nodes.body: Sarnhold sits at the foot of the spine like a fist on a table, and the thaw has turned its yard to a foot of grey slush. Two of the Compact's nine irons are in the captain's pack, wrapped in salt-cloth, and everybody in the district knows it. The Warden tower, the Reckoning coach and the Sable Guild's loading bay are all in sight of each other, and all three of them are watching the gate.

choices.label: Report to the Warden Commandant.
Answer the Reckoning legate's summons.
Hear out the Sable Guild at the guildhall.
Walk the thaw market first.
See to the company's own roster.
Go straight to the stables and the road out.
Ride out now, before anybody puts a hand on the pack.

nodes.body: The company is four hours west and downhill before Ilsabet says the word evidence out loud, and the arithmetic lands on all of them at once: a chartered company that has not reported is five people carrying stolen Warden property. They turn around in the dark and ride back up the way they came. The gate crew logs the hour of return, and that hour will be read out at every inquiry that follows.

choices.label: Turn back and sign in properly.

nodes.body: The provost's inspection is thorough because the provost has been told to be thorough. Three irons were expected in the pack and two are found, which the provost writes down twice. A queue of Guild carters waits behind the company for the whole performance, and the charter is read aloud in front of all of them.

choices.label: Declare the irons and let the provost seal them.
Declare the charter and nothing else.
Let Nyre answer as a sister of the Reckoning.
Walk past the provost on the charter's authority.

nodes.body: The irons are declared and sealed under a provost's wax and signed for in a book that the fortress keeps and the Guild reads. It is correct, complete and entirely irreversible. The fortress now knows exactly what the company carries, and so does everybody who was standing in the archway behind it.

choices.label: Go up to the Commandant.
Ask for the seals back before you go anywhere.

nodes.body: The charter is presented and nothing at all is volunteered beyond it. The provost reads it three times looking for a reason to be difficult and does not find one, which appears to disappoint him professionally rather than personally. The pack stays shut, and the queue moves on.

choices.label: Go up to the Commandant.

nodes.body: Nyre answers in the form her order uses, which the provost has to accept and clearly resents accepting. It gets the company through the gate in four minutes. It also puts the Reckoning's name on the company's arrival before the Wardens have theirs, which somebody in the coach yard notes down.

choices.label: Go up to the Commandant.

nodes.body: The pack is cut off a shoulder in the archway by somebody who knew exactly where the irons rode and did not have to look twice for them. Dellach has him against the wall in three steps and the pack back in four, which is fast enough to keep the irons and not nearly quiet enough. Every warden on the gate now knows what the Ninth Sword is carrying up the mountain.

choices.label: Take the pack straight to Thane.

nodes.body: The provost's seals are demanded back an hour after they were given, in front of eleven witnesses, which is a confession of second thoughts entered permanently into the record. The provost returns them without comment and writes the hour down. Nothing is suspended and nothing is forgiven, and the company climbs to the map room holding a charter that is now a favour rather than a right.

choices.label: Go up to the map room.

nodes.body: Iver Thane has been thirty years on the spine and has read Orr's letter twice. He does not believe the parts of it that are true, which he says out loud, and then asks the only question that matters to him: what does a company of five think it is going to do about a third door. He waits for an answer with his hands flat on the map.

choices.label: Tell him everything, in order, from Gallowmere.
Tell him what he needs to act on and no more.
Refuse to answer until the irons are receipted.

nodes.body: The whole account is given in order across a map table, from Gallowmere to Hollowmarch, and it takes two hours. Thane listens without interrupting once, which is unnerving. At the end he asks for the last part again, with the dates, and writes them into the margin of his own chart.

choices.label: Take his orders.

nodes.body: The account is given the way a soldier gives one: what is shut, what is loose, what is needed and how long there is. It takes eleven minutes. It is the only version Thane can act on before the thaw closes the lower road, and he starts acting on it before the company has left the room.

choices.label: Take his orders.

nodes.body: Thane decides, on reflection, that a company carrying two of the Compact's irons is evidence rather than a company. A fortress has a procedure for holding evidence. It takes Nyre two hours and a requisition citing her own order's interest to make that procedure inconvenient enough to abandon. Thane signs the orders instead, and signs them coldly, and the company rides out under a commander who has already tried once.

choices.label: Take the orders and go.

nodes.body: The orders are short and the charts beside them are not. Eleven lamp stations run up the Ninefold Road to the crown gate of Kar Ashen, and each one has an hour written against it in a hand that is not a Warden hand. A pencil line across the ninth station marks where Thane's last patrol turned back without a written reason.

choices.label: Read the charts with Vurma before you accept anything.
Take the orders as written and go.
Ask for a Warden column to come with you.

nodes.body: An hour with the charts and a dwarf pathfinder turns eleven stations into eleven questions, and Vurma gets nine of them answered by a man who has walked the road twice. The other two she marks with a circle and says she will answer on the ground. Thane watches the whole exchange and says nothing.

choices.label: Draw kit from the armoury.

nodes.body: The Warden column is requested, refused, and minuted. Thane has four hundred men for two hundred miles of spine and a written reason for the placement of every one of them, and he reads two of the reasons out. The company stands in a map room being thanked for its service, which is what a refusal sounds like when it is delivered properly.

choices.label: Go and draw what you can carry.

nodes.body: The quartermaster has been told to be generous and is not enjoying it. Crampons, spine rope, pitch, forty dwarf candles, a moor-iron pick and a warded haft come out onto the counter, and the haft has a Warden's initials filed off the ferrule. He does not explain the haft, and he books it out looking at the wall.

choices.label: Draw the climbing kit and the rope.
Draw the warded haft and the pick.
Draw nothing; the company is loaded already.
Draw everything and let him argue about it later.

nodes.body: Spine rope, crampons and forty candles, signed for in triplicate by a man who counts them twice. It is the least interesting transaction in Sarnhold. It is also the difference between the ice gallery being a route and being a paragraph in somebody's report next spring.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: A moor-iron pick and a warded haft come off the back rack, both cold in the hand in the way that ordinary iron is not. The quartermaster books them out without meeting anybody's eye. Ilsabet turns the haft over twice and says that whoever warded it knew exactly what it would be used against.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: Everything is drawn and nothing is signed for, on the reasonable grounds that there is no time, and the quartermaster swears his complaint before the provost within the hour. The charter survives the accusation. It does not survive it cleanly, and every piece of kit the company carries up the road is kit that is already the subject of a charge.

choices.label: Start the climb.

nodes.body: Prior Absolon Rell has come up from the mother house with a coach, four novices and a writ already drawn. He wants the two irons placed in the Reckoning's custody today, for safekeeping, and he has a receipt prepared with the company's names already entered on it in a clerk's hand. He is polite, and he is not in any hurry at all.

choices.label: Hear the writ out in full.
Tell him the irons are Warden property and watch his face.
Take the writ away to read it properly, and do not come back.

nodes.body: The writ is read out in full in a cold chapel with the company standing. Custody, safekeeping, indemnity, and then a clause about the count that Nyre stops him in the middle of, because she has read it twice already and can quote the rest of it from memory. Rell lets her finish, and then continues from where she stopped.

choices.label: Go through to the chapel.

nodes.body: The refusal is given plainly to a mother-house legate in front of four novices: the irons are Warden property and will be handed to a Warden. It costs the company its welcome in the chapter house before supper. By evening it has bought the company something with Thane that no amount of paperwork would have.

choices.label: Go through to the chapel.

nodes.body: Two irons go into a coach with the Reckoning's seal on the door, properly signed for, receipted in a hand that has plainly done this before. It takes Nyre until dusk and a point of custody law her own order taught her to get them out again, and the legate yields with a smile that says the matter is only postponed. The company keeps the irons and loses any illusion that the Reckoning is a neutral party.

choices.label: Go with Nyre to the chapel.

nodes.body: Sarnhold's chapel has a tally on its east wall in groups of nine that nobody in the fortress can account for. The chaplain has been counting them for six years as a devotional exercise and has never once asked what the count is of. He offers to show the company the wall the way a man offers to show visitors a garden.

choices.label: Read the east wall properly.
Leave it; you know what it says.
Ask the chaplain what he has been counting.

nodes.body: The east wall reads as nine hundred years of groups, cut by many hands, in the same system the company has now seen at Kar Duhn, Sixteen Mile and every gibbet post in between. The last group has eight strokes cut and a ninth begun. The mortar dust of the ninth stroke is still on the flagstones underneath it.

choices.label: Go and look at the reliquary.

nodes.body: The chaplain answers the question he has spent six years not asking, in front of his own congregation, and then he rings the bell. It empties the chapel in ninety seconds and fills the provost's office instead. The company spends the evening explaining a charter rather than reading a wall, and comes back to the wall at midnight with nobody watching.

choices.label: Come back to the relic wall later.

nodes.body: The chapel reliquary holds three tally-irons on velvet under glass, labelled as relics of the founding and dated to the legion. There is a fourth setting with its label already in place and nothing on the velvet. The label has a date on it, and the date is this spring.

choices.label: Take a tally-iron off the velvet.
Read the labels and take nothing.
Leave the reliquary alone entirely.
Break the glass; the fourth setting explains itself.

nodes.body: One tally-iron comes off the velvet, and it is cold as well-water and heavier than any relic has business being. The reliquary now has two empty settings in a row, which somebody will notice at the evening office. Ilsabet puts the iron in her own pack and starts, quietly, sorting the company's irons by gauge.

choices.label: Go on to the novices' dormitory.

nodes.body: Four labels read in a chaplain's careful hand; three name founding wardens with dates nine hundred years back. The fourth names nobody at all: it has an office, a term of nine years, and a date this spring, and the copperplate is fresh enough that the burr is still on the letters.

choices.label: Go on to the novices' dormitory.

nodes.body: The glass is broken in a Warden chapel to settle a question about a label, and the answer arrives from the direction of the empty setting rather than from the glass. It uses the captain's own name and the correct rank, once, and then stops. Nobody in the company sleeps properly again on this side of the spine, and the fourth setting is no longer empty when they look back from the door.

choices.label: Get out of the chapel.

nodes.body: Rell's four juniors sleep in a dormitory off the chapter house, and somebody has set out a jug of hot wine for the company's arrival, and four cups are poured; a fifth stands beside the jug, dry, with its own napkin. Two of the novices will not look at the tray at all.

choices.label: Refuse the wine and say why.
Drink it and watch which of them drinks too.
Take the jug and pour it out the window.

nodes.body: The wine is refused, out loud, with the reason given, and four novices look relieved rather than insulted. One of them follows the company into the corridor to say four words about the fifth cup, and then goes back inside before anybody can ask him a fifth. Nyre writes the four words down.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: The wine is drunk, and it is good wine; the night that follows is eleven hours of sleep nobody chose to take. In the morning the kit has been gone through with real care, and the provost's seals on the pack have been broken and re-set by somebody with the patience to match the wax.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: The jug goes out of a dormitory window in front of four novices of the mother house, which is satisfying for about nine seconds. Rell's complaint reaches the provost before the wine reaches the yard below, and the provost, who has read the charter, files it without comment. The company goes up the road with the Reckoning's mother house now holding a grievance in writing.

choices.label: Get on the road.

nodes.body: Bruk Sunder has a contract drawn before the company sits down. The Sable Guild will underwrite the whole expedition: kit, hands, provisions, a train as far as the fourth station. In exchange it wants the charts, the hours, and first claim on the crown road afterwards, and it has already had the clauses witnessed.

choices.label: Hear the offer out and let him finish.
Tell him the road is not the company's to sell.
Sign the underwriting and take the Guild's money.

nodes.body: The offer is heard out in full, which takes a quarter of an hour and includes three concessions Sunder did not have to make. That is the interesting part. A Guild factor who gives away three points unprompted is a factor who already knows what is up that road and has costed it.

choices.label: Go through to the chart room.

nodes.body: The refusal is given across a guildhall table: the road is not the company's to sell. Sunder takes it well, thanks the captain for the clarity, and has his clerk minute the exchange. Taking it well is worse than taking it badly, because it means he has a second plan and has had it for some time.

choices.label: Go through to the chart room.

nodes.body: The underwriting is signed and the Guild's money lands the same afternoon, which solves every practical problem the company has and creates one whose edges nobody can see. Nyre reads the third clause twice on the stairs and stops walking. The charter's authority, from this morning on, belongs to whoever holds the paper, and the company has just handed the paper over for a season's wages.

choices.label: Go and copy the charts before the Guild does.

nodes.body: The Guild chart room holds three surveys of the crown road that the Wardens do not have; two are old. The third is dated this spring and initialled by a surveyor whose name is on the Guild's own missing list, and it shows the crown gate closed and two ways into the outer ward that no Warden chart records.

choices.label: Copy the spring survey while Sunder is out.
Leave the charts; they are not yours yet.
Take the whole spring survey off the wall.

nodes.body: An hour of copying in Ilsabet's shorthand with Vurma reading elevations aloud beside her. The spring survey comes away as nine pages of the company's own. It shows a foundry chimney and a cistern channel, both of them entering the ward under its wall, and a note about the ninth hour in the surveyor's hand.

choices.label: Go down to the forge.

nodes.body: The spring survey comes off the guildhall wall entire, leaving a rectangle of clean plaster that is noticed inside the hour. The Guild's grievance reaches the provost's desk before supper and the charts are impounded as disputed property. Ilsabet has already copied the two sheets that matter onto the back of a kit list, which is the only reason the theft was worth anything at all.

choices.label: Take the copies to the forge.

nodes.body: The Guild forge is still hot at the ninth hour and the smith will cut anything for coin. She does not ask why a surface company wants a blank in the founding gauge, or what the two wrapped objects in the pack are, or why one of them is being measured against her own gauge plates while she works.

choices.label: Have a blank cut to the founding gauge.
Have the pick re-tempered and the haft rewarded.
Buy nothing here; the Guild sells twice.
Have the two irons copied while you wait.

nodes.body: A blank cut to the founding gauge, filed true and wrapped in salt-cloth, for eleven crowns. Ilsabet stows it herself. It is either the most useful object in the company's baggage or the single most damning thing in it, and which of those it turns out to be depends entirely on what happens at the crown door.

choices.label: Go through to the delvers' yard.

nodes.body: The pick is re-tempered and the warded haft is rewarded properly for the first time since Gallowmere, which costs a day's fee and most of an evening. The company gets both back better than they went in. In the first ice gallery above the fourth station, that evening pays for itself twice.

choices.label: Go through to the delvers' yard.

nodes.body: Two of the Compact's irons are handed to a Guild smith to be copied, and copies are made, and the originals are handed back. Nobody in the company can say afterwards, with any certainty, which pair went into the pack. Ilsabet settles it at the second station with a gauge and four hours of quiet work, and the answer is that they were lucky, and that luck is not a method.

choices.label: Go and find out what the delvers know.

nodes.body: The delvers' yard has four Sable Guild hands in it with opinions about surface companies holding dwarf irons. They are not keeping the opinions to themselves. Two of them recognise Vurma Kell as the pathfinder whose report their own foreman burned last spring, and the recognition does not improve anybody's temper.

choices.label: Let Dellach settle it in the yard.
Buy the yard a cask and let Vurma talk.
Put the Guild's own oath to them, in dwarf.
Draw steel in a Guild yard.

nodes.body: Four exchanges, a broken trestle, and a delver sitting down hard in the slush with his opinion substantially revised. The yard foreman calls it fair in front of everybody, because the alternative is the provost. Dellach's hand is split again, and Nyre binds it without comment, which is her way of commenting.

choices.label: Take the road.
Press it further while you are winning.

nodes.body: A cask is bought and Vurma is given the floor for eleven minutes, which is all she needs; by the end of it the yard knows exactly what its own foreman burned last spring and why. Two of the four will not look at him again, and one of them says so out loud in front of the others.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: The Guild's founding oath is recited back to the yard in dwarf by a hedge-thaumaturge with a southern accent, correctly, including the clause about surveys. The yard stops dead. Ten minutes later the company has a guide it did not ask for and did not pay for, standing at the gate with her own kit.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: Steel drawn in a Guild yard inside a Warden fortress engages two jurisdictions at once, and both of them respond inside the hour. The charter survives on the strength of who drew second and eleven witnesses who agree about it. The Guild's complaint and the provost's charge sheet reach Thane's desk together, and the company is on the road before either of them is answered.

choices.label: Leave before the paperwork lands.

nodes.body: A yard fight pressed past the point where it was already won turns four delvers into a Guild grievance, and the grievance into a knife that goes in under a rib in a slush-filled yard nobody was watching. It takes about four seconds. The captain of the Ninth Sword starts up the Ninefold Road nine days later with the stitches still in and a hand that will not close properly in the cold.

choices.label: Start the climb anyway.

nodes.body: The thaw market is mud to the ankle and the whole spine is selling what it has: rope, salt beef, dwarf candles, crampons, a stall of tally-irons labelled as scrap. A boy is selling lamp oil by the ninth rather than by the pint. That is not a measure anybody uses on the frontier, and nobody at the market finds it odd.

choices.label: Buy the stall's tally-irons as scrap.
Buy salt, oil and beef for a month.
Buy nothing and walk on to the taproom.
Ask the boy who taught him to sell by the ninth.

nodes.body: Nine tally-irons bought as scrap at the price of scrap, four of them founding gauge; Ilsabet spreads them on a bunkroom bed that night and sorts them into two piles without explaining either pile. In the morning one pile is in her pack and the other is back at the stall, sold on.

choices.label: Go on to the taproom.

nodes.body: A month of salt, oil and beef, loaded on the barrow and lashed down. It is the least interesting purchase anybody makes in Sarnhold and the one that decides how the ice gallery goes. Halt and Weem take the handles in turns and complain in alternation the whole way up the first switchback.

choices.label: Go on to the taproom.

nodes.body: The boy answers honestly, because he is nine and has no reason not to, and names the clerk who taught him the measure. The two men who have been standing behind his stall all morning decide the answer is worth following up. Kettle spends the afternoon making sure they follow up the wrong five people, which works, and costs him a tooth and the use of a hand for a week.

choices.label: Get off the market before dark.

nodes.body: The Hooked Lamp is full of Guild carters and off-duty Wardens, and one table of Rooks in charter colours. The story of Kar Duhn is being told at the bar by three people who were not there, badly, with the names wrong. It is the fourth time this month, and it has improved with each telling in every way except accuracy.

choices.label: Correct the story, quietly, with names.
Buy the room a round and let the story run.
Take the argument outside with whoever is telling it.

nodes.body: The story is corrected with names, dates and the actual sequence, by somebody who was standing in the room when it happened. The bar does not enjoy it. The correction reaches Thane's clerk before the company reaches the door, and it reaches Corrow's people at their own table in about nine seconds.

choices.label: Go over to the Rooks' table.

nodes.body: A round is bought and the bad version is left standing, which costs four crowns and buys the room's goodwill. It is the first entirely sensible thing anybody in the company has done in Sarnhold. The version being told gets worse over the evening and nobody in the Ninth Sword corrects a word of it.

choices.label: Go over to the Rooks' table.

nodes.body: The company wakes in the provost's cells with the pack inventoried in somebody else's handwriting and two entries on the list that nobody in the company recognises. The irons are all still there, counted and countersigned, which is considerably worse than missing. Getting out takes the charter, an apology and most of the morning, and half the yard is waiting to watch them do it.

choices.label: Out to the yard.

nodes.body: The Rooks lieutenant was at Hollowmarch and lost four people there, and he wants the company to explain, out loud, in front of the room, whose orders those four died under; it is a fair question asked in an unfair place. The room goes quiet enough to hear the fire, and Dellach puts his cup down flat.

choices.label: Let him have it out with fists in the yard.
Answer the question honestly, in front of the room.
Buy the four dead a round and name them.
Tell him to take it to his captain.

nodes.body: A yard fight against a man with a real grievance, which is the worst kind to win. The company wins it on points and loses it in every other respect, and the lieutenant goes down twice and gets up twice. Nyre binds two sets of knuckles afterwards and says nothing at all about either of them.

choices.label: Take the bunkroom.
Keep going until he stops getting up.

nodes.body: The question is answered honestly in front of a full room: whose orders, what those orders were, what the company learned, and what it did with what it learned. It takes four minutes. The lieutenant listens to all of it, says one sentence at the end of it, and goes back to his own table.

choices.label: Take the bunkroom.

nodes.body: Four dead are named aloud with a round bought for each, in the old free-company form that predates the Rooks and the Wardens both. The lieutenant accepts it because there is no version of him that could refuse it. Both companies drink standing, and afterwards nobody in the room raises Hollowmarch again.

choices.label: Take the bunkroom.

nodes.body: The grievance is sent up to Corrow rather than settled in the room, which is procedurally correct and a good deal slower than the weather. Corrow's written complaint arrives two days later and is filed, and the inquiry it asks for is scheduled for after the passes close. The company keeps its charter and starts the climb knowing a chartered rival now holds a paper trail with their names in it.

choices.label: Turn in for the night.

nodes.body: The yard fight is continued past the point of decision, in slush, in front of Wardens, and the Rooks lieutenant is slow getting up the third time. The provost arrives before there is a fourth. What the company keeps is its charter, and what it acquires is a reputation on the spine for not knowing when a thing is finished, which travels up the road considerably faster than the company does.

choices.label: Get to the bunkroom.

nodes.body: The fortress bunkroom is warm from the kitchen flue, the door bars from inside, and the pack goes under the captain's head; there is a whole night available for the first time since the Deep Road. Outside, the spine stands over Sarnhold with the Ninefold Road on it as a thread of lamps going up into cloud.

choices.label: Take the full night and let the watch go.
Sleep in shifts anyway; the pack is the pack.

nodes.body: One whole night on a straw mattress in a warm stone room with the door barred and no watch kept, which everybody in the company has learned the value of the hard way; nobody dreams about counting. In the morning five people pick up their kit like people who intend to come back for the rest of it.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: The company is two hands short since Hollowmarch and there are forty applicants in the yard, because Sarnhold is a fortress town in a thaw and work is work. At the front of them is Ossa Vend's cousin Mira with her own lighting pole, and behind her a Warden veteran called Hask who has been up the road twice.

choices.label: Take Ossa's cousin and one Warden veteran.
Take nobody; five who know is better than seven who do not.
Hire fast; take the first six who can carry.

nodes.body: Mira Vend is hired at a half share with her own pole, and Hask at a full one because he has been up the Ninefold Road twice and does not pretend to have enjoyed either trip. Both of them ask about the hours before they ask about the money, which is the only qualification that matters.

choices.label: See to the kit.

nodes.body: Forty applicants are refused in one sentence each, which takes an hour and is the correct decision. Five people who have survived two doors together do not need two strangers learning the count on the ice stair. The company goes up the spine at exactly the strength that came down off Hollowmarch.

choices.label: See to the kit.

nodes.body: The hiring yard is worked through at the end of a long day, and one of the forty turns out to be a Reckoning novice under instruction with a writ folded into his boot. Kettle finds it that night rather than above the ice gallery nine days later, which is the difference between a problem and a burial. The novice comes off the roster and goes straight back to Rell with everything he has already seen.

choices.label: Draw kit and go.

nodes.body: The company's kit is spread on a fortress floor for the first honest inventory since Gallowmere. Two irons in salt-cloth, three books, a bag of tally-die fragments, and rope that has been up two mountains too many. Written out on a slate, it is a strange list for a chartered company and a very clear one for an inquiry.

choices.label: Replace the rope and the reservoirs.
Split the irons between two packs.
Load out as you are; there is no time.
Leave one iron with the fortress strongbox.

nodes.body: New spine rope, two clean reservoirs and a spare wick roll, for eleven crowns. It is a boring purchase. In the crevasse above the ice stair it is the difference between a crossing and a paragraph, which is a sentence Vurma says out loud while she coils the new rope and which nobody argues with.

choices.label: Take the night watch.

nodes.body: The two irons are split between two packs on Ilsabet's insistence, which halves what a single theft can take and doubles the number of people who can be robbed. She argues for it anyway, on the grounds that the second risk is a fight and the first is simply an ending, and the company agrees with her.

choices.label: Take the night watch.

nodes.body: One iron is left in the fortress strongbox for safekeeping, receipted properly, with two Wardens on the door. On the ninth night the strongbox is opened by two Wardens whose cloaks do not fit them, and Kettle, who has not trusted a strongbox since Kar Duhn, is asleep across the passage. He gets the iron back and one of the cloaks, and the man wearing it goes over the wall rather than answer for it.

choices.label: Get some sleep while you can.

nodes.body: The last night in Sarnhold, and the spine stands over the fortress in moonlight with the Ninefold Road visible on it as a thread of lamps going up into cloud; you can count nine of them from the wall. The ninth is the highest, and it is lit two hours before any chart in the fortress says it should be.

choices.label: Sleep. The road can have you in the morning.
Sit up with the charts and the company.

nodes.body: A full night's sleep taken deliberately by five people who have learned what not taking one costs. Nobody sits up with the charts. In the morning everybody's hands work, which sounds like nothing and is the difference between the ice stair and the bottom of it.

choices.label: Hold the company council.

nodes.body: The company council is held in a fortress stable because it is the only room nobody else wants. The question is how the Ninth Sword goes up a road with eleven counted stations on it and a closed gate at the top, and every option on the table is bad in a different direction.

choices.label: Go up openly, on the charter, station by station.
Go up as Guild carters with the train.
Go up by the smugglers' adit and skip the stations.
Go up split, in two parties, one day apart.

nodes.body: The decision is to go up openly on the charter, station by station, signing the book at each one. It is slow, it is legal, and it gives the road nine days' notice of the company's arrival. Dellach argues for it on the grounds that the alternative is arriving somewhere as smugglers, and he is not wrong.

choices.label: Take the road.
Send word ahead to the stations that you are coming.

nodes.body: The decision is to go up inside the Guild train as carters, which puts forty witnesses around the company and forty pairs of hands within reach of the packs. Kettle argues for it and does not pretend to like the second half of it. Ilsabet's only condition is that the irons travel on her back and not on a wagon.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: The decision is to split the company one day apart, which is what Thane would advise and what nobody in the room likes. It halves what a single ambush takes and it means somebody walks the ice gallery without Ossa. The argument about which half goes first runs for a quarter of an hour and settles nothing.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: The council runs until the Guild train has gone, the weather has turned, and the crown door's nine days have quietly become six. Nobody makes a bad decision and nobody makes any decision at all, which is worse. They start the climb three days later than the road wanted them to, and every station above will be that much colder for it.

choices.label: Get on the road.

nodes.body: Word is sent ahead to eleven counted stations that a chartered company is coming up on the charter, station by station, which is courteous and entirely correct. It is read at the fourth station by exactly the wrong clerk. By the time the company reaches the third station everything above it has had four days' notice, and the fourth station's book has a page torn out of it.

choices.label: Start the climb.

nodes.body: There are no horses for the spine above the fourth station and the stables know it. What is available is one hand-barrow with a broken shaft, two mules on hire, and a place on the Guild train loading in the next yard. The Guild's fourth wagon is loaded with sealed crates and the wagon-master will not discuss its manifest.

choices.label: Take the barrow and mend the shaft yourself.
Buy two mules as far as the fourth station.
Carry everything and take no wheels at all.
Take a place on the Guild train.

nodes.body: The barrow shaft is mended with a spliced ash haft and wire in an hour, and Vurma pronounces the repair better than the original in the tone she uses for things she intends to be asked about later. It carries four hundred pounds up nine switchbacks without complaint, which is more than the porters manage.

choices.label: Go and look at the wagons.

nodes.body: Two mules hired as far as the fourth station, with a boy to bring them back down. It buys the company four days of not carrying and costs it four days of not being quiet, because a mule on dwarf paving can be heard from a station away and both of these have opinions.

choices.label: Go and look at the wagons.

nodes.body: At the second station the fourth wagon's load shifts and one crate's seal splits, and the company sees what it has been helping to haul up a mountain. The wagon-master's account of the discovery, given later, does not mention the company at all. They come off the train at the third station on their own feet, a day behind where they would have been, knowing exactly one thing more than they did.

choices.label: Get off the train and walk.

nodes.body: The Guild train is loading for the crown road: eleven wagons, forty hands, and a wagon-master who cannot account for the fourth wagon's manifest and has stopped pretending to try. He is not lying. He simply has a bill of lading that lists weights against nine entries and no description against any of them.

choices.label: Read the manifest properly with Nyre.
Break the fourth wagon's seal and look.
Leave the Guild's business to the Guild.

nodes.body: The manifest is read line by line by a Reckoning sister who has spent two books learning what to look for. Nine entries in a hand she has now seen in three fortresses. One entry with no weight recorded against it at all, which in a Guild manifest is not an omission but a category.

choices.label: Go and find the scouts.

nodes.body: The fourth wagon's seal is broken in a loading yard in front of forty Guild hands, which costs a fight, a fine and the Guild's cooperation for the whole spine. Inside are nine crates of founding-gauge blanks packed in chaff. The fine is eleven crowns and the company pays it in the yard, in coin, without arguing.

choices.label: Go and find the scouts.

nodes.body: Guild business is left to the Guild, and the fourth wagon goes up the Ninefold Road a full day ahead of the company. Everything that happens at the fourth station afterwards happens because of what was inside it, and the company reads the first part of it in a station book. They will walk into the rest in four days, having chosen not to know.

choices.label: Find the scouts who came down.

nodes.body: Thane's three road scouts are in the map room because there is nowhere else in Sarnhold they are allowed to be; between them they have walked to the ninth station and back this year. None of them will go past it for any money the Wardens have, and all three of them say so in the same words.

choices.label: Ask them what is at the ninth station.
Ask them for the way in that is not the gate.
Press the one who has been past the ninth station.

nodes.body: The ninth station described by three people who have stood in it: lamps lit two hours early, a count that runs backwards, and a station book signed every single day since autumn in the same hand; none of them saw who signs it. All three of them looked, which is why none of them will go back.

choices.label: Go and write your letters.

nodes.body: The way in that is not the gate, given reluctantly and drawn on a slate: the foundry chimney at the outer wall, ninety feet, staples at the bends, coming out in the ward's slag yard. The oldest scout adds a warning about the ninth hour and then rubs the slate clean with his sleeve before anybody can copy it twice.

choices.label: Go and write your letters.

nodes.body: The scout gives up the route he has already refused twice, in front of his own officer, because he is pressed until refusing costs him more than telling. The company gets the route it came for. It also gets a Warden complaint that reaches the provost by evening, because a man broken in front of his officer will always find a way to be heard.

choices.label: Say your goodbyes and go.

nodes.body: The last hour before the road goes on the free-company custom that has never once been optional: letters written and left with a fortress clerk against the company's return. There is a book for it. It has four hundred letters in it, and eleven of them have been collected by the people who wrote them.

choices.label: Write the letters and hand them in.
Do not write them. You are coming back.
Write one, and read it aloud to the company.

nodes.body: Five letters written in a fortress hall and handed to a clerk, sealed, dated and entered in the book. Nobody reads anybody else's. Dellach's takes the longest, Kettle's takes four lines, and Ilsabet writes two and hands over both, which nobody comments on and everybody notices.

choices.label: Take the road.

nodes.body: One letter is written and read aloud to the company in a fortress hall, which is not the custom and cannot be undone. It is well written, which makes it a good deal worse. Five people go up the Ninefold Road the following morning already grieving themselves, and the third station is where that begins to show in how they walk.

choices.label: Start the climb.

nodes.body: First light at the foot of the Ninefold Road, and the spine stands over Sarnhold in cloud with eleven counted stations above and a crown gate at the top of them; the road itself is dwarf paving nine feet wide, in good order, swept. Three ways go up from this first switchback, and the company has to pick one now.

choices.label: Take the road proper, station by station.
Take the ice stair up the shoulder and rejoin above.
Take the smugglers' adit under the first four stations.

nodes.body: The first counted station above Sarnhold is a lamp bracket, a bench, and a signing book on a chain, and the book has been signed every day this winter. Six ways go up the spine from here and all six of them reach the crown gate. The scouts' opinion, given in the map room, was that none of them is safe and two of them are worse than the others.

choices.label: Take the switchbacks on the road proper.
Take the ice stair up the shoulder.
Go by the counted villages on the shelf road.
Take the smugglers' adit into the rock.
Cross by the old span and the watchtower.
Go up ahead of the weather coming off the summit.
Sign the book, turn round, and go back down.

nodes.body: The book is signed and the road refused in the same movement, which is at least honest arithmetic, and the company gets four miles back down before it turns round again. What turns it is Nyre, and one sentence about what the count is actually for. They come back to the foot of the ice stair having lost half a day and any right to call the decision brave.

choices.label: Go back and take the ice stair.

nodes.body: Nine switchbacks of dwarf paving climb out of the treeline in thaw meltwater running an inch deep over the stone. The drop grows behind each turn until the fortress is a grey mark below. A Guild train's ruts are a day old in the slush, and they cut every corner the company is looking at.

choices.label: Keep to the paving and take the turns wide.
Cut the corners on the scree between turns.
Rope the company for the exposed sections.
Run the switchbacks before the meltwater freezes.

nodes.body: Corner-cutting on wet scree saves the best part of an hour and puts everybody's ankles on notice for the rest of the climb. Hask remarks that he has done exactly this on both his previous trips and paid for it both times. He does it again anyway, which tells the company something about Hask.

choices.label: Go on to the scree field.
Cut the last corner too, over the drop.

nodes.body: The paving is taken properly, turn by wide turn, in meltwater that has opinions about boot leather and none at all about the company's schedule. It costs an hour. Nobody turns an ankle, nobody goes down, and the barrow arrives at the scree field upright with its load still lashed.

choices.label: Go on to the scree field.

nodes.body: The company is roped through four exposed turns on Vurma's insistence, which costs a half hour and makes everybody feel faintly ridiculous. On the third turn Mira's feet go out from under her on glazed stone. She goes down eleven inches instead of two hundred feet, and after that nobody mentions the rope again.

choices.label: Go on to the scree field.

nodes.body: The switchbacks are run in the last of the light with meltwater going to glass behind every boot, and the fourth turn refuses that pace exactly as it has refused it since the legion cut the road. Ilsabet goes over the edge to the length of the rope and is hauled back up in the dark by four people who cannot see her. Her pack is somewhere below and nobody goes down for it.

choices.label: Go on across the scree.

nodes.body: The last corner is cut over the drop because the first four worked, which is exactly how this road takes people, and the scree there is scree over ice over nothing at all. Kettle goes with it as far as the ledge below and stops there, alone, without making any sound the others could have used to find him. It takes forty minutes to get him up and he is not right for the rest of the day.

choices.label: Cross the scree field.

nodes.body: A live scree field crosses the road for two hundred yards, moving quietly on its own account in the thaw. The Guild train's wheel-track runs into the middle of it and does not come out the other side, which is the single most informative thing anybody has seen since the treeline.

choices.label: Cross one at a time, slowly, in the wheel-track.
Cross together and fast while it is quiet.
Go under the field by the drainage culvert.

nodes.body: Five separate crossings at a walking pace, one person at a time, with the field talking under everybody's boots the whole way. It takes ninety minutes. It gets five people and one barrow across a moving slope that swallowed a Guild wagon, which is the entire argument for doing it slowly.

choices.label: Go on to the cairn.

nodes.body: The field is crossed at a run, all five together while it is quiet, and it stays quiet for the whole two hundred yards. It costs the company its wind and one reservoir lamp, which goes down the slope in eleven bounces and is still audible after it is out of sight.

choices.label: Go on to the cairn.

nodes.body: The culvert under the scree field is four feet high, half full of meltwater, and entirely full of the reason the Guild train's wheel-track stops in the middle of the field above it. The company is nine feet inside before anybody's lamp reaches the far end. Getting out backwards through four feet of headroom is what the next eleven minutes are, and everybody's hands are cut raw by the end of them.

choices.label: Get out and go up to the cairn.

nodes.body: A cairn stands at the third station's turning, built not of loose stone but of station-book pages weighted under one flat slab; the top page has nine names on it in a clerk's hand and a tenth begun. It has been rained on and it has not been moved, and the mortar of the slab is fresh.

choices.label: Read the pages under the stone.
Leave the cairn as you found it.
Take the cairn apart properly.

nodes.body: Nine names read off station-book pages in a wind that wants them, and all nine are Wardens; all nine signed in at the fourth station this winter, in the correct form, with times. None of them signed out at the fourth station or anywhere else on the road, and the tenth name is only half written.

choices.label: Go on up into the wind.

nodes.body: The cairn is taken apart properly to see what it was built over, which takes twenty minutes of careful work. Under the slab is a station book with four hundred pages in it, and under the book is a hand, and the hand is still holding the pen it was signing with when the slab went on. The book comes with them, and nobody rebuilds the cairn, and nobody can say afterwards why not.

choices.label: Go on into the wind gap.

nodes.body: The wind gap above the third station is eighty feet of dwarf cutting through which the spine funnels an entire valley's air, and has done since the founding. It arrives in cycles rather than gusts. Ossa has crossed it eleven times and starts counting the cycle out loud before anybody asks her to.

choices.label: Wait out the gust cycle and cross in the lull.
Crawl it, roped, under the worst of it.
Send the barrow through first on a line.
Walk it upright; it is only wind.

nodes.body: The lull is counted out by somebody who has crossed this gap eleven times, and then used. Ninety seconds, she says, and it is ninety seconds, and the whole company is through with eleven to spare. On the far side she goes back to counting under her breath and does not stop for a mile.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.
Go back for the barrow in the next lull.

nodes.body: Eighty feet of crawling on a roped line with the wind taking the breath sideways out of everybody's mouths. It works. Nobody discusses it afterwards, and Dellach in particular does not discuss it, having spent the last twenty feet of it on his stomach with his shield over his head.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: The barrow goes through first on a line and arrives on the far side upside down and one cask lighter, which is a better outcome than any of the alternatives available. The cask is somewhere below the gap. Halt watches it go and says a sentence that Nyre declines to write in her book.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: The gap is walked upright by people who have been on a spine road for a day and a half and believe they understand it; the gust arrives at the sixtieth foot. The dwarves cut this gap to survive that gust and cut it for nothing else at all, which is a distinction the company works out too late.

A return trip into the gap for the barrow, in what looks like the next lull and is not, and what it is is the pause the cycle makes before its worst, which Ossa knows and does not have time to say. Her count reaches four before the noise takes the rest of the sentence off the ridge.

The ice stair is four hundred dwarf steps up the shoulder, glazed a finger thick, with an iron handline that stops at the halfway post for reasons nobody has recorded. Outside the handline there is two thousand feet of nothing. The steps are cut deep and the glaze has filled every one of them level.

choices.label: Cut steps in the glaze the whole way up.
Use the handline as far as it goes and trust the crampons.
Go up the rock beside the stair instead.

nodes.body: Two hours of step-cutting with a pick, one person working and four standing in the cold waiting to move up, and it is the slow way. It is also the way people come back from, which Vurma says once at the bottom and does not need to say again anywhere on the stair.

choices.label: Go on to the glass gallery.

nodes.body: The handline to the halfway post and crampons above it, which is fast and puts the whole company's weight in turn on eleven inches of dwarf ironwork that the mountain has been working at for nine hundred years. It holds. Everybody looks at the fixing bolt on the way past, and nobody says anything about it.

choices.label: Go on to the glass gallery.

nodes.body: The rock beside the stair is sound rock with good holds, and it carries a nine-hundred-year glaze of black ice on every one of them, indistinguishable from wet stone until a gloved hand is already committed. The second hold is where the company finds that out, and Dellach takes the weight of two people on one arm for as long as it takes. He will not use that arm properly again for a month.

choices.label: Get onto the glass gallery.

nodes.body: The glass gallery runs the road inside the mountain for a mile, and the wall on the right is ice rather than rock: clear ice, nine inches of it, with lamp niches burning steadily on the far side. The niches are dwarf-cut and the lamps in them are lit, and there is no way in to any of them from this side.

choices.label: Walk the gallery straight through, lamps down.
Chip through to a niche and see what feeds it.
Wait at the mouth for the ninth hour to pass.
Break the wall ice and take the shortcut.

nodes.body: A niche is chipped open through nine inches of clear ice, which takes twenty minutes and produces a lamp with clean oil and a trimmed wick behind it. There is no passage behind the niche and no soot on its roof. Nothing at all in the gallery explains how either the oil or the trimming got there this winter.

choices.label: Go on to the crevasse.
Take the lamp out of the niche.

nodes.body: A mile of gallery walked with the company's own lamps hooded, past nine niches burning behind nine inches of ice. Nobody speaks after the fourth one. At the far end Ossa says that her father counted eleven niches on this stretch and that she has counted nine every time she has walked it since.

choices.label: Go on to the crevasse.

nodes.body: An hour at the gallery mouth waiting out the ninth hour, and the file passes inside: nine lamps, unhurried, in step, and a count that does not go up. From outside, through nine inches of ice, it is a procession of lights and a rhythm. The company watches the whole thing without one person suggesting they go in.

choices.label: Go on to the crevasse.

nodes.body: The wall ice is broken for a shortcut through a mile of gallery, and those nine inches have been holding the mountain's meltwater off this road since the founding. It stops holding it in the fourth minute. The company is halfway through the breach when the gallery begins filling behind them, and they come out at the crevasse soaked to the skin at four thousand feet with the light already going.

choices.label: Get to the crevasse.

nodes.body: A lamp is taken out of a niche behind nine inches of ice, because it is a lamp and the company needs lamps, and the nine niches of the gallery go dark in order behind them. The count that starts in the dark afterwards is not on the far side of the ice, and it is closer than the far wall. They run the last two hundred yards, and the lamp is still in the pack, and nobody has suggested putting it back.

choices.label: Run for the crevasse.

nodes.body: The ice has pulled away from the rock across the whole shoulder, leaving a crevasse forty feet down to blue and no bottom that a lamp can find. There is a snow bridge at the narrow end and a Guild ladder frozen into the ice at the wide one, with its lashings still on it.

choices.label: Cross on the Guild's frozen ladder.
Cross the snow bridge roped and one at a time.
Jump the narrow end; it is four feet.

nodes.body: The Guild's ladder is chopped free and laid across, and it holds five people and a barrow, which it does not deserve to do. Vurma refuses to look at it while anybody is on it and refuses to explain why until the last person is over, at which point she explains at some length.

choices.label: Go on to the ice lamps.

nodes.body: The snow bridge is crossed roped, one at a time, on hands and knees. The fourth person over puts a leg through it and is pulled out by the harness in eleven seconds, which is nine seconds faster than the drill and about as fast as anybody has ever done it.

choices.label: Go on to the ice lamps.

nodes.body: Four feet is jumped at the crevasse's narrow end by somebody who has been walking uphill in crampons for six hours, which is the problem. The landing lip is snow over nothing, and it has been waiting all winter for exactly that piece of reasoning to arrive and put its full weight on it.

The ice-lamp station above the crevasse has nine brackets cut into the ice wall itself, all nine burning, and a station book on a chain under a slate roof; the book is dry. The last four weeks of it have been signed by the same hand every single day, at the same time, to the minute.

choices.label: Read the last four weeks of the book.
Sign the book and go on.
Take the book off the chain and carry it.

nodes.body: Four weeks of station book read in a wind that wants the pages, holding them down with both gloves, and the same hand every day; the same time to the minute. And the hours for each day written in the column before the day they were kept, which means the book is a schedule rather than a record.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: The station book comes off its chain and goes into a pack, because it is evidence and evidence is what wins arguments with Wardens. It is Warden property and the only record of who has come up this road. It is missed at the next station, by the person who has been signing it, within the hour.

Highfold is the first of the counted villages on the shelf road: forty houses, a green, and nine lamps burning on that green at midday for no reason the daylight explains. The headman's wife counts the company in at the gate, out loud, and she does not stop counting when she reaches five.

choices.label: Ask her plainly what the lamps are for.
Say nothing and ask for a bed and bread.
Order the lamps put out on Warden authority.

nodes.body: The question is asked plainly on a village green and answered just as plainly by a woman who has lived inside the arrangement her whole life. The lamps are the rent. Highfold has paid it since her grandmother's time, it is paid in the ninth month, and she is puzzled that anybody official has finally come to ask.

choices.label: Go on to the shrine.

nodes.body: Bread, cheese and a barn floor bought for coin, with no questions asked in either direction. The village goes about its afternoon around the company as though the company were weather. Two children follow Ossa's lamp-pole about all afternoon, and one of them can already recite the station hours.

choices.label: Go on to the shrine.

nodes.body: Nine lamps are ordered out on Warden authority in a village that has kept them lit for nine generations. Forty people do not argue, and do not put them out, and do not let the company leave before the ninth hour. They are apologetic about all three of those things and entirely immovable on the last, and the company spends the hour on the green learning what the lamps are counting.

choices.label: Go and look at the shrine.

nodes.body: The village shrine is a dwarf road-marker older than the village, with a Reckoning cross fixed to its face by four modern nails. Under the cross the marker's base carries a tally cut in groups of nine, and the tally goes back further than the cross, the village, or the order that put the cross there.

choices.label: Read the base of the marker.
Leave the shrine; you have read three of these.
Prise the cross off and read what is under it.

nodes.body: The marker's base is read with a glove off: nine hundred years of groups, in the same system the company has now seen at four doors; the last group has eight strokes cut and a ninth begun. Over the top of all of it somebody has fixed a Reckoning cross, and the nails are less than ten years old.

choices.label: Go on to the barn.

nodes.body: A Reckoning cross is prised off a dwarf marker in front of a counted village, which manages to be sacrilege to two orders at once, and forty people watch it happen without moving. The company spends the ninth hour explaining itself on a village green, which is precisely where nobody in Highfold wants anybody standing at that hour. What they learn from standing there is worth more than the cross, and it costs the village something to teach them.

choices.label: Go and look at the barn.

nodes.body: The barn at the village's upper end is the one thing the headman's wife asked the company not to open; there are nine bootprints in the mud of its doorway going in. There are none at all coming out, and the mud is soft enough that a print from yesterday would still be sharp.

choices.label: Open it and go in with lamps up.
Watch it from the lane until the hour turns.
Go round it and count the roof beams from outside.
Fire it where it stands.

nodes.body: The barn opens on nine of them standing in the straw in Warden cloaks, drained to paper, hands folded, boots paired at the wall. The fourth from the left turns its head with the deliberate courtesy of a clerk noticing a visitor at a counter. Nobody in the company gets as far as raising a weapon.

choices.label: Go on to the headman.
Ask it which station it signed at.

nodes.body: An hour in the lane watching a barn door, and at the hour's turn the door opens from the inside; nine of them come out and go along the shelf road in file, unhurried, in the wrong direction for a village and the right one for the road above it. The barn door closes itself afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the headman.

nodes.body: The roof beams are counted from the lane, which gives nine, and the barn's footprint is paced out along the wall, which gives nine by nine; it is a dwarf building with a village barn's roof on it. Nobody in Highfold will say who built it, and two people say, unprompted, that it was here first.

choices.label: Go on to the headman.

nodes.body: The barn is fired where it stands with nine of them in the straw, and it goes up beautifully, and the straw makes it quick. Forty villagers watch from their doorways without any expression at all and then go back inside. At the ninth hour the company understands what the barn was for and what it was holding, and by then there is nothing to be done about it but find the headman.

choices.label: Go and find the headman.

nodes.body: A question is asked of something standing in straw, and it is answered: a station name, a date, and then the captain's own name with the correct rank and the correct company. The other eight turn their heads together to hear the rest of the exchange, and there is a great deal of the rest of it.

The headman of Highfold has been expecting somebody official for nine years and has a ledger ready on the table for when they came. He wants the company to carry his village's accounts down to Sarnhold and to be witnessed accepting them. He has had the witnessing clause written out for six of those nine years.

choices.label: Take his ledger and witness it properly.
Refuse; you cannot carry a village's paperwork up a mountain.
Read his ledger through on the green before you decide.

nodes.body: A village ledger is taken and witnessed on the green in front of forty people, which takes eleven minutes and adds four pounds to the barrow. It puts Highfold's arrangement into the Warden record for the first time since the arrangement was made. Two households ask to have their own names added while the ink is out.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: The refusal is given honestly, with a promise to send a Warden clerk in the spring. The headman has heard that promise from two previous officials and writes today's date beside it in his ledger anyway, which is not sarcasm. It is a record, and he keeps records, and that is the whole problem.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: The headman's ledger is read on his own green and the company's arrival is in it, in advance, in the hand that signs the station books. Forty people are standing between the green and the road by the time anybody has finished reading the entry. None of them is armed and all of them are apologetic.

The smugglers' adit is a dwarf drainage bore that runs under the first four stations: four feet high, half flooded, entirely unlit, with a Guild rope still rigged in the entrance and its far end out of sight. The Guild's own charts do not admit it exists. The scree field's wheel-track came from somewhere near here.

choices.label: Take it on the Guild's rigged rope.
Rig your own line and go slow.
Send Kettle in first to find the roof-falls.
Take it fast; four stations is four days.

nodes.body: The Guild's rope is taken on trust, which works for six hundred feet. Then it ends in a splice somebody made in the dark, over water of unknown depth, with the tail of the original rope hanging free beside it. Whoever made that splice was standing where the company is standing now, and was not going on.

choices.label: Come out at the drift head.
Splice on and keep going.

nodes.body: The company's own line is rigged and paid out properly, which costs three hours in a four-foot bore and means everybody comes out at the same time as everybody else. Halt complains for the first hour and stops in the second, when the line takes his weight at the first roof-fall and holds it.

choices.label: Come out at the drift head.

nodes.body: Kettle goes in first and comes back in forty minutes with three roof-falls counted, two crawlable and one that needs digging, and an opinion about the water that she delivers in a single word. She also comes back with her lamp out and does not immediately explain why, and nobody presses her on it.

choices.label: Come out at the drift head.

nodes.body: The third roof-fall arrives at chest-deep water in the dark with the whole company already past the second one, and there is no room at all to turn round in a four-foot bore. It takes eleven hours to move enough stone to pass, working by feel, in relays, in water. Everybody comes out of the far end, and nobody says anything for the first mile of the drift.

choices.label: Go on into the drift.

nodes.body: Somebody else's splice is trusted a second time, in the dark, over water, by people who have already got away with it once. The second splice is where the first rigger stopped, and the reason he stopped is on the far side of it, and it has been waiting for the rope to be trusted again. What the company leaves in the water is two packs and the last of its lamp oil.

choices.label: Push on along the drift.

nodes.body: The adit opens into a dwarf gallery nine feet wide, and the gallery floor has been swept. Not worn: swept, recently, along its whole visible length, in a bore that nobody has officially entered since the survey. There is no broom in sight and the sweeping runs uphill and downhill in both directions.

choices.label: Follow the swept floor uphill.
Cross the gallery and get back into the bore.
Follow the swept floor downhill instead.

nodes.body: The swept floor is followed uphill for a quarter mile to a lamp niche with a broom leaning against the wall beside it; the bristles are dry. There is a candle stub in the niche that is still warm to the back of a hand, and the sweeping continues past the niche in the same direction.

choices.label: Go on to the cache.

nodes.body: The gallery is crossed at a run and the bore re-entered on the far side, wet to the waist again inside four steps. Nobody says anything at all about the swept floor. Ilsabet writes two lines in her book about it that evening and reads them to nobody, which is how the company knows they are bad lines.

choices.label: Go on to the cache.

nodes.body: The swept floor is followed downhill, which is the direction the sweeping was going, and after eleven minutes it arrives at what is being swept toward. It also arrives at what has been doing the sweeping, and at roughly how long it has been at the work. The company goes back up the drift a great deal faster than it came down, and it goes back up one lamp and one pack lighter.

choices.label: Get back up to the cache.

nodes.body: A smugglers' cache fills a side bay: eleven crates under tarpaulin, nine of them Guild-marked and two of them marked not at all. Above the crates a lamp bracket has been screwed into dwarf stone by somebody who did not care what dwarf stone thinks about screws, and there is a fresh lamp in it.

choices.label: Open the two unmarked crates.
Open a Guild crate and take supplies.
Leave the cache and go on to the deep bay.
Take the lamp bracket off the wall for the oil.

nodes.body: The two unmarked crates open on founding-gauge blanks packed in straw in one, and nine lamp reservoirs in the other, filled and sealed with wax. The wax is dated. The date is a week from today, which is not a thing anybody in the company can immediately explain and not a thing anybody wants to discuss in a side bay.

choices.label: Go on to the deep bay.

nodes.body: A Guild crate is opened and salt beef, candles and two coils of line come out of it. Nyre leaves a note in the lid recording exactly what was removed, by whom, and under what authority, which is the sort of thing that seems absurd in a smugglers' cache and reads extremely well at an inquiry.

choices.label: Go on to the deep bay.

nodes.body: A lamp bracket is unscrewed from dwarf stone for the sake of a pint of oil, and it comes away with nine hundred years of the wall's own arrangement behind it. The bay's roof takes that personally and immediately, with no warning at all, which is the thing dwarf stone is famous for and everybody forgets. Two packs are under it and the company is not, and that is the whole of the good news.

choices.label: Move on before the rest comes down.

nodes.body: The bore widens into a chamber the survey does not show, and something that has been eating the smugglers' cache for a season lies asleep across the only way out. It is the size of a plough horse and the wrong shape for one, and its breathing sets the water in the floor moving on a slow count.

choices.label: Take it while it sleeps.
Go over it along the ledge above the exit.
Put the last of the Guild's salt beef down and go past.
Wake it and fight it in the open bay.

nodes.body: A killing is attempted on something asleep, which goes extremely well for four seconds, and after that it is eleven minutes of noise in a stone chamber with a pick and a poleaxe and no room at all to swing either properly. It ends. Two people can walk afterwards without help, and the thing does not get up.

choices.label: Come out on the shelf road.
Finish it rather than leave it wounded.

nodes.body: The ledge above the exit is eleven inches wide and taken in the dark with the thing breathing underneath at a pace that does not change while five people go over the top of it. Nobody breathes on the ledge. Everybody breathes at the far end, which is when the pace underneath changes.

choices.label: Come out on the shelf road.

nodes.body: The last of the Guild's salt beef goes down eleven feet from the exit, and the transaction is accepted without any negotiation. The company walks past something that watches them go with its chin on its paws. Kettle says afterwards that the whole arrangement felt professional, which is the word that stays with everybody.

choices.label: Come out on the shelf road.

nodes.body: A thing is woken deliberately in a stone chamber with one exit, by a company that wanted the fight on its own terms. In a room with one exit the terms belong to whatever lives in the room. It takes four minutes for that to become clear and rather less than that for it to stop mattering.

The wounded thing is finished rather than left, which is correct practice and takes four minutes longer than the company has. The noise of the first four seconds has been travelling up the bore the whole time, and something at the top of the bore has been coming down toward it since the second minute.

The old span at the fifth station crosses two hundred feet of air on a dwarf deck with its parapet long gone, and the deck is sound. A Guild sign at each end forbids more than two people on it at once, in three languages, and the sign at the near end has been repainted this year.

choices.label: Cross two at a time as the sign says.
Cross all together and quickly.
Go down to the ford and up the far side.

nodes.body: Three crossings of two, done slowly, with the deck ringing under boots in a way that stone should not ring; nobody looks over the edge, which takes some doing on a deck with no parapet. On the far side Hask says that the sign is not a Guild sign at all and shows them the mason's mark.

choices.label: Go on to the watchtower.

nodes.body: The whole company crosses at once against a Guild sign's advice, and the deck carries them, because dwarves built it to carry a train. It costs a cask off the barrow when the deck's ring changes pitch in the middle and everybody moves at once. Nobody suggests doing that again on the way back.

choices.label: Go on to the watchtower.

nodes.body: The ford below the old span is a spine river in a thaw, crossable in late summer by people who know it and in the second week of a thaw by nobody at all. The company establishes this with four people already committed and the fifth on the bank paying out a rope that is not long enough. They get everybody back to the near bank, and it costs them the afternoon and both spare coats.

choices.label: Go up to the watchtower instead.

nodes.body: The fifth station's watchtower is empty, its door barred from the outside, and its lamp lit; inside, the signing book lies open on the table at a page dated tomorrow, with the ink dry. There is a stove that has been out for a week and a chair that has not, and the tower is warm.

choices.label: Read the book's page dated tomorrow.
Take the lamp oil and the tower's spare rope.
Bar the door again and go on up.
Wait in the tower for whoever wrote tomorrow's page.

nodes.body: Tomorrow's page, read today: five arrivals entered in advance in a clerk's hand, with times against each. One of the entries is the company's own number. The time against it has not happened yet, and the ink of it is as dry as the ink of every other entry on the page.

choices.label: Go on to the pass.

nodes.body: Four gallons of station oil and forty feet of spare rope taken from a Warden tower and signed for in the book under today's date, which is the correct procedure. Under tomorrow's date, in the same book, in the other hand, the taking has already been recorded, along with the quantities.

choices.label: Go on to the pass.

nodes.body: The page is written at the ninth hour from the inside, by a hand that comes up through the floor hatch to do it and goes back down afterwards. The company is in the room for all of it and not one of them can move. In the morning the hatch is bolted from below, the page is signed in a hand Nyre recognises, and nobody suggests reading further back in the book.

choices.label: Get up to the pass.

nodes.body: The pass at nine thousand feet is the last of the road above cloud, and from it the crown gate of Kar Ashen is visible for the first time as a black notch in the ridge four miles on; weather is building behind the summit. Ossa looks at it for a while and gives it two hours, and then revises that to one.

choices.label: Push over the pass before the weather lands.
Dig in below the pass and let it pass over.
Go round the pass by the high traverse.
Send Hask over alone to find the gate road.

nodes.body: The pass is taken at a run in the last hour before the weather lands, and it works. It is also the point at which the mountain stops being scenery for everybody in the company at once. Nobody who was on that ridge in that hour ever describes it afterwards to anybody who was not.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.
Keep going through the first hour of the storm.

nodes.body: A hole is dug below the pass and roofed with the tarpaulin, and five people sit in it for eleven hours while the weather goes over the top of them making a sound like a mill. Nobody sleeps. Everybody comes out able to walk, which is the entire purpose of a hole in the ground.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: The high traverse round the pass adds four miles and a thousand feet of climbing and keeps the company out of the wind for all of it. Ossa says her father called it the long way and used it every single time. Her father walked this road for thirty years and died in bed, which she also mentions.

choices.label: Go on to the crown gate road.

nodes.body: Hask is sent over the pass alone to find the gate road, on the reasonable grounds that he has been up twice; the weather lands between him and the company in the fourth minute. There are eleven hours of nothing afterwards, and then a clear morning, and then four days of looking that turn up his pack.

The storm's first hour is walked into on the strength of having beaten the pass, which is exactly the sort of reasoning that gets people onto a ridge at nine thousand feet in weather. It takes the top layer off the snow and puts it into everybody's lungs. The company is strung out over a quarter mile inside ten minutes.

The last camp below the crown gate is in the lee of a dwarf revetment a mile short of the arch, and from it nine lamps are visible burning on the gate in cloud; they have been burning since the company first saw the notch. Nobody in the camp suggests that anybody is trimming them.

choices.label: Sleep properly; the gate can wait a night.
Break camp at once and go up in the dark.

nodes.body: A real night's sleep in the lee of dwarf stonework, with a brazier, two watches and the packs in the middle, and it is the last sleep on the near side of the crown gate. In the morning five people stand up able to walk to a closed door and think clearly about what to do with it.

choices.label: Go up to the crown gate.

nodes.body: The weather off the summit arrives early and arrives on the shelf road, with nine hours of daylight left and no shelter marked on any chart between here and the eighth station. Visibility goes to eleven feet in about four minutes. Ossa gets her pole onto the road's outer edge and keeps it there.

choices.label: Go on through it on the road, roped.
Get off the road and dig in on the lee side.
Run for the eighth station and hope it is manned.

nodes.body: Nine miles walked roped in whiteout with a lamp-lighter's pole feeling out the road edge the entire way. It is the worst day anybody has had since the Barrow Moor and nobody is lost on it, which is entirely down to a nineteen-year-old with her father's pole and her father's method.

choices.label: Go on to the shelter.

nodes.body: A hole dug in the lee of the road bank and roofed with the tarpaulin, and eleven hours of five people breathing each other's air while the spine works itself out overhead. Dellach tells the whole of a story about a siege at Rell's Gate, badly, twice, and everybody is grateful for it.

choices.label: Go on to the shelter.

nodes.body: A run is made for the eighth station on the strength of it probably being manned, and the eighth station is four hundred yards off the road on a spur, which is on the chart and not in anybody's memory of the chart. The company looks for it in whiteout for two hours, which is ninety minutes longer than the weather allows. They find a rock shelter instead, and two of them cannot feel their feet by the time they are inside it.

choices.label: Get into the shelter.

nodes.body: A dwarf shelter is cut into the road bank at the eighth station: benches, a flue that draws properly, a wood store still stacked, and nine lamp brackets with nine trimmed lamps in them. The wood is dry. Somebody restocked the store recently and did not sign anything, and the shelter has been swept.

choices.label: Light the flue and take four hours.
Take nothing and go straight on up.

nodes.body: Four hours with a fire in a dwarf flue, dry socks all round and hot water for everybody's hands. The wood store's own tally is on the wall, restocked eleven days ago according to the marks, by somebody who did not put a name to it. The tally is kept in groups of nine, like everything else on this road.

choices.label: Go on to the wolves' ground.

nodes.body: The ninth station's ground has spine wolves denning in its old revetments, and four of them are sitting in the road watching the company come up. They are not hunting. They are sitting in the road, in a line, in the way that animals sit when they have been fed on a schedule at a particular place.

choices.label: Break through them with shields and noise.
Back off the road and go round their ground.
Put meat down and walk through slowly.
Shoot the nearest one and see what the rest do.

nodes.body: Four spine wolves broken through with shields, noise and a poleaxe, which works and costs Dellach a forearm laid open to the bone. Nyre gets it closed in the road with the light going. Two of the wolves run and two do not, and nobody in the company enjoys any part of the eleven minutes.

choices.label: Go on to the ridge.
Follow the ones that ran and finish them.

nodes.body: A mile off the road round the wolves' ground in snow to the thigh, which costs two hours and everybody's legs and not one drop of blood. Hask, who has been up this road twice, says he did the same thing both times and that the wolves have been in those revetments longer than the Wardens have been on the spine.

choices.label: Go on to the ridge.

nodes.body: Salt beef goes down in the road and the company walks through at the pace of a funeral; four wolves eat eleven feet away without hurrying. One of them does not eat at all and watches the pack on Ilsabet's back the whole way past, and turns its head to keep watching it afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the ridge.
