nodes.body: One wolf is shot in the road to see what the rest do, which is a question with a well-known answer to anybody who has wintered on the spine. Four become eleven inside a minute, in open country with no cover and one shield between five people. The road at that point is nine feet wide.

The runners are followed off the road and finished in their own revetment, which is thorough. It also puts five people in a dwarf ruin at dusk with the den behind them, and the den is occupied by the part of the pack that did not come out to sit in the road in the first place.

The last ridge below Kar Ashen carries the road along its crest with the whole spine dropping away into cloud on both sides. The crown gate is a quarter mile above, lit, with its nine lamps clear now. Anything standing at that gate can see the entire length of the crest, and the crest has no cover on it at all.

choices.label: Walk the crest in the open.
Traverse below the crest on the north side.
Wait for cloud and go up inside it.
Go up the crest at a run; it is a quarter mile.

nodes.body: The north traverse below the crest is snow to the thigh and out of sight of the gate, and it takes an hour to cover a quarter mile. It arrives with the company below the arch rather than in front of it, in the shadow of the gate's own revetment, which is worth every minute of the hour.

choices.label: Go up to the crown gate.
Traverse further and try to get above the gate.

nodes.body: The crest is walked in the open in full view of a lit gate a quarter mile above, which is either confidence or a formality depending on who is watching. Nothing interrupts it. The nine lamps burn steadily the whole way and nobody comes out of the arch, and that is somehow worse than an interruption.

choices.label: Go up to the crown gate.

nodes.body: Cloud is waited for and then used: forty minutes of it. The company arrives at the gate's revetment inside the weather with nobody's lamp visible from anywhere. Vurma calls it the first competent thing anybody has done since Sarnhold, which is unfair to Ossa and everybody lets it stand anyway.

choices.label: Go up to the crown gate.

nodes.body: A quarter mile of crest at nine thousand feet, taken at a run by five people carrying packs, in the dark. A Guild survey marked the cornice on the left hand in spring, and nobody has marked it since, and the survey is in the company's own pack in Ilsabet's shorthand copy.

The traverse is pushed further to get above the gate, out onto the north face proper, which is not a route and was never a route. It resembles a ledge for its first eleven feet. After that it resembles nothing at all, and there is no way back along it in the dark for people carrying packs.

The crown gate of Kar Ashen is a dwarf arch the width of the road driven into the ridge, with nine lamps burning on nine brackets in cloud and a scraped Warden shield nailed to the post; the gate itself stands open exactly a hand's width. The bar is on the inside, set down neatly, out of the way.

choices.label: Go in by the open gate.
Go round to the foundry chimney under the wall.
Take the cistern channel under the outer ward.

nodes.body: Inside the crown gate, Kar Ashen's outer ward is not a ruin. It is inhabited: lamps lit on every corner at midday, a tally-yard working, a market open, four hundred people going about a morning under a mountain. Nobody runs. Nobody raises an alarm. Two children stop to look at the company and are called away by name.

choices.label: Take the gatehouse stair and the wheelhouse.
Cross to the tally-yard and its clerks.
Follow the cistern channel under the ward.
Try the garrison barracks on the wall.
Walk into the ward market.
Find the yardmaster and ask who runs this.
Turn round and go back out through the gate.

nodes.body: The crown gate is reached, the ward is seen, and the road is taken back down inside the hour. It is a decision Thane will accept and enter in the record without comment. It is also four hundred people the company looked at and left, and nobody in the Ninth Sword ever manages to describe them to anybody.

The gatehouse stair inside the arch is manned by two gate wardens in cloaks that fit them properly, with a signing book on a lectern. A queue of ward children waits beside them to have their lamps refilled from a common reservoir. One of the wardens holds out a pen and asks, politely, for the company's number.

choices.label: Sign the book like any traveller.
Ask the wardens who signs the book above them.
Ask the children what the lamps are for.
Refuse to sign and go past them.

nodes.body: The book is signed and countersigned by a gate warden who reads the entry twice and checks the pack; then he writes a number in the margin against it. The number is not the number of people in the company, and when he is finished he blots it and turns the book face down.

choices.label: Go up to the wheelhouse.
Ask him what the number against your entry means.

nodes.body: The question about who signs above them is answered without hesitation and without resentment: the yardmaster, and above him the chapel, and above the chapel the crown clerk. That clerk has held the office since this warden's grandfather was on this gate. He says it the way a man recites a chain of command he trusts.

choices.label: Go up to the wheelhouse.

nodes.body: Nine ward children with nine lamps explain the refill rota with the patience of people who have never once been asked about it; two of them argue about whose turn the ninth lamp is. The eldest settles it by saying that the ninth lamp is not anybody's turn, and none of them finds that strange.

choices.label: Go up to the wheelhouse.

nodes.body: A refusal to sign a signing book inside a working city, in front of two gate wardens and thirty witnesses who all stop what they are doing. The ward does not need violence. It has a gate, the company is inside it, and the crown clerk's household arrives at the gatehouse before anybody has reached the second street.

The question about the number in the margin is asked, and a gate warden answers it honestly while reading his own entry upside down. It is the number the crown clerk requires against an arrival, he says, and it is always the same number, and the number is nine. Then he asks the company to wait.

The gate's wheelhouse holds a dwarf capstan the size of a small room, oiled this week, which closes the crown gate, and its pawl is chained back with a Warden chain, and the chain has been cut once and mended with a Guild splice. Nothing else in the room has been touched in a century.

choices.label: Jam the ratchet so the gate cannot be closed.
Leave the wheel alone and look at the chain.
Cut the chain and drop the pawl now.

nodes.body: The ratchet is jammed with the moor-iron pick and a wedge of dwarf oak, quietly, in four minutes. It is the single most useful four minutes anybody spends in the outer ward. Whatever else happens now, nobody in Kar Ashen can shut the crown gate behind the company without a mason and an afternoon.

choices.label: Go on to the foundry.

nodes.body: The Warden chain is examined properly: cut once with a cold chisel and mended with a Guild splice. That dates the cutting to this spring and the mending to the same week as a Guild survey whose surveyor is on the Guild's own missing list, which is a coincidence Vurma refuses to call one.

choices.label: Go on to the foundry.

nodes.body: The pawl is dropped on a dwarf capstan the size of a room, and the crown gate closes with a noise that the whole ward hears and the whole city below it feels. It announces, to four hundred people, that somebody has arrived who does not want that gate open. They respond to it as a municipal matter.

The foundry under the ward wall has eleven inches of standing water on its floor and four furnaces that have been cold since the founding. There is something living in the casting pit at the far end. The ward feeds it on the ninth, from a bucket, on a rota, and the rota is chalked on the wall by the door.

choices.label: Go through fast along the moulding floor.
Go round by the pattern shop and the chimney.
Put down what the ward puts down and walk.
Empty the casting pit with the pumps and see.

nodes.body: A fast crossing of a flooded moulding floor, with something coming out of the casting pit behind at a pace that suggests it has done this many times and expects to be outrun. It does not hurry. It is still coming when the company reaches the slag door, and it stops at the doorway as though the doorway were a rule.

choices.label: Go on to the slag heaps.
Turn and hold the doorway rather than run.

nodes.body: Round by the pattern shop, which is dry and full of nine-hundred-year-old casting patterns for key-irons in every gauge the Compact has ever used, hung in order on the wall. At the far end it opens onto the foundry chimney's base, and the chimney has iron staples in it going up into the dark.

choices.label: Go on to the slag heaps.

nodes.body: The ward's own offering is put down at the pit's lip, the way the lamp-children do it, and the arrangement is accepted without complaint. Eleven minutes of walking past a casting pit follow. Kettle counts the steps out of habit and stops at nine, and starts again from one, and nobody asks her to explain.

choices.label: Go on to the slag heaps.

nodes.body: The casting pit is emptied with the ward's own pumps to see what has been in there, which takes two hours of pumping and is a reasonable use of an afternoon. In the last four inches the company gets its answer. It is standing in a drained pit on a flooded floor when the answer arrives at the ninth hour.

A doorway is held on a flooded moulding floor instead of running, which is the correct tactical choice against nearly everything. It is the wrong one against something that has been fed at a fixed hour for nine hundred years and has never once had to chase anything anywhere.

The slag heaps behind the foundry are warm, nine hundred years deep, and sorted. Founding-gauge blanks lie tipped out among the slag where the mint has been discarding rejects since before the legion, and a tally board at the yard gate records how many were tipped in each century, in nines.

choices.label: Dig the reject blanks out of the slag.
Take a slag sample for Ilsabet and go.
Leave the heaps; they are somebody's records.
Dig into the heap where it is warmest.

nodes.body: Four reject blanks dug out of warm slag, each mis-struck in a different way and each still heavy and cold in the hand. Ilsabet lays them out that evening in the order of their errors and says that whoever cut them was learning, and that the fourth one was cut by somebody who had stopped learning.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: A slag sample taken and read over a candle by a hedge-thaumaturge who has been doing this since the Barrow Moor. The mint has been cutting irons continuously for nine hundred years. It stopped, entirely, eleven days ago, and the last of the slag on the heap is still warm enough to prove it.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: A dig into the warmest part of a nine-hundred-year slag heap, which is warm because it is still working. What it has been working on is the mint's other rejects, the ones that were not blanks, and the heap gives way under the digging in the way that a stack of anything gives way under digging.

The tally-yard is working: eleven clerks at standing desks, a weighing floor, and a queue of ward families waiting to have their household counts entered for the month. It is a municipal office. It has a bench for waiting, a rail for queueing, and a jug of water, and everybody in it is entirely calm.

choices.label: Join the queue and have the company counted.
Go straight to the head clerk and show the charter.
Tip a clerk's desk over and stop the queue.

nodes.body: The company is entered in the ward's count as five, which a clerk does without looking up from his desk. Then he corrects it, at the bottom of the entry, to nine, without being asked and without explaining. When Nyre asks him why, he says that arrivals are entered at nine, and goes on to the next family.

choices.label: Go and look at the scales.

nodes.body: A Warden charter is presented to the head clerk, who reads it, thanks the captain for producing it, files a copy in the correct box, and continues the morning's counting, and a charter is a document. The count is the count. He does not appear to see any conflict between those two facts at all.

choices.label: Go and look at the scales.

nodes.body: A clerk's desk is tipped over in a working tally-yard in front of eleven clerks and forty families. The queue reforms around it. Two of the waiting families help the clerk pick his papers up, and the ward's own constables arrive within the quarter hour with a form already partly filled in.

The yard's weighing floor holds a dwarf balance with nine pans, in daily use, and it weighs nothing that can be seen. A clerk stands beside it entering a result in a book after each empty weighing, and the ninth pan hangs a quarter of an inch lower than the other eight.

choices.label: Read over the clerk's shoulder.
Leave the scales; you will not like the answer.
Stand on the ninth pan yourself.

nodes.body: The clerk's book, read over his shoulder: nine columns, one per pan, and in each column a name and a weight, and today's ninth column is blank. The pan under it is sitting low, and the clerk is waiting, pen in hand, for whatever it is that fills in the ninth column at the hour.

choices.label: Go on to the clerks' hall.

nodes.body: A company captain stands on the ninth pan of a dwarf balance in a working tally-yard, which the clerk records without any comment at all. It produces a weight. It also produces a name, entered in the ninth column in the clerk's neat hand, and the name is not the captain's.

The clerks' hall behind the yard holds eleven people keeping the ward's arithmetic, and at the end desk an old woman who has been copying the crown ledger for forty years. She has kept every copy. She has them in date order in a cupboard behind her, and she is the only person in Kar Ashen who has ever expected to be asked for them.

choices.label: Ask the old woman for the copies.
Ask her what happens to a household that falls behind.
Take the copies off her desk while she is at the yard.

nodes.body: The copies are handed over without argument by a woman who has waited forty years for somebody to ask for them. She wants a receipt. She writes the receipt herself, in triplicate, and signs all three, and keeps one, and hands the other two to the company with the cupboard's key on top of them.

choices.label: Go through to the cells.

nodes.body: The answer is given flatly across a desk, without any softening: a household that falls behind is carried by the ward for three months. After three months it is entered in the ninth column. After it is entered in the ninth column it is not a household, and the ward re-allots its rooms.

choices.label: Go through to the cells.

nodes.body: Forty years of crown-ledger copies taken off an old clerk's desk while she is at the yard, which is quicker than asking. It is noticed inside the hour, because she checks the cupboard hourly and has done for forty years. The ward's constables hold the company in the clerks' hall until the crown clerk can come up.

The ward cells under the clerks' hall are nine in a row, and eight of them are occupied by people who have fallen behind and are waiting quietly, with their households' tokens around their necks; the ninth is standing open. It has been swept, and it is warmer than the corridor.

choices.label: Open the eight and get them out.
Talk to the eight through the grilles first.
Look into the ninth cell.
Take the ninth cell's occupant's place and see what comes.

nodes.body: Eight cell doors opened with Kettle's picks in under two minutes, and eight people who do not come out, and the arrangement is that they are carried down on the ninth and their households are cleared; they have families in this ward. Two of them ask the company to close the doors again before the count.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.
Carry them out anyway, over the objections.

nodes.body: Eleven minutes through the grilles with eight people who are entirely reconciled to the arrangement and are worried about something else. What worries them is whether the company's arrival will disrupt the schedule. A disrupted schedule means arrears, and arrears fall on the households that are still standing.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: The ninth cell, looked into: swept, warm, empty, with nine tally-marks cut into the plaster at eye height and a fresh tenth begun. The sweeping has been done from the inside, which is clear from the direction of the marks in the dust, and the tenth mark is at the height of a man's shoulder.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: The ninth cell is entered deliberately and its door pulled to, because somebody in this company needed to know what a swept cell is for. The ninth hour arrives exactly on schedule to collect what is in it. The tenth tally-mark is finished from the outside, afterwards, by whoever does the finishing.

Eight people are carried out of ward cells over their own objections and their families' objections both. The ward does not fight the company for them. The schedule appoints eight others by the ninth hour, and it adds the carriers to the list, because the list has always had a provision for carriers.

The cistern channel under the outer ward is a dwarf conduit four feet high running full, with an inspection grating every hundred feet. The water in it is warm and comes down from somewhere above the city. It does not smell of stone. Everybody notices that at the same moment and nobody says it out loud.

choices.label: Wade it upstream to the ward gratings.
Go along the maintenance ledge above the water.
Follow the warm water down instead of up.

nodes.body: A quarter mile waded upstream in warm water against a current that has come off something the size of a mountain. It arrives under the ward at a grating that lifts from below, which means somebody uses it from this side and has greased the hinge. Everybody's legs are warm afterwards for an hour.

choices.label: Go on to the drowned quarter.

nodes.body: The maintenance ledge above the water is eleven inches wide and slick with nine centuries of mineral, and it is taken in the dark with the current going the other way underneath. Halt slips at the third grating and is caught by Hask. The catching is the loudest thing that happens in the conduit.

choices.label: Go on to the drowned quarter.

nodes.body: The warm water is followed downstream instead of up, on the entirely reasonable grounds that the source is what matters and the source can be found from either end. The conduit's outfall is where the ward's ninth-hour deliveries go, and the company arrives at it four minutes before the hour does.

The drowned quarter under the ward is eleven streets of dwarf housing flooded to the lintels, with lamps burning above the waterline in every ninth window. There is a boat chained at the steps and a pole beside it. The water is warm, and the lamps are trimmed, and nobody is at any of the windows.

choices.label: Take the chained boat and pole the streets.
Wade the shallow street by the temple wall.
Climb the roofs and cross the quarter above it.
Break into a lit ninth-window house.

nodes.body: A chained boat cut loose and poled down eleven flooded streets, past lit ninth windows with nobody at them; the water is warm and does not smell the way water smells. Nyre reads the street names off the door lintels as they pass and stops reading them aloud at the fourth street.

choices.label: Go on to the pump house.
Put in at one of the lit houses on the way.

nodes.body: The shallow street by the temple wall is thigh-deep the whole way, and the temple's east wall carries a tally in groups of nine from the waterline right up to the roof line. The lower groups are underwater and legible through it, which means the water arrived after the counting started and did not stop it.

choices.label: Go on to the pump house.

nodes.body: The roofs of the drowned quarter are crossed above the water in the dark, dwarf slate holding under boots the whole way. From up there the ward's whole lamplight is visible, and nine of the windows below are lit, and their pattern across eleven streets is not random and is not a pattern of habitation.

choices.label: Go on to the pump house.

nodes.body: A lit ninth-window house is broken into above the waterline. Inside there is a table laid for nine, with a ninth place set and untouched. The other eight places are occupied by the household that fell behind three months ago and has been carried since, and all eight of them look up at once.

The boat is put in at one of the lit houses on the way past, because a lamp in a window means somebody, and somebody might be helped. The somebody turns out to be the arrangement rather than a household. It is a considerable relief for the first four seconds, and then it is not.

ending.title: Put In At the Lit House

nodes.body: The ward pump house still works: nine dwarf pumps in a row with three of them turning, and a maintenance book that has been kept faithfully by hand for nine hundred years; the book is on a shelf, in date order, in nine volumes. The current volume is open at today's page and today's page is filled in.

choices.label: Read the maintenance book from the back.
Start the other six pumps and drain the quarter.
Take the pump house tools and go.
Stop the three that are turning.

nodes.body: The maintenance book, read from the back: nine hundred years of entries, one hand per century, every bearing and every repack recorded. The current hand starts eleven days ago, in the middle of a page, without any handover note. In nine hundred years of this book that has never happened before.

choices.label: Go on to the eel channel.

nodes.body: A dwarf toolkit taken out of a working pump house: spanners, a bearing puller, and a spool of the wire the dwarves used for gauge work. Vurma values the wire above everything else the company has picked up in three books and says so, and lashes it inside her own coat rather than to the barrow.

choices.label: Go on to the eel channel.

nodes.body: Three working pumps are stopped in a pump house that has kept eleven streets from filling for nine hundred years. The water is coming up through the drowned quarter's roofs inside the hour. The ward's response is to send its constables to the pump house rather than to the water, which tells the company who it is dealing with.

The eel channel behind the pump house is a dwarf sluice full of pale eels nine feet long, farmed by the ward and fed on a rota, and a farmer stands on the walkway with a bucket at the ninth hour; the walkway is eleven inches wide. The bucket is heavy enough that he carries it with both hands.

choices.label: Take the walkway past the farmer.
Ask the farmer what he feeds them.
Wait for him to finish the ninth-hour feed.
Kill the eels and be done with it.

nodes.body: The walkway is crossed with a farmer's bucket going into the channel alongside, and eleven feet of pale eel coming up out of the water for the contents. The contents are not fish, and were not fish yesterday either. Nobody in the company looks down after the first look, and Mira does not look at all.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.
Ask him whose turn the bucket was.

nodes.body: The farmer answers the way a man answers a trade question: the eels take what the ward's ninth column allots, and he has farmed them for thirty years and his father did before him, and the yield feeds four streets. He is proud of the yield, and there is no reason for him not to be.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: An hour on the walkway watching the ninth-hour feed from beginning to end, which is what it takes to understand the arithmetic properly. By the end of it the company knows what the ward's count is, what it is for, and what happens to the part of it that the eels do not take.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: Nine feet of pale eel is attacked in its own sluice by a company that has had enough of the arrangement, on a walkway eleven inches wide, with eight more eels in the water. The first one is killed. It is in the water rather than out of it by then, and so is the person who killed it.

The farmer is asked whose turn the bucket was, and he answers, and the name is one the company heard through a cell grille an hour ago. He waits politely for the next question with the empty bucket in his hands, and the next question does not come, because nobody in the company can find it.

The ward's garrison barracks on the wall holds forty bunks with twenty occupied, and the militia in it salutes a Warden charter properly. The sergeant has held this wall for the crown clerk for nineteen years. He is competent, his men are turned out, and his standing orders are on the wall in a frame.

choices.label: Ask the sergeant to put the ward under Warden orders.
Ask him what the militia is holding the wall against.
Rest the company here on the charter's authority.
Try to arrest the sergeant on the charter.

nodes.body: The ward goes under Warden orders on paper, which the sergeant accepts, salutes and files. Then he explains, without any insolence at all, that the order cannot be executed, because the militia's count is kept by the crown clerk and not by him. A man cannot be ordered out of a column he is entered in.

choices.label: Go up onto the wall.

nodes.body: The answer is given on the wall itself, with the sergeant pointing outward and then downward. Not the road, and not the spine. What his militia holds this wall against is the ninth-hour file coming up out of the city below, and his whole standing order, framed on his wall, is to let it through.

choices.label: Go up onto the wall.

nodes.body: A ward militia sergeant is arrested on a Warden charter in his own barracks in front of twenty of his men. The twenty do not intervene, which is worse than if they had. The crown clerk's constables arrive within the hour to take custody of everybody in the room, including the charter.

The ward wall's inner walk looks down over the city proper, and the city proper is lamplit all the way to a darkness at its centre that the lamps stop short of. Four things in Warden cloaks are coming up the stair to the walk, in step, at a marching pace, and the walk is eleven feet wide.

choices.label: Hold the stair head with shields.
Get off the walk into the barracks.
Give them the road and stand aside.
Go over the parapet onto the roofs.

nodes.body: A stair head held with shields against four things that fight like drilled men, because that is what they were; it costs blood and it buys the walk. Afterwards Dellach sits down on the parapet and says that the third one used a Warden's fourth-form guard on him, correctly, and that he learned it in the same school.

choices.label: Go on to the bell tower.
Follow them back down the stair.

nodes.body: The barracks door is taken at a run, and twenty militia close it behind the company and then stand at their posts as though nothing at all is passing on the walk outside. Something passes on the walk outside. It takes about ninety seconds, and not one of the twenty looks at the door.

choices.label: Go on to the bell tower.

nodes.body: The road is given and the company stands aside against the parapet while four of them go past in step, close enough to touch, close enough to smell the lamp oil in their cloaks; none of the four turns a head. The fourth one is a foot shorter than the others and wearing a militia issue belt.

choices.label: Go on to the bell tower.

nodes.body: The parapet is gone over onto the drowned quarter's roofs in the dark, which is nine-hundred-year-old dwarf slate over eleven feet of warm water. It has been holding that water in the dark for a long time without being walked on, and it does not object at the first boot or the second.

Four of them are followed back down the stair into the city proper, which is where they were going anyway. At the bottom of the stair the rest of the shift is forming up for the ninth hour, in a yard, in nines, and the company arrives in the middle of the forming up.

The ward bell tower holds a dwarf bell the height of a man, rung on the ninth hour every ninth day; its rope has been spliced by nine generations of ringers and every splice is different. The ringer's log hangs on a nail beside the rope, and it is full, and it has entries in it for next month.

choices.label: Cut the bell rope and take it with you.
Ring it now, off the hour, and see what happens.
Leave the bell; it is not the arrangement.

nodes.body: The bell rope is cut and coiled, nine generations of splices in forty feet of hemp, which is a museum in a bag; it stops nothing at all. The ward's ringers keep a spare rope and have kept one since the founding, and it is on the shelf under the log, and the ringer offers to fetch it.

choices.label: Go and take a billet.

nodes.body: The bell is rung once, off the hour, which empties the ward's streets in ninety seconds. Four hundred people go indoors without hurrying and without shouting, in the manner of a town that has drilled this. Then the crown clerk's constables arrive at the tower door with a form and no particular urgency.

choices.label: Go and take a billet.

nodes.body: The bell is left alone and the tower's own log is read instead, which lists every ringing for nine hundred years. Tomorrow's ninth-hour ringing is already entered, with the ringer's name against it. So is the company's number, in the column the log keeps for what the ringing is for.

The ward's travellers' house is clean and warm, with nine beds in the room, and eight are stripped; the ninth is made up, unoccupied, and kept that way, with the blanket turned down. The housekeeper says the room sleeps eight and does not explain the ninth bed, and does not appear to think it needs explaining.

choices.label: Take four beds and leave the ninth alone.
Sleep in the ninth bed out of principle.

nodes.body: A night in a warm ward billet with four beds used and the ninth left made. Nothing happens. Everybody sleeps better than they will admit to in the morning, and in the morning the ninth bed has been slept in and remade, and the housekeeper has already changed the linen and does not mention it.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: The ward market at midday sells bread, iron, rope, and lamp oil by the ninth. There is a stall selling tally-blanks to households the way a stall elsewhere sells nails: in bundles, by gauge, with a discount for quantity. The stallholder has a queue and a ledger and a boy to run errands.

choices.label: Ask the blank-seller who buys them.
Buy nine blanks and ask for a receipt.
Turn the blank stall over and scatter it.

nodes.body: The blank-seller answers as a tradesman answers: households buy them for the ninth-column entries, one per name. He has sold four hundred this season, he expects to sell nine more today, and he keeps a book because the crown clerk's household audits him. He is entirely willing to show anybody the book.

choices.label: Go and talk to the beggars.

nodes.body: Nine blanks bought at market price with a written receipt in the seller's own hand, itemised, dated and signed. It costs eleven pence. It is, on any reasonable assessment, the single plainest piece of evidence anybody has taken off this mountain in three books, and it fits in a coat pocket.

choices.label: Go and talk to the beggars.

nodes.body: The blank stall is turned over in a working market, and four hundred people stop what they are doing, and then they pick the blanks up, one at a time, and hand them back to the seller. It takes about four minutes. Afterwards they all look at the company, and go on looking, and nobody says anything.

The ward's uncounted sit at the market's edge and are in no column at all: nine of them, fed on the market's leavings, entirely willing to talk to strangers for bread. They are not treated badly. They are simply not in the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what the ward means by being a person.

choices.label: Buy them bread and hear the whole ward's history.
Ask specifically how somebody becomes uncounted.
Ask nothing; you are being watched from the yard.

nodes.body: Bread bought and an hour given, and nine uncounted deliver the ward's history from underneath: which families were cleared, in which years, what the crown clerk's hand looks like, and which of the ward's officials can be relied on. It is better intelligence than the Wardens have collected in nineteen years.

choices.label: Go on to the ward gaol.

nodes.body: The question about becoming uncounted is asked, and the oldest of the nine answers it in one sentence: you are uncounted when your name has been entered and taken. Then he says, without any drama at all, that this is true of all nine of them, and that two of them were taken this spring.

The ward gaol is not the cells: it is a proper stone gaol with a gaoler, a book, and four prisoners in for ordinary crimes. At the end of the row there is a Warden in a cell who has been there since autumn, and whose entry in the gaol book has no charge written against it.

choices.label: Get the Warden out of the end cell.
Question him through the door first.
Leave him; you cannot carry a prisoner up a mountain.

nodes.body: A Warden of Thane's own command comes out of a ward gaol on a charter, four months in, thin and entirely lucid. He can name every officer of the crown clerk's household from memory, in order of seniority, with the hours they keep. He has had four months in a stone room to memorise it.

choices.label: Go and find the lamp-keeper.

nodes.body: Eleven minutes through a cell door with a man who has had four months to arrange what he would say if anybody ever came, and the hours, and the file, and the crown clerk; where the mint's die is kept and who holds the key to the rack. He says all of it twice, in the same order, to be sure it is remembered.

choices.label: Go and find the lamp-keeper.

nodes.body: A Warden is left in a ward gaol because a prisoner is a burden on a mountain, which is defensible and which the gaoler writes in his book as the company declining custody. The crown clerk reads that entry the same evening. He now knows the company came, looked at his prisoner, and left him there.

The ward's lamp-keeper holds the oil rota and the hour book, and is the only person in Kar Ashen who can say precisely when the ninth hour falls, because the hour is not the sun's hour and never has been; she is nine years old. Her mother held the book before her and taught her the reckoning.

choices.label: Ask her for the hour book.
Ask who taught her the rota.
Take the hour book and go.

nodes.body: The hour book is handed over by a nine-year-old on the strength of a Warden charter she cannot read, because a charter is a grown-up thing and she has been taught to cooperate with grown-up things. It has the rota for the next nine days in it, and a note in an adult hand about the crown door.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: The answer comes from a child who does not understand that any of it is remarkable, and her mother taught her the reckoning, and her mother was taught by the crown clerk himself, who teaches every keeper personally. She has met him twice. She says he is kind and that he checks her arithmetic.

choices.label: Go on to the deep stair.

nodes.body: An hour book is taken off a nine-year-old lamp-keeper without asking. She reports it, because reporting it is her job and she was taught the reporting along with the reckoning. The crown clerk's household is on the ward stair within the hour, and it arrives at the walking pace it always uses.

ending.title: Reported, Because It Is Her Job

nodes.body: The yardmaster of the outer ward administers four hundred people and their counts, and he has been expecting a Warden company since the ninth station's book was signed. He has tea ready and two chairs set out. He is neither stupid nor cruel, and he has run this ward for nineteen years without a riot.

choices.label: Sit down and hear how he justifies it.
Put the charter on his table and take the ward.
Ask him what happens to him if the count fails.

nodes.body: Two hours of tea and justification from a man who has thought about it more than anybody in the company has, and the ward is fed, warm, lit and safe. Nobody is taken who has not fallen behind. And the alternative, he says, setting down his cup, is Hollowmarch, and he can describe Hollowmarch, and he does.

choices.label: Go and see the ward stores.

nodes.body: The charter goes on the table and the ward is formally under Warden authority, which the yardmaster accepts with visible relief and enters in his own book with the time. Then he explains what it changes about the ninth hour, which is nothing, and asks whether the company would like to see the rota.

choices.label: Go and see the ward stores.

nodes.body: The question is asked of a yardmaster about his own position if the count fails, and he answers it honestly, because he has answered every other question honestly. He is the ninth column's first entry and has been for nineteen years. That is what the office is. That is why nobody else applied for it.

The ward stores hold nine hundred years of grain, oil and salt in dwarf bins, better stocked than Sarnhold and better kept. There is a written allocation for every household on the wall. There are also nine bins at the end of the row that are not allocated to anybody, and the storekeeper's list skips them.

choices.label: Open the nine unallocated bins.
Take stores for the descent and sign for them.
Leave the stores; the ward will need them.
Fire the oil bins and burn the ward's rota.

nodes.body: The nine unallocated bins are opened, and eight are full of founding-gauge blanks packed in chaff, and the ninth is full of household goods: boots, coats, a child's mitten, sorted by size and stacked in nines. It is not a store of the dead's belongings. It is a store of the not-yet, sorted in advance.

choices.label: Go on to the kiln.

nodes.body: A month of stores drawn and signed for at ward prices, which the storekeeper enters without comment and totals correctly. It is the last honest transaction anybody in the company makes in Kar Ashen. The storekeeper insists on giving the correct change for it, in ward coin, counted twice.

choices.label: Go on to the kiln.

nodes.body: The oil bins are fired to burn a rota, in a stone city with nine hundred years of oil in it. The fire does not spread, because dwarf stores are cut to contain exactly this and every bin has its own stone lip. What it does is tell four hundred people what the company is, in one afternoon, permanently.

The ward kiln is hot and tended, with a firing on: nine saggars in the chamber and a kiln-master who will not open it before the hour. He cannot say what is in the saggars, and he means that literally. He loads what he is given, fires it, and hands over what comes out, and has for eleven years.

choices.label: Open the kiln now and look in the saggars.
Wait for the firing to finish with him.
Take the kiln-master's book and go.
Break the saggars where they stand.

nodes.body: A kiln opened four hours early, which ruins the firing and the kiln-master's month. Inside are nine saggars, and in each saggar a set of tally-blanks bedded in sand, and every blank already cut with a name. The names are in a hand the company has now seen in four fortresses and one mint.

choices.label: Go on to the ward watch.
Take a saggar's contents with you.

nodes.body: Two hours of waiting with a kiln-master who talks about clay the entire time, cheerfully and at length. The firing is drawn at the proper hour and nine saggars are opened in front of the company by a man who genuinely did not know what he has been firing, and who has to sit down afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the ward watch.

nodes.body: The kiln-master's book, given willingly: nine firings a season, one on each ninth day, and the same nine names entered as the customer every single time for nineteen years. He has never met the customer. The order comes down with the clay, and the clay comes from the crown clerk's household.

choices.label: Go on to the ward watch.

nodes.body: Nine saggars are broken in a hot kiln chamber with a moor-iron pick, which destroys nine sets of cut blanks and takes about a minute. The ward's arithmetic treats destroyed blanks as arrears rather than as a loss. Arrears fall on whoever is nearest to them, and the company is standing in the kiln chamber.

A saggar's contents are taken out of a working kiln: nine cut blanks in sand, still hot enough to need gloves. The ninth blank in the set is cut with a name that the captain has been carrying in a pack since Gallowmere, and it is cut properly, in the founding hand, with the correct rank.

The ward watch house stands at the head of the deep stair and keeps the city's own log; the log for tomorrow has already been written, in the crown clerk's hand, and it is on the desk under a rule. The watch sergeant does not stop the company reading it and does not offer it either.

choices.label: Read tomorrow's log entry.
Sign in for the deep stair and go down.
Take the log and carry it down with you.

nodes.body: Tomorrow's entry, read at a watch house desk: the ninth-hour file, its numbers, its route through the ward, and at the bottom of the page a company of five entered as arriving at the crown door. The hour against that last entry has been left blank, and the blank has been ruled, ready.

choices.label: Go down the deep stair.

nodes.body: The city log is taken off a watch house desk and carried down the deep stair, because the log is the case. The watch reports it at once, because the log is the city and a city cannot be without its log. The company goes down into Kar Ashen with the whole city awake behind it.

ending.title: The Log Goes Down With You

nodes.body: The deep stair at the ward's inner edge is nine feet wide and cut for traffic, dropping in long flights into the counted city itself; there is lamplight all the way down, on both walls, at intervals. The air coming up is warm and smells of forge and stone and something underneath both of those.

choices.label: Go down in order with lamps lit.
Go down at the ninth hour behind the file.
Rope the stair and send Kettle a flight ahead.

nodes.body: The counted city opens at the deep stair's foot: nine streets radiating from a plaza, nine hundred lamps, a great chapel on one side and a working mint on the other, and eleven thousand people live inside the arithmetic here, and there is a fountain. There are children. There is a queue outside a municipal office, and the queue is orderly.

choices.label: Go to the great chapel.
Go to the mint where the irons are cut.
Walk into the market of the counted.
Find the archive and read the whole thing.
Follow the aqueduct into the lower city.
Find the city's own Wardens.
Take the baths; you are filthy and half dead.
Turn round and take the stair back up.

nodes.body: The plaza is seen, the city counted at a glance, and the stair taken straight back up before anybody has crossed the square. It is the last moment at which this could still be called a reconnaissance. Everybody in the company knows that at the time, and four of them say so on the stair.

The great chapel of Kar Ashen is Reckoning-built over dwarf foundations and holds four thousand. There is a service in progress. The entire congregation is counting in unison, in nines, in a rhythm the company has heard in a barn on the shelf road and in a barracks at Sixteen Mile and in a gallery under a moor.

choices.label: Sit through the service to the end.
Interrupt it and ask who wrote the liturgy.
Take the celebrant aside afterwards and press him.

nodes.body: A full hour of a liturgy that is arithmetic set to plainsong, four thousand voices keeping a count in nines, and at the end there is a form of words that names the debt, the term and the collateral, in that order. Nyre knows the tune. It is her own order's evening office with the numbers changed.

choices.label: Go through to the choir.

nodes.body: A service interrupted from the aisle by a Warden charter. A celebrant who stops mid-phrase, answers the question fully, and invites the captain to read the liturgy's colophon for himself. Then he resumes the count from exactly where he left it, and four thousand people come back in on the correct number.

choices.label: Go through to the choir.

nodes.body: The celebrant is pressed in his own vestry about who wrote the liturgy, and he answers. The name is on a signed requisition in the company's own pack. Four thousand people are still counting on the other side of the vestry door, and the count does not falter when the door opens.

The choir loft above the nave holds nine cantors who keep the count for the whole city in shifts, and have kept it from that loft, without a break, since the founding, and there are nine chairs, and there is a water jug. There is a slate for the shift change, and the shift change is timed to the second.

choices.label: Read the cantors' shift roll.
Leave the loft; you have heard enough of it.
Stop the count. Put a hand over the ninth cantor's mouth.

nodes.body: The shift roll, read in a choir loft: nine hundred years of names in nine-hour shifts, four hundred pages of them; the last page lists next month's shifts, filled in as far as the twentieth, with nine blanks at the bottom. The blanks are ruled and waiting, and the ruling was done in the same ink.

choices.label: Go and find the confessor.

nodes.body: The count is stopped in the great chapel of Kar Ashen for nine seconds by a hand over a cantor's mouth; the whole city hears it stop, because the whole city is keeping time to it. Eleven thousand people turn toward the chapel at once, and what they do next is not violent and is not slow.

The chapel's confessor is an old man with a lifetime of the city's private arithmetic in his head. He will talk to a Warden company because he has been waiting forty years for somebody official to ask, and he says so before anybody has asked. He has a chair set out for it, and a jug, and a pen.

choices.label: Hear his whole account, on the record.
Ask only who the crown clerk is.
Ask him to name the families who fell behind.

nodes.body: Four hours in a confessional with a man who has kept a city's secrets professionally, and who gives up all of them at once in a flat voice, in order, with dates. Ilsabet writes as fast as she can and misses none of it. At the end he asks whether that was useful, and then asks it again.

choices.label: Go and look at the reliquary.

nodes.body: The crown clerk is named: it is an office, not a person, held for nine hundred years by a succession of holders. The current one is a man the confessor christened himself, forty-one years ago, and has confessed every ninth day since. He gives the name, the house, and the hours at which he can be found.

choices.label: Go and look at the reliquary.

nodes.body: The confessor is asked to name the fallen-behind families out loud in his own chapel, and he does it, all four hundred of them, in order, from memory, over the course of an hour. The ninth name in the list is his own, and he says it in the same voice as the other three hundred and ninety-nine.

The chapel reliquary of the counted city holds eight tally-irons on velvet in a case built for nine. Under the ninth setting there is a plate, engraved, and the engraving is not yet complete: an office, a date this spring, and a space for a name. The burr is still on the letters.

choices.label: Read the ninth plate's engraving.
Take an iron off the velvet.
Leave the case; you have two of these already.
Break the case and take all eight.

nodes.body: The ninth plate, read through glass: an office, a term of nine years, a date this spring, and a blank where a name goes. The engraver stopped at the blank rather than leaving the whole plate for later, which means the office was expected to be filled and the filling was expected to be soon.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: One founding iron comes off the velvet in a chapel with four thousand people in it, and nobody stops it. Two of the cantors watch the whole thing from the loft without breaking the count. Afterwards there are two empty settings in the case, and the plate under the ninth is still not finished.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: A reliquary case is broken in the great chapel and all eight founding irons are taken at once, which is the entire holding tally of a door somewhere in this mountain. The city's response is not violence. It is a bell, rung once, and then the whole congregation standing up together and turning round.

The mint of Kar Ashen is working: nine hearths, a rolling floor, gauge benches, eighty smiths on shift. At the far end the crown die stands under a hood on a dwarf anvil, with two of the crown clerk's household beside it who are not smiths and are not armed and do not appear to do anything at all.

choices.label: Go in openly on the charter.
Go in through the coal yard at shift change.
Send Kettle over the roof to the die.
Walk in and demand the die on Warden authority.

nodes.body: The coal yard at shift change is forty smiths going out and forty coming in, and five strangers crossing a mint floor in the middle of it with nobody looking at anything except their own hands. It works because a mint at shift change is the least observant place in any city, including this one.

choices.label: Go on to the die room.
Take a hearthman's apron and stay for the shift.

nodes.body: The mint is entered openly on a Warden charter, which the mint-master reads, accepts and files. Then he shows the company the floor himself, at length, with professional pride. There is nothing on it he considers illegal and he has never been told that anybody thinks otherwise.

choices.label: Go on to the die room.

nodes.body: Kettle goes over the mint roof and down into the die room's clerestory, which takes forty minutes and a great deal of patience. It puts one member of the company inside the only room in Kar Ashen that actually matters, with a view of the die, the rack, and the two who stand beside them.

choices.label: Go on to the die room.

nodes.body: The crown die is demanded on Warden authority in a working mint in front of eighty smiths. The two of the household beside it step back rather than forward, which is the first warning. The eighty smiths put down their tools and form up in nines, which is the second, and there is no third.

Kettle surrenders the borrowed apron and takes a place on the line instead, and a full shift teaches him the gauge, the tally, and the particular rhythm of the die. It also enters five strangers on the shift roll, and the roll is reconciled against the count when the closing bell goes. Nobody in Kar Ashen argues with a count, so the company departs the mint as recorded labour rather than as thieves.

The die room holds the crown die bolted to a dwarf anvil under a hood, four cut irons cooling in a rack beside it, and a ledger on a stand listing what has been cut this season and what is still to cut, and the hood is up. The ledger is open. Everything in the room is exactly where the rota says it should be.

choices.label: Take a cut iron off the cooling rack.
Read the season's cutting ledger.
Take nothing and go through to the smiths.
Take the crown die itself off the anvil.

nodes.body: A cut iron off the cooling rack, founding gauge, still warm through a glove; its tally matches the crown door's own ring, which Ilsabet establishes in four minutes with a wire and a rubbing. Its flank is blank where a name goes, and the blank has been filed smooth in readiness.

choices.label: Go on to the smiths.

nodes.body: The season's cutting ledger, read at the stand: nine irons cut, eight distributed to the ring, and the ninth entered as held pending the appointment of a hand. The entry is dated eleven days ago. It is the day the slag heap went cold, and the day the pump house's maintenance hand changed.

choices.label: Go on to the smiths.

nodes.body: The crown die is unbolted from its anvil in the middle of a working mint: forty pounds of dwarf steel that decides what every iron in this mountain says; the mint stops. All eighty of them stop at once, without a signal, and turn round, and the room is a hundred feet long with one door.

The mint's smiths are eighty people who have cut irons here father to daughter for nine hundred years, and their foreman would like to know what a Warden company thinks it is doing on his floor. He asks it reasonably. He is holding a two-pound hammer while he asks, because he was using it.

choices.label: Fight your way across the floor to the far door.
Put the charter to the foreman and argue it out.
Have a blank cut for you, here, on the crown die.
Fire the hearths' oil store and go out in the smoke.

nodes.body: Eleven minutes of fighting across a mint floor against people who work with hammers for a living, in a room with nine open hearths in it. It reaches the far door. It costs blood, and it costs the company any possibility of ever being welcome in this city again, and it does not get anybody the die.

choices.label: Go on to the blank store.
Go back for the die once the floor is clear.

nodes.body: An argument with a mint foreman conducted entirely in trade terms: gauge, tally, warrant and standing order. He wins two points of it. He loses the third, which is whether a standing order signed by an office rather than a person can be produced on request, and he stands aside and writes down that he did.

choices.label: Go on to the blank store.

nodes.body: A blank is cut for the company on the crown die by a foreman who has been asked correctly, in trade form, with the gauge specified. He does it because the request was made properly and the die does not care whose hand pulls the lever. He also, unasked, files the flank smooth.

choices.label: Go on to the blank store.

nodes.body: A hearth's oil store is fired to make smoke to escape in, in a mint with nine working hearths and nine hundred years of oil in its floor seams, and the smoke works. What the smoke does not do is confuse eighty people who know exactly which of the two doors anybody would run for.

A return is made across a cleared mint floor for the die, on the reasonable grounds that the fight has already been had. The second shift is coming in through the coal yard door at the ninth hour with the whole household behind it, and the company is standing at an anvil with a spanner in its hands.

The blank store behind the mint holds nine hundred years of uncut blanks in dwarf bins, sorted by gauge, and a ledger of issues going back to the founding; there are four entries for this spring. They are in a hand the company has seen on requisitions at Rell's Gate and on a chart at Sarnhold.

choices.label: Read the spring issues.
Take blanks and go on to the wyrm gate.
Burn the issue ledger where it stands.

nodes.body: Four spring issues, read at the store's own desk: three to the ring, and one to a name that Nyre stops reading aloud halfway through. It is the legate who came up to Sarnhold with a coach and a writ to take custody of the company's irons for safekeeping, and the issue predates his arrival by a month.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: The issue ledger is burned in a dwarf blank store to destroy the record, which takes four minutes and works completely. It also destroys the only document connecting a mother-house legate to a mint under a mountain. The company understands that about four minutes after the last page has gone.

The market of the counted is a market like any market, with bread and iron and cloth, except for the ninth stall in every row; the ninth stall sells nothing. It has a clerk at it and a ledger and a queue, and the queue moves briskly, and people thank the clerk when they reach the front of it.

choices.label: Join the ninth stall's queue and watch.
Buy food and rope and ask nothing at all.
Clear the ninth stall and send the queue home.

nodes.body: An hour in the queue at a stall that sells nothing; eleven people in turn give the clerk a name, receive a token, and thank him. The twelfth is a child on her own, who gives a name that is not hers, receives the token, and carries it away in both hands as though it were hot.

choices.label: Go on to the pens.

nodes.body: Food, rope and lamp oil bought at fair prices in a market under a mountain, from people who make change correctly and wish the company a good afternoon. Eleven thousand people go about their day around it. The whole transaction takes twenty minutes and is the most disturbing twenty minutes in the book.

choices.label: Go on to the pens.

nodes.body: The ninth stall is cleared and its queue sent home by a Warden company acting on a charter, and the queue goes home; it comes back at the ninth hour. The stall is staffed again by then with a different clerk and the same ledger, and the day's entries have all been made up from the tokens already issued.

The pens below the market are for stock, and they hold stock, and the ninth pen holds nine people, fed and warm, with their households' tokens on cords around their necks, and there is straw; there is a water trough with a cover on it. The stockman keeps all nine pens to the same standard and is proud of it.

choices.label: Open the ninth pen.
Talk to them over the rail first.
Buy the whole ninth pen from the stockman.
Cut the stockman down and take his keys.

nodes.body: The ninth pen is opened, and nine people stay in it. The eldest explains to a Warden captain, with real patience and no bitterness at all, why leaving would cost nine other households their tokens, and what happens to a household without a token, and how long it takes.

choices.label: Go on to the auction.
Carry the youngest out over her objection.

nodes.body: Eleven minutes over a rail with nine people who are calm, informed and entirely uninterested in being rescued. What they want is for the company to carry a letter down to a family at the eighth station. They have written it already. It is four lines long and it is not about them.

choices.label: Go on to the auction.

nodes.body: The ninth pen is bought outright from the stockman at market rate, receipted, with nine tokens handed over and nine names struck from a book. It takes eleven minutes and empties the company's purse entirely. The stockman gives a proper receipt and asks whether the company wants the pen as well.

choices.label: Go on to the auction.

nodes.body: The stockman is cut down in his own pens for a set of keys; he is one man with a stick, and it takes four seconds. He was also a father of four, the pens are municipal property, and the hue and cry closes nine streets between the market and the deep stair within the quarter hour.

The youngest of the ninth pen is carried out over her own objection and her household's. Her household's tokens are struck the same afternoon, because a pen short at the count is arrears. The eight who remain make up the difference, and they were told that would happen, and they told the company so.

The arrears auction is held on the ninth of every month in a hall off the market, and it is held with perfect courtesy, and households that have fallen behind bid their own names against each other for another month's grace. There is a rostrum, a clerk, and a bell. Nine hundred people attend, and most of them are not bidding.

choices.label: Sit at the back and watch the whole auction.
Bid on every lot until the money runs out.
Break up the auction from the floor.

nodes.body: An hour at the back of an arrears auction, conducted throughout with the manners of a livestock sale in a good market town; four names are sold. Two of them are bought by the crown clerk's own household, which bids by paddle, and which does not bid against itself, and which pays over the odds both times.

choices.label: Go on to the ledgers.

nodes.body: Every lot is bid on until the purse is empty, which buys four households a month of grace and costs the company everything it has. It also raises the reserve on every remaining lot, because the room has now learned that there is outside money in it. The auctioneer adjusts accordingly and apologises for doing so.

choices.label: Go on to the ledgers.

nodes.body: An arrears auction is broken up from the floor by a Warden company. It adjourns politely, with the auctioneer thanking the company for its attendance. It reconvenes at the ninth hour in the chapel undercroft with the same lots, plus nine more, and the nine more are the households that spoke up in the hall.

The auction hall's ledgers fill nine hundred years of shelving, one volume per decade, recording every name sold in this city since the founding, and it is a continuous record in a single institutional hand, and there is an index. There is a reading desk. There is a lamp with a shade on it for readers.

choices.label: Read the current century and take notes.
Take the ledgers and go on to the archive.
Compare the hand against the requisitions in your pack.

nodes.body: A century of arrears read in ninety minutes by two people taking notes: the rate, the cycle, the household names, and the one fact that matters most. The rate has doubled since Kar Duhn shut, and doubled again since Hollowmarch, which means the company's own two books are in this ledger as a cause.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: The auction ledger's hand is held against a Reckoning requisition from the company's own pack, in front of the hall clerk, on his own desk; the two hands match. The hall clerk looks at both of them for a long moment, and then quietly leaves the room, and does not come back with what he went for.

The city archive occupies nine floors of dwarf shelving with nine hundred years of Kar Ashen's arithmetic on it, four archivists, and a public reading room; it is entirely open to any citizen who asks, and there is a request slip. There is a trolley. There is a rule about not taking lamps between the stacks.

choices.label: Ask for everything on the crown door.
Ask for the founding charter of the arrangement.
Set the archive alight and end the arithmetic.

nodes.body: A request for everything on the crown door is filled in forty minutes. The archivist brings eleven boxes up on a trolley. She asks, on the way past, whether the company would like the founding volume as well, since most people who ask for the boxes turn out to want the volume.

choices.label: Go through to the stacks.

nodes.body: Nine floors of dwarf shelving are set alight to end an arithmetic. The arithmetic survives, because it is kept in nine places and this is one of them. What does not survive is a city's own history of itself, and the company is remembered for exactly that, correctly, for as long as anybody remembers anything.

The founding volume is kept in a dwarf vault at the bottom of nine floors, behind a door that has stood open for nine hundred years; the step into it has been worn into a groove. There is a lectern, a chair, and a lamp bracket, and the bracket has a lamp in it that is lit.

choices.label: Go down and read the founding volume.
Have Ilsabet copy the relevant clauses only.
Take the founding volume off the mountain.

nodes.body: Four hours in a dwarf vault with the founding volume, and it is not a contract. It is a set of engineering specifications. It describes the doors as containment, the count as a maintenance schedule, and the hands as an operating crew, and it does all of that in the flat prose of people writing for successors.

choices.label: Go on to the index.

nodes.body: Nine clauses copied in Ilsabet's shorthand, which is the smallest defensible extract and the one an inquiry will actually read. It takes an hour rather than four. She copies the clause numbers, the volume's shelf mark and the vault's own catalogue number as well, because she has been thinking about courts since Hollowmarch.

choices.label: Go on to the index.

nodes.body: The founding volume is taken out of its vault, which the archive permits, because the archive permits any citizen to borrow. The archive's standing order also requires the borrowing to be reported to the crown clerk within the hour, along with the borrower's name. The archivist fills the slip in while the company watches.

The archive's index is kept on nine thousand slips in nine cabinets, cross-referenced by name, household and year. Any citizen can use it. The system is simple, well maintained, and entirely comprehensive, and it works in both directions, which is a property of indexes that nobody in the company has thought about before today.

choices.label: Look up the company's own five names.
Look up the crown clerk's office holders.
Look up nothing; the index reads both ways.

nodes.body: Five names looked up in a nine-thousand-slip index, and all five found, with arrival dates. Behind them, filed in the same drawer in the same hand, there is a sixth slip. It has the company's number on it, a date this week, and a cross-reference to a shelf mark in the crown ledger's own series.

choices.label: Go and find the archivist.

nodes.body: The index is consulted for the crown clerk's office holders, which produces nine slips in good order, and in the same drawer there is a tenth slip, blank except for a date and two words. The words are pending appointment. The date is today, and the slip has been in that drawer since before the company reached the gate.

The senior archivist has been in this building fifty years, knows exactly what her archive is, and has spent her whole professional life keeping it complete against the possibility of a day like this one. She says that in the first minute. She has a folder ready, with tabs in it, and the folder is not thin.

choices.label: Ask her to certify copies for a Warden inquiry.
Ask her what she thinks the count is for.
Ask her to come down the mountain and testify.

nodes.body: Nine certified copies made, sealed and signed by an archivist of fifty years' standing, with her office stamp and her personal seal on each one. In a Warden court it is worth more than everything else the company has picked up in three books put together, and she makes ten and keeps one herself.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: The answer of somebody who has read all of it: the count is a maintenance schedule for a containment, the containment has been maintained, and she would like the company to understand that she is not defending it. She says the last part twice, and then asks whether that was clear, and asks it again later.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: An archivist of fifty years' standing is asked to come down a mountain and testify, and she agrees, and goes to pack a bag. She is entered in the ninth column before the company reaches the wyrm gate, which takes about four hours, and her folder is back on its shelf by the following morning.

The city aqueduct brings warm water down from somewhere above the crown door and runs the whole lower city on it. There is an inspection walkway along its channel, with markers every hundred yards. The water is warm enough to steam in the lamplight, and it is the reason the baths exist, and the mills, and the eels.

choices.label: Follow the walkway up toward the source.
Cross the channel and go down into the lower city.
Swim the channel; it is warm and quiet.

nodes.body: A mile of inspection walkway upstream, the water getting warmer under the hand every hundred yards. At the ninth marker the channel's stonework changes: dwarf work below it, and above it something older and better, cut without tool marks. Vurma looks at it for a long time and declines to identify it.

choices.label: Go on to the sluice.

nodes.body: The channel is crossed on a maintenance plank and the lower city entered from above, which is quieter and dirtier and puts the company among the uncounted rather than the counted. Nobody up here has a token. Nobody up here is in a column. It is the only part of Kar Ashen where anybody looks at strangers.

choices.label: Go on to the sluice.

nodes.body: A warm quiet channel is swum for a quarter mile because it is warm and quiet; the grating at the far end turns out to be a filter rather than a gate. What it filters is why the water below it is warm, and the swimming has been downstream of that filter for the whole quarter mile.

The great sluice divides the aqueduct nine ways for the nine quarters, with a keeper's hut, nine gates and a log book. The keeper has held the gates for thirty years and knows every allocation by heart. He is pleased to have visitors and offers tea, and the tea is made with the aqueduct's own water.

choices.label: Ask the keeper what is upstream.
Shut the ninth gate and see who complains.
Open all nine gates and flood the quarters.
Read the sluice log for the last nine days.

nodes.body: The keeper answers while he works, because the gates need working: upstream is the crown cistern, above the cistern is the door, and the water is warm because it comes off the door. It has always come off the door. His father told him that, and his father had it from the keeper before him.

choices.label: Go on to the mills.
Ask him what the water tastes of in the ninth week.

nodes.body: The ninth gate is shut, which dries one quarter in forty minutes. It brings not constables but nine householders with buckets, who ask the company, reasonably and with some embarrassment, to open it again, and who explain what the quarter uses that water for and how long the cisterns hold.

choices.label: Go on to the mills.

nodes.body: Nine days of sluice log, read at the keeper's table: the same allocations every day, in the same hand. On the ninth day of each cycle the whole flow is diverted to the crown cistern for two hours. Tomorrow is a ninth day, and the diversion has already been entered, in advance, with the hours.

choices.label: Go on to the mills.

nodes.body: Nine sluice gates are opened at once to flood nine quarters, which is nine hundred years of arithmetic drowned in an afternoon. It works exactly as intended. Eleven thousand people lose their homes to a company that came up here to help them, and the count is unaffected, because the count was never in the buildings.

A sluice-keeper is asked what the water tastes of in the ninth week, and he answers honestly out of thirty years of tasting it, because a keeper tastes his water and that is the job. The company stands in his hut with his tea going cold in their hands and understands the aqueduct at last.

The mill row on the aqueduct runs nine mills, and eight of them are grinding grain; the ninth mill's stones are turning on nothing at all. Its miller stands outside in the lane because he will not go in while it is running, and he has not gone in while it is running for nine years.

choices.label: Go into the ninth mill with him.
Stop the ninth mill's wheel yourself.
Ask him what the ninth mill grinds.
Go past the mills entirely; the door is above.

nodes.body: The ninth mill entered with a miller who has not been inside it while it was working since he inherited it, and it is grinding; it has a hopper. The hopper has been fed on the ninth of every month for as long as the mill has stood there, and the feeding is done by somebody else, at night.

choices.label: Go on to the quiet room.
Look in the hopper.

nodes.body: The miller answers at his own door, plainly: the ninth mill grinds what the ninth column allots, the flour goes to the chapel, and he has never eaten the chapel's bread. Neither has his family. Neither, he says, has anybody on this row, and he would rather the company did not either.

choices.label: Go on to the quiet room.

nodes.body: The mill row is walked past at speed with nine wheels turning and one of them turning on nothing. It is the correct decision and it takes four minutes. Nobody in the company is able to leave it behind afterwards, and two of them raise it again that evening without meaning to.

choices.label: Go on to the quiet room.

nodes.body: The ninth mill's wheel is stopped by a company that has had enough; that stops the chapel's bread, which stops the liturgy's own offering, which stops the count at the evening office. The crown clerk's household is on the mill row within the hour, and it does not arrive angry, which is worse.

A look into the ninth mill's hopper, taken deliberately by somebody who had been told what was in it and needed to see for himself. The hopper is full. The mill goes on working while the looking happens, because a mill does, and nobody standing on that floor is able to move for eleven seconds.

A dwarf rest-house stands on the mill row: empty, clean, nine beds, a stove laid ready, kept by the city for travellers because the city keeps everything properly. There is a book to sign. There is a jug of the aqueduct's water on the table, and nobody in the company touches it.

choices.label: Take four hours and the stove.
Press on; the door is nine hours off.

nodes.body: Four hours in a warm dwarf rest-house on clean beds, taken deliberately by a company that has learned three books' worth of lessons about arriving at doors tired. Nobody signs the book. Everybody sleeps, and Kettle takes both watches and does not tell anybody until afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: The city's Warden post exists. It is manned by six Wardens of a garrison posted here nine years ago, who have heard nothing from Sarnhold since, and who come to attention when they see a charter because they have been waiting nine years to have a reason to. Their uniforms are mended and clean.

choices.label: Bring them under Thane's orders and take them with you.
Ask them why they never sent a report.
Arrest the whole post for dereliction.

nodes.body: Six Wardens brought under a Commandant's written orders, who fall in gratefully and badly. They have not drilled in nine years. They will be a liability everywhere on this mountain except in front of the crown door, and their sergeant knows both halves of that and volunteers anyway.

choices.label: Go on to the gibbets.

nodes.body: The answer comes from a sergeant who has drafted eleven reports in nine years and sent every one of them, and they went down with the couriers, on the schedule, because the couriers are the post; the schedule is the crown clerk's. None of the eleven ever arrived, and he has kept the drafts.

choices.label: Go on to the gibbets.

nodes.body: A whole Warden post is arrested for dereliction by a chartered company, which is legally sound and practically insane. It puts six men in their own cells. It also puts the company on the crown clerk's list twice over, once as arresting officers and once as the only Wardens now unaccounted for in the city.

The gibbet row in the ninth street is where the counted city hangs its criminals, and nine cages hang there, and eight are occupied; the ninth stands open with a step under it and a plate on it that has not been filled in. The cages are clean, and the row is swept, and there is a rail for the public.

choices.label: Read the plates on the eight cages.
Cut the eight down and be done with it.
Stand under the ninth cage and look up.

nodes.body: Eight plates read in order: eight names, eight crimes, and every one of the crimes the same crime, which is refusing an entry in the ninth column. All eight are dated within the last two months. The oldest of them is dated eleven days after Hollowmarch, which is when the rate doubled.

choices.label: Go on to the kennels.

nodes.body: Eight gibbet cages are cut down in the ninth street of a city of eleven thousand, which is a public act performed in public. The city does not treat it as a rescue. It treats it as arrears, because eight cages empty at the count is eight entries short, and arrears fall on whoever is standing nearest.

ending.title: Cut Down in the Ninth Street

nodes.body: The city kennels hold the crown clerk's household's hounds; they are not hounds. The kennel-master is the only man in Kar Ashen who goes armed as a matter of routine, and he is armed with a stick, a horn and a set of keys, which tells the company what he is actually for.

choices.label: Kill the kennel-master and free the kennels.
Go past the kennels along the wall.
Show him the charter and ask what they are for.
Open the kennels and let them out.

nodes.body: The kennel-master is killed at his own door, which takes eleven seconds because he is one man with a stick. It leaves the company standing between an open kennel and a street with nine hundred people in it, holding a set of keys nobody in the company knows the order of.

choices.label: Go on to the cages.
Go in and finish what is in the kennels.

nodes.body: The kennels are passed along the wall at the pace of a funeral. Nine of them come to the bars in order as the company goes by, one after another, keeping pace on the inside. None of them makes any sound at all, and that is the part Kettle mentions afterwards, twice.

choices.label: Go on to the cages.

nodes.body: The charter is shown to a kennel-master who reads it and answers without embarrassment: they are for households that run; there have been nine this year. None of the nine got further than the second street, and he does not say that as a boast, and he does not appear to think it is one.

choices.label: Go on to the cages.

nodes.body: The crown clerk's kennels are opened by a company acting on principle, in a city with nine hundred people in the street outside. Nine of them go into that street ahead of anybody's ability to warn it. What follows is not the company's fault in intention and is entirely the company's fault in fact.

A decision is taken to go into the kennels and finish what is in them, which is nine of them in a stone run eleven feet wide with one door. It is the last tactical decision anybody in the Ninth Sword makes on this street, and it is made by people who know better and do it anyway.

The cage yard behind the kennels holds nine transport cages on wheels. Four are loaded and sealed for the ninth-hour delivery. A manifest is chained to the yard gate, weather-proofed under a slate, and the yard has been swept, and the cages' wheels have been greased this week.

choices.label: Read the manifest on the gate.
Break the four loaded cages open.
Take a cage and go up in it yourselves.

nodes.body: The manifest, read at the gate: four cages, nine names, a delivery time and a destination. The destination is the crown door itself, at the ninth hour tomorrow. The names are entered in the household form, with ages, and two of them are ages the company would rather not have read.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: Four sealed transport cages are broken open in a yard behind the kennels, and nine people get out. All nine ask, immediately and unanimously, to be put back in before the yard's own count is taken. They are not hysterical about it. They explain the arithmetic, twice, and then they ask again.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.
