nodes.body: The company rides up to the crown door inside a sealed transport cage on the ninth-hour delivery, in place of the nine, which is an excellent plan for arriving. It has no provision whatsoever for the arrival, or for the fact that a sealed cage is sealed from the outside by people who count.

The city baths are dwarf-built, fed off the warm aqueduct, open to any citizen and full at midday, and they are also indifferent to a Warden company standing filthy in the doorway with four days of the spine on it, and there is a rail for kit. There is soap. There is an attendant who asks nothing.

choices.label: Take the baths and let the company be human for an hour.
Skip it; there is a door nine hours above you.

nodes.body: An hour in a dwarf bath fed by water that comes off the crown door, which nobody enjoys once Vurma says that sentence out loud, and which gets four days of the spine off five people regardless, and everybody is cleaner. Nobody is comfortable. Ilsabet washes twice and does not explain why.

choices.label: Go and find the surgeon.

nodes.body: The city surgeon is competent and has set the company's kind of injuries before. She wants nothing in return except that somebody official finally write down what she has spent nineteen years treating. She says so while she is laying out instruments, without looking up, in the tone of somebody who has rehearsed it.

choices.label: Have her treat the company properly.
Take her statement and have Ilsabet witness it.
Refuse; she reports to the ward like everyone.

nodes.body: Two hours with a competent surgeon: Dellach's forearm resewn properly, Mira's ankle strapped, everybody's frostbite dressed and two of Kettle's fingers splinted. The company is genuinely capable again for the first time since the pass. That is worth more than anything else in this city.

choices.label: Go and look at the beds.

nodes.body: A surgeon's statement, taken and witnessed: nineteen years of injuries, their pattern, their timing, and the nine cases a year that arrive on the tenth of the month having spent a night in a cage, and she signs it; she asks for a copy. She puts the copy in her own case file where it will be found.

choices.label: Go and look at the beds.

nodes.body: A city surgeon is refused on the assumption that she reports to the ward. She does, honestly and openly, because that is her post. Her ward return for the day therefore records a Warden company that declined treatment and looked ill, with a description, and the return goes up at the hour.

The surgeon's ward holds nine beds, and eight have patients in them. The ninth is made up with a chart already hanging on its rail and a name written on the chart in a clerk's hand, and the bed has been made up like that, with that chart, since before the company came down the deep stair.

choices.label: Read the name on the ninth chart.
Leave the ward; you know what it says.
Take the chart off the rail and pocket it.

nodes.body: The ninth chart, read off its rail: a name, an age, an admission date of tomorrow, and a treatment plan consisting of the single word none; the hand is the one that has signed every requisition in the company's pack. The name is one of the nine on the cage yard's manifest.

choices.label: Go on to the wyrm gate.

nodes.body: A chart is taken off a ward rail, which the surgeon reports, because a missing chart is a missing patient and she is required to account for both. The company's own description goes into a city report at the exact hour it most needed not to be in one, and the report is copied twice.

The wyrm gate stands at the counted city's lowest street, a dwarf arch with the whole city's warm air going up through it and nine lamps burning on it, and there is no guard; there has never been a guard. Beyond it the wyrm-road goes down along Ashendrel's own flank, and it is nine miles long.

choices.label: Go down the wyrm-road in order.
Go down along the scale-wall side.
Go down with the couriers at the hour.

nodes.body: The wyrm-road is a dwarf gallery cut along Ashendrel's own flank for nine miles, and the left wall is worked stone with lamp niches in it. The right wall is not a wall. It is warm, it is plated, and it moves once every nine minutes, and the dwarves cut the whole gallery to the width that movement allows.

choices.label: Take the scale-wall side and read as you go.
Fall in with the couriers on the road.
Go by the bone galleries below the road.
Take the span across the flank's fold.
Go to the eye, where the road passes its head.
Find the stewards who keep this stretch.
Go by the wing-vault at the road's shoulder.
Turn round. Nine miles of this is not survivable.

nodes.body: Nine miles of moving wall is refused inside the first two hundred yards, which is not cowardice by any definition a Warden would use in a report. The company goes back up to a counted city it cannot fix and a gate it cannot close. It does that with two irons and a folder full of certified copies.

The scale-wall stretch is plated in overlapping scale the size of doors, warm to the hand at four feet. Along the joint between rock and hide the dwarves have cut nine hundred years of inscriptions: maintenance notes, in nine hands, running the whole length of the stretch at shoulder height.

choices.label: Read the joint inscriptions as you walk.
Keep to the far wall and do not touch anything.
Put a hand flat on the scale and hold it there.
Cut a scale free and take it.

nodes.body: A mile of joint inscriptions read at walking pace, which is nine hundred years of maintenance notes on a living wall. The last hand is recent. It records that the ninth-minute movement has been increasing since autumn, gives figures, and stops in the middle of a sentence about the fold at the four-mile mark.

choices.label: Go on to the vent.
Stop and copy the last hand's notes in full.

nodes.body: A mile walked with the whole company pressed to the worked wall, touching nothing and breathing shallow. The right-hand wall moves twice in the course of it, exactly on the count, and each time the gallery narrows by about a foot and then returns to what it was.

choices.label: Go on to the vent.

nodes.body: A palm flat on warm scale for nine seconds, which is what a dwarf maintenance note instructs the reader to do. It gives a pulse, a temperature and a rhythm. Ilsabet takes all three, writes them down, and says that what she has just performed is a diagnosis and not a greeting.

choices.label: Go on to the vent.

nodes.body: A scale is cut free off the flank with a moor-iron pick, for evidence, which takes eleven minutes of quiet careful work. It leaves a gap the size of a shield in something nine miles long. Nine miles is large enough that nobody expects it to notice, and it is not large enough for that.

A stop is made in the middle of the scale-wall stretch to copy nine hundred years of notes properly, which takes an hour and forty minutes, and that is eleven ninth-minute movements. The first ten stop where the others did. The eleventh is the one the last hand's unfinished sentence was about.

A breath-vent crosses the road: a fissure in the flank that exhales every ninth minute at a temperature that has glazed the gallery roof above it into something like enamel. There is a dwarf shutter frame in the wall and no shutter in it. The frame's hinges have been greased within the year.

choices.label: Cross in the interval, one at a time.
Wedge the frame and cross under cover.
Cross now, together, and be done with it.

nodes.body: Five crossings in five intervals, counted by Ossa, each one taking eleven seconds of running and about nine years of anybody's composure. The intervals hold. She counts every one of them out loud from the far side, and her voice does not change, which is the only reason the fifth person moves at all.

choices.label: Go on to the heat stretch.

nodes.body: The shutter frame is wedged with a barrow plank and a wire line, which holds the worst of one exhalation off the road and is comprehensively destroyed by it. It buys the whole company a single crossing at once instead of five. The plank comes out of the frame in two pieces and neither piece is found.

choices.label: Go on to the heat stretch.

nodes.body: The vent is crossed together to save four intervals, by five people who have counted the rhythm for a quarter of an hour and are entirely confident in it. The ninth minute arrives on the eighth. Nobody has done anything wrong except assume that a living thing's rhythm is a clock.

The heat stretch is four hundred yards where the flank runs close and the gallery's air sits at the limit of what people can walk through; the dwarves put water butts at each end and one in the middle. The butts are stone, they are refilled from the aqueduct above, and the refilling is on a rota.

choices.label: Soak everything at the butts and walk it fast.
Wait for the flank to shift and go in the cool.
Walk it dry; it is four hundred yards.

nodes.body: Everything soaked at the butts and four hundred yards walked at a fast march, arriving at the far end steaming with the water gone out of every garment. Everybody's lips split. Nobody stops in the middle, which is the whole discipline of the stretch and the reason the middle butt exists.

choices.label: Go on to the shed skins.

nodes.body: Two hours of waiting for the flank to shift off the gallery wall, which it does. It drops the stretch to something survivable and costs the company a quarter of its remaining margin against the ninth hour. Hask, who has never been down here, says he would wait four hours, and nobody argues.

choices.label: Go on to the shed skins.

nodes.body: Four hundred yards of the heat stretch walked dry, because it is only four hundred yards; the middle butt is empty. The last hundred yards is where the road's own maintenance crews found the people who tried this before, which is recorded in the relay's book in the flat prose such books use.

A shed-skin bay opens off the road, and the city has stacked nine hundred years of Ashendrel's sheddings in it like cordwood, sorted by year, with a tally board at the door; the plates are light as horn and warm. There is a barrow in the bay for moving them and a chalk mark showing this year's stack.

choices.label: Take a plate of shed scale for evidence.
Read the tally board's years.
Leave the bay; it is a store, not a find.
Go deep into the stack to the founding-year layers.

nodes.body: A plate of shed scale the size of a shield, light as horn and warm to the hand, wrapped and lashed to the barrow. It is the single best piece of physical evidence anybody has taken off this mountain. It cannot be argued with, cannot be forged, and cannot be explained by anybody's paperwork.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: The tally board, read at the bay door: nine hundred years of shed years, one entry per nine; the last three entries are close together rather than nine years apart. The last of the three is dated this autumn, and somebody has put a query mark beside it in a different chalk.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: A dig back through nine hundred years of stacked shed scale to reach the founding layers, which are at the bottom under everything else. It is a bay with one door and a stack that has been settling since the legion, and the settling has been waiting for exactly this kind of curiosity.

A courier post on the road: nine bunks, a lamp rack, a tally desk, and four couriers eating a meal. They look up at a Warden company with the mild interest of civil servants whose office has received an unexpected visitor, and one of them stands to fetch two more cups without being asked.

choices.label: Sit down and eat with them.
Show the charter and ask for their schedule.
Take them prisoner and get the schedule that way.

nodes.body: A meal shared with four couriers on the wyrm-road, which produces the schedule, the hours, the crown door's routine, and one piece of advice about the ninth minute at the fold. That advice saves somebody's life within the hour, and the courier who gives it does not know he is doing anything remarkable.

choices.label: Go on to the file.

nodes.body: A charter shown, and a schedule handed over without argument by people who consider themselves entirely legitimate. They have no reason not to. They add a copy of the crown door's maintenance rota, unasked, and offer to walk the company down as far as the tithe hall, which is the end of their stretch.

choices.label: Go on to the file.

nodes.body: Four couriers are taken prisoner on the wyrm-road for a schedule they would have handed over on request. The post fails to report at the hour. A road whose whole arithmetic is hours notices a missing report considerably faster than it notices a missing person, and it notices this one within nine minutes.

The ninth-hour file comes up the wyrm-road: nine lamps, nine carriers, four sealed cages on a trolley, and a steward at the head of it with a book. He has the company's number in the book. He has had it since the ward gatehouse, and he checks it against the company as he comes up.

choices.label: Stop the file and open the cages.
Stand aside and let it pass; count it.
Fall in behind it and follow it down.
Kill the steward and scatter the carriers.

nodes.body: The file is stopped and four cages opened, and nine people get out and stand in a dwarf gallery, entirely unwilling to go either up or down. Both directions are somebody's arrears. The steward waits with his book open while the argument happens, and makes a note of its duration.

choices.label: Go on to the relay.
Send them back up the road on their own.

nodes.body: The file counted past at eleven feet: nine lamps, nine carriers, four cages, one steward. Every one of the carriers is somebody the company saw in a ward market two days ago, and two of them nod, politely, in passing, because they were sold bread by the same stall.

choices.label: Go on to the relay.

nodes.body: The file followed down at forty paces on its own rhythm, which teaches the company the door's approach, the steward's routine, and the precise place on the road where the carriers stop being carriers. It is a hundred yards short of the tithe hall, and it is marked, and the mark is dwarf work.

choices.label: Go on to the relay.

nodes.body: A steward is killed on the wyrm-road and nine carriers are scattered into a nine-mile gallery with a living wall down one side of it. It is a rescue in intention and a dispersal in fact. None of the nine reaches either end of the road, and the company hears two of them for a long time.

Nine freed people are sent back up the road alone and unescorted, with the city's own count due at the hour. Between them and any street they know are the crown clerk's kennels. The company understands the arithmetic of that about ten minutes after the last of them is out of sight.

A relay station is cut into the worked wall: a lamp rack, a rota board, a water butt, and a dwarf plaque listing the road's maintenance standards in nine clauses. The plaque is bronze and it is polished. Somebody polishes it, on a rota, and the rota for the polishing is on the board.

choices.label: Read the nine clauses on the plaque.
Sign the rota and go on.
Take the rota board off the wall.

nodes.body: Nine maintenance clauses read off dwarf bronze: temperature limits, the shutter schedule, the ninth-minute discipline, and clause nine. Clause nine specifies what must never be carried past this point and gives the reason. The reason is one sentence long and it is about irons, and the company is carrying two.

choices.label: Go on to the lamp store.

nodes.body: A rota board is taken off a relay wall on the wyrm-road, which is how the whole stretch knows which shutters are wedged and which butts are filled; the next shift needs it in about four hours. The next shift comes down anyway, without it, on the assumption that the board is where boards are.

The road's lamp store holds nine hundred reservoirs on dwarf shelving, filled and sealed, enough to light this gallery for a century. Nine of them stand on a separate shelf at the end. Those nine have names written into the wax of their seals, and the writing is recent and the names are legible.

choices.label: Take the nine named reservoirs.
Take plain reservoirs for the company and go.
Leave the store alone entirely.
Break every reservoir on the shelves.

nodes.body: Nine named reservoirs taken off a separate shelf, each sealed with a name pressed into the wax. Nyre reads them aloud one at a time as they come down. She stops reading aloud after the fourth, and puts the remaining five into the pack herself, and writes all nine into her book afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: Four plain reservoirs taken and signed for in the store book, which is the correct procedure and takes a minute. The store book is audited by the crown clerk's household every ninth day. The company's hand is now in it, dated, with the quantity, in the middle of a page of ordinary withdrawals.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: Nine hundred sealed reservoirs are broken on dwarf shelving to deny the road its light, which takes a quarter of an hour of committed work. The store floods with oil. Dwarf floors drain toward the flank rather than away from it, for reasons the founding volume explains in a clause nobody has read.

The bone galleries lie below the road: nine hundred years of what the arrangement has not digested, stacked and sorted by the city, with a working ledger at the entrance and a lamp above the ledger. The stacks are labelled by year. The labels are municipal tags, wired on, in the ward's own numbering.

choices.label: Read the bone ledger's last nine pages.
Take a labelled bone for the inquiry.
Go straight through and up to the road.
Go deeper, to where the stacks are still warm.

nodes.body: Nine pages of a bone ledger, read at the entrance: a mortality record kept to municipal standard for nine hundred years. This century includes four Warden patrols and nine Reckoning couriers. All of them are tagged, shelved and cross-referenced to the archive's index by household and year.

choices.label: Go on to the gullet.

nodes.body: One labelled femur taken with its municipal tag still wired to it. It is an evidentiary object of a kind no Warden court has ever been offered. A bone with a city's own reference number on it, cross-referenced to a ledger, in a series that runs for nine hundred years without a gap.

choices.label: Go on to the gullet.

nodes.body: A walk deeper into the bone galleries, to where the stacks are still warm, which is where this season's are; at that depth it is not a store. It is a working area, with a schedule, and the schedule's next entry is at the ninth hour, and the company is standing in the middle of the workspace.

Where the flank folds, the gallery has to pass through the fold: forty feet of dwarf tube with hide above and below it, and a shutter at each end. Both shutters work. Both are meant to be set by hand before anybody crosses, and the setting takes about a minute each, and the interval is nine.

choices.label: Go through in the interval with both shutters set.
Go through fast with the shutters left open.
Send the barrow through first and watch it.

nodes.body: Both shutters set by hand and forty feet crossed in a single interval, which is exactly how the road was designed to be used. It works precisely as designed, which is the first time in three books that anything has done that, and Vurma says so on the far side with real feeling.

choices.label: Go on to the teeth.

nodes.body: Forty feet crossed at a run with both shutters left open, which is nine seconds of the worst heat and pressure anybody in the company has felt. Everybody survives it. Everybody's eyebrows are gone, and Halt's coat is scorched through at the shoulder, and nobody suggests going back for the barrow.

choices.label: Go on to the teeth.

nodes.body: The barrow is sent through the fold first as a test, which is sensible, and the fold closes on it at the fourth second rather than the ninth. That tells the company the interval has changed, and does not tell them what it has changed to, and the road has four more folds on it.

The tooth gallery is where the road passes a mouth-fold, and nine of the teeth stand through the worked wall like pillars, and they are polished at hand height by nine hundred years of couriers touching them for luck; the ninth is the most polished. There is a worn patch in the floor in front of it.

choices.label: Walk it without touching anything.
Touch the ninth tooth, as everybody does.
Sound the teeth with a hammer and listen.
Take a tooth chip for Ilsabet.

nodes.body: A gallery walked with everybody's hands in their armpits, which is the only sensible way to walk it. It takes eleven minutes and feels a great deal longer. Nobody touches anything, and at the far end Mira asks whether the luck works, and nobody in the company has an answer for her.

choices.label: Go on to the nest.
Go back and touch it after all.

nodes.body: The ninth tooth touched the way nine hundred years of couriers have touched it, palm flat, briefly. It produces nothing at all: a smooth patch under the hand, a slight change in the gallery's air, and a very small sound from somewhere further down the road that does not repeat.

choices.label: Go on to the nest.

nodes.body: The teeth sounded with a hammer and listened to along the wall, which tells Vurma the fold's thickness and the flank's tension. It also tells her one further thing, which she does not say out loud until the company is past the gallery and then says twice, in different words both times.

choices.label: Go on to the nest.

nodes.body: A tooth chip is taken with a hammer and a cold chisel, in a gallery where nine hundred years of couriers have known better than to try. The fold's response arrives before the second blow lands, which means it did not arrive because of the second blow, and everybody understands that at once.

A return is made down the gallery to touch the ninth tooth after all, because the company has come nine miles and somebody wants the luck. The tooth is warmer on the second visit than it was on the first. It is the only thing in the gallery that has changed, and it has changed for one person.

A stewards' nest is built into the flank's fold: nine bunks, a stove, a small shrine, and nine of the crown clerk's household asleep in shifts between deliveries, and the stove is lit, and there is a kettle on it. The shrine has nine niches and eight tokens, and the ninth niche is warm.

choices.label: Go past them in their sleep.
Wake the shift leader and talk to him.
Take the nest quietly, one bunk at a time.
Fire the nest and go on down.

nodes.body: Nine sleeping stewards passed at the pace of a minute hand, in single file, with the barrow carried rather than wheeled; the ninth of them is awake the whole time. His eyes are open and he watches the company go by without moving at all, and he does not raise the alarm.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.
Go back and deal with the one who was awake.

nodes.body: A shift leader woken and spoken to, who turns out to be a working man of fifty with a family in the counted city. He answers every question put to him. He asks in return only that the company not make his shift late, because a late shift is arrears and arrears fall on the shift.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: A nest taken one bunk at a time, in silence, which works for eight of them. It is the ugliest eleven minutes in three books. Nobody in the company ever describes it to anybody afterwards, including in the report, where it appears as one sentence with no adjectives in it.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: A stewards' nest is fired in a fold of the flank, which puts smoke into a gallery whose only ventilation is the flank's own breathing. The flank breathes in. It takes about a minute and a half, and the company is in the same gallery as the smoke for all of it.

A return is made to deal with the steward who was awake, which is the correct tactical instinct and is why tactical instincts should be examined. It puts the company back inside a nest of nine, of whom eight are now also awake, in a chamber with one door and a stove between them and it.

A dwarf bridge crosses a fissure in the flank where the road cannot follow the hide: two hundred feet of span over something that is not rock and is not still. The deck is sound and the parapet is intact. The road standard, cut into the abutment, is two people at a time, and it has been obeyed for nine hundred years.

choices.label: Cross two at a time as the road standard requires.
Cross all together, quickly, and be over it.
Go down into the fissure and across the bottom.

nodes.body: Three crossings of two on a dwarf span over a fissure that exhales twice while the company is on it. Everybody survives. Nobody looks down, which takes discipline on a span with a parapet you can see through, and Dellach goes last and takes the longest and says nothing at all afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the span's far works.

nodes.body: The whole company crosses at once against the road's own standard, and the span carries them, because dwarves built it to carry a train. It costs everybody a memory they did not want, which is the moment in the middle when the fissure exhales and the deck's ring changes pitch under five sets of boots.

choices.label: Go on to the span's far works.

nodes.body: A descent is made into the fissure to cross at the bottom, on the reasonable grounds that a bottom is more solid than a span; the bottom of this fissure is the part of the flank that the fissure is in. That is obvious from the third rung down and the rope is above the second.

The span's far works hold a dwarf winch house, a stack of replacement timbers dated by century, and a maintenance crew's hut with a kettle still warm on its stove; the hut door is open. The log is on the table under a lamp, and the last entry in it stops in the middle of a sentence.

choices.label: Search the hut and read the crew's log.
Take the winch's wire rope; you will want it.
Wait for the crew to come back to the kettle.
Cut the span behind you and burn the timbers.

nodes.body: The crew's log, read at their own table: nine hundred years of span repairs in a professional hand. The current entry stops mid-sentence. The sentence is about a movement in the fissure that has no precedent in the book, and the writer had got as far as giving it a measurement.

choices.label: Go on to the pillars.
Wait for whoever was writing it.

nodes.body: Ninety feet of dwarf wire rope taken off a winch drum, which is the single most useful object on the wyrm-road and weighs forty pounds. Vurma carries it herself, coiled across her chest, without being asked and without complaining, for the remaining four miles.

choices.label: Go on to the pillars.

nodes.body: Two hours in a warm hut waiting for a maintenance crew that does not come back; the kettle goes cold. The log entry stays mid-sentence under the lamp, and at the end of the two hours Ilsabet closes the log, which she says afterwards was the only respectful thing available.

choices.label: Go on to the pillars.

nodes.body: A dwarf span is cut behind the company and the replacement timbers fired, to close the road. It works. It also strands the company nine miles down a gallery with one exit and removes the only route by which anybody could ever come down to it, which was the road's other purpose.

A wait is kept for whoever was writing the log, and at the ninth minute the fissure's movement arrives, and the writer comes back up out of it to finish the sentence. He has the pen. He finishes the sentence, and the measurement in it is correct, and he does not stop when the company speaks to him.

The pillar hall is where the dwarves propped the gallery roof: nine hundred years of columns, each one carved with the year of its raising and the names of the crew who raised it. There are forty of them. The newest is this spring's, and its stone is a different colour from all the others.

choices.label: Read the last nine columns' inscriptions.
Walk the hall and touch nothing.
Cut a column's inscription out for the record.

nodes.body: Nine column inscriptions read, one per century, in order, which is a labour history of this gallery. The last one was raised this spring by a crew of nine whose names are cut into it. The ninth name has been chiselled out again afterwards, cleanly, by somebody who knew how to do it.

choices.label: Go on to the camp.

nodes.body: An inscription is cut out of a load-bearing dwarf column for the record, which removes eleven pounds of stone from a pillar holding a gallery roof under a mountain. The pillar accepts that for about four hours. The company is two miles further down the road when it stops accepting it.

A dwarf way-camp stands in the pillar hall: benches, a flue that vents somewhere clever, water from a cistern, and nine bunks with blankets folded on eight of them. The ninth bunk's blanket is on the floor beside it, folded differently, by somebody in a hurry who then did not come back.

choices.label: Take six hours and the flue.
Press on; the door is four miles down.

nodes.body: Six hours in a dwarf way-camp with a working flue, taken by a company that has learned to take them. It is the last sleep anybody in the Ninth Sword gets before the crown door. Everybody knows that at the time, and everybody sleeps anyway, which is its own kind of professionalism.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: The road passes the head in a worked gallery with one wall of dwarf stone and one wall that has an eye in it. The eye is nine feet across and lidded. The lid has been open since autumn, according to the relay's book, and the gallery has a ledge cut below the sight-line for people who would rather not be seen.

choices.label: Stand in front of it and let it look at you.
Go past below the sight-line, on your belly.
Speak to it. It is awake and it is listening.

nodes.body: Nine minutes standing in front of a nine-foot eye that does not blink and does not move, because it does not need to do either. At the end of it every person in the company knows, without being told and without discussing it, that they have been counted individually rather than as five.

choices.label: Go on to the dream gallery.

nodes.body: A hundred yards crossed on bellies below the sight-line with packs pushed ahead, and the dwarves cut the ledge for exactly this and nine hundred years of couriers have used it; it works. Halfway along, Kettle stops and puts her forehead on the stone for four seconds and then goes on.

choices.label: Go on to the dream gallery.

nodes.body: A company captain speaks aloud to a nine-foot eye in a dwarf gallery, and is answered. The answer does not arrive as sound. It arrives as arithmetic, laid into the head directly, and it is an offer with a term, a rate and a security, and the security is standing in the gallery.

The dream gallery lies below the head, and nine hundred years of couriers have written on its walls what they heard here: in nine hands, in eleven languages, layered over each other. It is all the same three sentences. Ossa has seen the wall before and has never read the sentences, and says so.

choices.label: Read the walls properly with Ilsabet.
Walk it fast with your ears stopped.
Add your own line to the wall.

nodes.body: The wall read properly with a lamp and a translator: the same three sentences in eleven languages, which are an offer, a term and a price. Every courier who has ever walked this gallery has heard them, in their own tongue, in their own head, and has come out and written them down.

choices.label: Go on to the whisper stretch.

nodes.body: A line is added to nine hundred years of the dream gallery's wall by somebody in the company who wanted to answer. The answer is read. That is what the gallery is for and always has been: not a memorial, but a correspondence, and the correspondence has been one-sided for nine hundred years until now.

The whisper stretch runs four hundred yards where the flank's breathing makes words out of the gallery's echoes, and the words come in the voices of people the company has buried. It is not a trick of the ear. Everybody hears different voices, and everybody's voices are accurate, including the pauses.

choices.label: Walk it with the count called aloud to drown it.
Walk it in silence and let it say what it says.
Answer the voice that sounds like Ferrin.

nodes.body: Four hundred yards walked with Kettle calling a marching count aloud the whole way, which drowns most of it and does not drown all of it. Everybody afterwards agrees that it worked. Nobody afterwards says which of the voices got through, and Kettle's count does not falter once in four hundred yards.

choices.label: Go on to the pact ledge.

nodes.body: Four hundred yards walked in silence, listening, because the alternative is walking through it deaf. Everybody hears something different. Nobody discusses it. Nyre stops once, halfway, for about three seconds, and then walks on, and nobody asks her about it then or afterwards.

choices.label: Go on to the pact ledge.

nodes.body: A voice is answered in the whisper stretch, because it sounded like somebody's brother and it used the name he used. The answering is the transaction. The rest of the company walks the remaining four hundred yards alone, and arrives at the far end at the correct strength minus one.

A dwarf ledge widens the road below the head, and here the flank's own voice comes clearly. It is the place the offer is made, and the ledge has been cut wide for it, with a bench, because the offer takes some time to state properly and has been stated nine times before to nine hands.

choices.label: Hear the terms out in full and write them down.
Refuse to hear them and walk on down the road.
Accept the terms on the spot.

nodes.body: The terms heard out in full and written down by a hedge-thaumaturge whose hand shakes for the first time in three books, and the count ends; the doors open. The arrears of nine hundred years are paid once, in one payment, and the frontier is free of the whole arrangement afterwards, permanently.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: The terms refused unheard, out loud, by a captain who has learned in three books what merely hearing an offer costs. The flank accepts the refusal without any apparent interest in it, which is worse than argument. The bench on the ledge stays empty and the road goes on down.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door road.

nodes.body: Terms are accepted on a dwarf ledge without being written down. The company has been nine miles inside a living thing and cannot reasonably be blamed for wanting it over. The payment begins immediately, because immediately was one of the terms, and nobody had written the terms down.

A steward station stands at the road's four-mile mark: nine of the crown clerk's household with a rota, a lamp rack and a ledger. None of them is armed. None of them is afraid of a Warden company, and the senior of them stands up and asks whether the company would like the rota read out.

choices.label: Take the station by force and hold it.
Go past on the charter and let them log it.
Have Nyre put the Reckoning's own question to them.
Kill them all; they are the arrangement.

nodes.body: A station taken by force from nine unarmed civil servants, which takes ninety seconds and involves no weapons. The company finds it harder afterwards than any fight in three books, and two of them say so out loud, and Hask, who has been a Warden for twenty years, says nothing at all.

choices.label: Go on to the tithe hall.
Make them sign the station over formally.

nodes.body: A charter presented at a steward station, logged, countersigned and handed back with directions. They add a warning about the ninth minute at the fold and an offer of hot water, and the senior steward walks the company to the edge of his stretch and points out the marker where his rota ends.

choices.label: Go on to the tithe hall.

nodes.body: The Reckoning's own question is put to nine stewards by a sister of the order, in the form her rule prescribes. Four of them cannot answer it. One of them answers by resigning his post on the spot, in writing, on the station's own paper, and walking up the road alone without a lamp.

choices.label: Go on to the tithe hall.

nodes.body: Nine unarmed stewards are killed at a station four miles from the crown door, because they are the arrangement. That is true. It also turns a Warden company into the thing the counted city has always said would come down the road one day, and the city's version of the story is now correct.

A station is signed over formally under duress by nine civil servants, in triplicate, with the company's names on all three copies. It is a document that will be read at an inquiry with exactly the emphasis anybody would expect. One of the three copies goes up the road within the hour.

The tithe hall is the road's last widening: nine alcoves where the ninth-hour deliveries wait their turn, four of them occupied, and a steward with a book calling the order, and the alcoves have benches. The occupied ones are quiet. The steward calls the order the way a clerk calls a queue.

choices.label: Stop the calling and empty the alcoves.
Ask the steward how the order is decided.
Take the book and read the whole delivery order.

nodes.body: The steward explains the order of calling: by arrears, oldest first, with households given nine days' notice served by the chapel, and he has served four hundred of those notices. He does not enjoy it. He has a system for it, and he explains the system, because it is the part he can defend.

choices.label: Go on to the shrine.

nodes.body: A delivery book taken and read: nine hundred years of order, kept properly. Today's page has four names on it. Tomorrow's page has five, and five is not a number this book has used in nine hundred years, and the fifth entry is a company rather than a household.

choices.label: Go on to the shrine.

nodes.body: A tithe hall's calling is stopped and four alcoves emptied by force; four people will not leave the hall. The steward enters the interruption in his book, with the time, and then calls the next four, because there is a next four and the hall has nine alcoves and only four were full.

The road's own shrine stands at the last bend: dwarf work, older than the Compact, with nine niches, and eight hold founding tokens. Under the ninth there is a plate, and the plate is in the founder's own hand, which nobody in the counted city has been able to read for four hundred years.

choices.label: Read the plate under the ninth niche.
Put one of your own irons in the ninth niche.
Leave the shrine; you have read three of these.

nodes.body: The founder's plate read: not a dedication but an instruction. It tells whoever holds the ninth hand what the office is actually for, in four sentences, and then it says what happens on the day nobody holds it. The fourth sentence is the reason the founders built the door with a hollow behind it.

choices.label: Go on to the lamplighter.

nodes.body: One of the company's own carried irons is set in the road shrine's ninth niche. The niche accepts it. So does the road's whole arithmetic, immediately and without comment, and the iron is now in somebody else's schedule, in a niche, four hundred yards from a door it was not cut for.

The road's last lamplighter is a woman of sixty who has walked this stretch every ninth day for forty years. She knows the interval, the fold, the eye and the door. She is not afraid of any of them and she is not sentimental about any of them, and she is carrying a pole and a wick knife.

choices.label: Ask her to walk the company down to the door.
Ask her what she has seen at the door itself.
Ask her to come down the mountain and testify.

nodes.body: Forty years of the wyrm-road's experience walking at the head of the company for the last four miles, correcting three things in the first quarter mile. It is worth more than the wire rope, the charter and both irons together. She does it because she was asked politely and nobody ever asks her anything.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door.

nodes.body: Her account of the door: the ring, the hours, the household, the four deliveries a month. And the one time in forty years that the ring was opened, and what came out of it, and how far up the road it got before it was persuaded back, and who did the persuading and what it cost him.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door.

nodes.body: A lamplighter of forty years' standing is asked to leave the road and testify, and she refuses, and her reason is one sentence about the ninth day and who lights the lamps if she is not there to light them; it is not a rhetorical question. She waits for an answer to it, and there is not one.

The wing-vault is at the road's shoulder, where the flank's forelimb folds against the rock. The dwarves cut the gallery through the fold with nine props and cut a warning into the lintel above it. The warning is in three languages and the third is the founders' hand, and it is the shortest of the three.

choices.label: Read the lintel warning and obey it.
Go through fast on the props' inside line.
Wait for the fold to open and go in the gap.
Cut a prop out; it is in the way of the barrow.

nodes.body: The lintel warning read and obeyed to the letter: through in threes, on the ninth minute, hands off the props. It is the only method by which anybody has ever come out of this vault, which the warning says in its second sentence, and which nine hundred years of practice has not improved on.

choices.label: Go on to the claw gallery.
Go back for the barrow through the vault.

nodes.body: The props' inside line taken at speed, which is eleven feet from the fold and works. Everybody's ears ring afterwards from a movement that happens a yard behind the last person through, and the last person through is Halt, who does not speak for the next quarter of an hour.

choices.label: Go on to the claw gallery.

nodes.body: The fold's opening waited for and then used, which costs forty minutes. It gives the company a clean, wide, entirely undramatic crossing. Vurma calls it the first competent thing anybody has done today, which is unfair to three other people and which nobody bothers to contest.

choices.label: Go on to the claw gallery.

nodes.body: A dwarf prop is cut out of a wing-vault because the barrow will not fit past it; the vault has nine props and moves on a nine-minute count, and it was cut with nine because nine is what it takes. The eight that remain hold for two of those counts, which is longer than anybody expected.

A return is made through the wing-vault for the barrow, alone, on the ninth minute, by somebody who counted correctly on the way through the first time. On the way back he counts from the wrong end of the interval, which is an error of about four seconds and is the whole margin the vault allows.

The claw gallery is where a foreclaw the size of a gatehouse comes through the worked wall, and the dwarves have cut the road around it with nine feet of clearance. The clearance is measured and marked on the floor. It was nine feet when it was cut and it is nine feet now, which is the reassuring part.

choices.label: Take the nine feet of clearance carefully.
Go over the claw where the road is widest.
Wait; it moved last week and may move again.

nodes.body: Nine feet of clearance taken one at a time, with the barrow passed hand to hand around the claw's curve. It is exactly as much clearance as the dwarves said and not one inch more. Everybody's back is to the stone for the whole passage, and nobody's coat touches anything.

choices.label: Go on to the hoard.

nodes.body: The claw climbed over at the road's widest point, which is quicker by four minutes and puts five people's boots on something that has not been walked on since the founding. It notices being walked on. It does not do anything about it, which is not the same as not noticing.

choices.label: Go on to the hoard.

nodes.body: An hour is spent waiting to see whether a foreclaw will move again, in a gallery whose only feature is the claw. It moves at the fifty-first minute, in a direction the dwarves did not cut clearance for, which is the direction they cut the gallery's roof line to allow instead.

The hoard bay is not treasure. It is nine hundred years of what the counted city has sent down and Ashendrel has not consumed: sorted, stacked, catalogued by the stewards, and shelved by year, with a desk at the entrance and a catalogue on the desk in nine volumes.

choices.label: Take the catalogue and nothing else.
Take what is portable and valuable.
Take nothing and go on to the door.
Look for the two Warden patrols in the stacks.

nodes.body: A nine-hundred-year catalogue taken off a steward's desk: four pounds of it, in nine volumes, in a professional hand. It is a receipt for everything the frontier has paid into this mountain. It is also the only document in existence that names all of it, item by item, with dates and provenance.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door.

nodes.body: Forty pounds of portable value taken out of a hoard bay by people who have not been paid since Sarnhold. It is fair salvage by every free-company standard on the frontier. It will read very badly in a report, and Nyre says so while it is being loaded, and it is loaded anyway.

choices.label: Go on to the crown door.

nodes.body: The hoard stacks are searched for the two lost Warden patrols, and they are found: catalogued, tagged, shelved by year, in good order. The company is standing in front of that shelf when the ninth-hour delivery arrives at the bay to add to it, on schedule, with a trolley and a book.

The last bend of the wyrm-road opens on the crown door of Kar Ashen, standing in a socket ring at the end of it, and nine sockets, and eight filled; the ninth worn bright and empty. Behind you are nine miles of flank, and on the other side of that door is whatever the flank is attached to.

choices.label: Go up to the ring and look at the sockets.
Speak to it before you touch anything.
Walk straight into the ring and get it done.

nodes.body: The socket ring is a dwarf chamber the size of a chapel, with the crown door in one wall and nine sockets set in a ring around it. Eight are filled and warm. The whole apparatus is in daily working use: there is a rota on the wall, a clerk's desk with a lamp on it, a scaffold on the frame and a gallery above with people standing at the rail.

choices.label: Go to the sockets and read the ring.
Find the keeper's chair and whoever sits in it.
Answer the voice that has started speaking.
Deal with the stewards working the ring.
Look at the last works: the die, the forge, the wedge.
Go to the masons' scaffold on the door frame.
Find the watchers in the gallery above.
Walk out. You have seen enough to report.

nodes.body: The socket ring is seen, counted and left. The company walks nine miles back up a living gallery with a complete description of the crown door, a folder of certified copies, two irons that fit nothing here, and nothing done. Thane files the description. It is the best intelligence the Wardens have ever had and it changes nothing at all.

At arm's length the ring resolves into detail: eight founding irons seated in eight warm sockets, each with a tally cut into its exposed face. The ninth socket is empty and worn bright around the mouth. In the floor in front of it there is a groove worn by nine hundred years of somebody standing in exactly one place.

choices.label: Read the tallies on the eight seated irons.
Measure the ninth socket against your own two.
Test the eighth iron's seating with a hand.
Draw an iron now, while nobody is looking.

nodes.body: Eight tallies read at arm's length, one per iron, and they are not eight marks of ownership. They are eight parts of one instruction, and read in order they say exactly what the ninth iron is required to say and why. Ilsabet reads them twice and then puts her hand out for the company's own two irons.

choices.label: Go on to the eighth socket.
Read them again in the reverse order.

nodes.body: The ninth socket measured against Kar Duhn's iron and Hollowmarch's, with a wire and a straight edge, and both fit the socket's gauge. Neither fits its tally, which is cut for this door and no other. That tells the company precisely what the crown door will accept and precisely what it will not.

choices.label: Go on to the eighth socket.

nodes.body: A hand laid flat on the eighth iron's seating: warm, firm, and moving a sixteenth of an inch under the palm on the nine-count; the maintenance notes call that working properly. It is the first time in three books that anybody has touched one of these things while it was doing its job.

choices.label: Go on to the eighth socket.

nodes.body: An iron is drawn out of the crown ring on impulse while nobody appears to be looking, in a chamber that has been continuously staffed for nine hundred years. Nobody has ever needed to look. The ring itself keeps the count, and it registers a socket going empty considerably faster than any of the people in the room do.

Eight tallies are read again in reverse order, which is not how they are meant to be read, and the founders' plate says they must never be read that way, in a clause nobody in the counted city can translate. In reverse they are not a set of instructions. They are a sentence, and reading it aloud completes it.

The eighth socket is the one the maintenance rota lists as due; its iron stands a sixteenth proud of the collar. The stone collar around it is cracked in a curve, and a mason's chalk mark rings the crack with this week's date beside it, and the lead pot on the forge is already warm.

choices.label: Pack the crack with lead as the rota says.
Leave it; a chalk mark means somebody is coming.
Draw the eighth iron and look at the collar.

nodes.body: A cracked collar packed with lead off the barrow by a company that has read the rota and can follow instructions. It takes an hour of unglamorous work with a ladle and a cold chisel. It is the single most useful hour anybody spends in this chamber, and the mason says so afterwards, twice.

choices.label: Go on to the ninth iron.

nodes.body: A chalk mark left alone and the mason's arrival waited for, which costs two hours. What it produces is a mason, his apprentice, and a conversation about the crack that changes the company's plan entirely, because he explains what the crack means and what it will do and how long the door has.

choices.label: Go on to the ninth iron.

nodes.body: The eighth iron is drawn to inspect a cracked collar, which is exactly the inspection the rota forbids, for exactly this reason. The collar goes the rest of the way as the iron clears it. The rota's wording, which nobody read to the end, was that the collar carries the iron and not the reverse.

The ninth iron is in the chamber and not in the door: cut, tallied, and held in a rack under the keeper's own hand, waiting for the appointment of a hand to seat it; there is a plate above the rack. The rack has nine slots and eight are empty, and the ninth iron sits in the ninth slot.

choices.label: Take the ninth iron off the rack.
Read the appointment plate above the rack.
Leave it in the rack; it is not loose by accident.
Take the rack, the plate and the iron together.

nodes.body: The crown iron off the rack and into a hand: founding gauge, cut with the crown tally, its flank filed blank where a name goes. The whole chamber's arithmetic turns, quietly and without any drama at all, toward whoever is holding it. Everybody in the room notices the turn, including the people at the rail.

choices.label: Go on to the collar plate.

nodes.body: The appointment plate, read above the rack: an office, a term of nine years, a set of duties in nine clauses, and a signature line. Across the signature line somebody has written the word held, in a hand that has been holding it for nineteen years, which is twice the term the plate specifies.

choices.label: Go on to the collar plate.

nodes.body: The rack, the plate and the iron are all taken together, on the sound principle that evidence should be complete. That removes the entire appointment apparatus of a nine-hundred-year office in one movement. It also constitutes the appointment, because the apparatus is not a record of the office and never was.

Above the ring the door's collar plate is dwarf bronze with nine clauses on it: the founding specification of what this door is, what it holds, and what the nine hands are for; it is polished. It has been polished, on a rota, by people who cannot read it, for four hundred years.

choices.label: Read all nine clauses with Ilsabet.
Read only the ninth clause.
Prise the plate off; it is the whole case.

nodes.body: Nine clauses read in full: containment, maintenance, the schedule, the hands, the arrears. Then clause nine, which describes what the founders expected to happen on the day the count stopped, and what they built into the door against that day. It is the most useful sentence anybody has read in three books.

choices.label: Go on to the decision.

nodes.body: A founding collar plate is prised off a door frame with a moor-iron pick, because it is the whole case and cases need exhibits. It is not a plaque. It is a fitting, and it has been holding the frame's upper collar into the rock since the founding, and the frame has been spreading since autumn.

The keeper's chair is a clerk's chair at a clerk's desk beside the ring, and it is occupied. The crown clerk of Kar Ashen is working through a delivery ledger by lamplight, nineteen years into a nine-year term. He looks up when the company comes in, and marks his place, and does not stand.

choices.label: Sit down opposite him and let him talk.
Show him the charter and take the desk.
Put a knife in front of him and ask for the iron.

nodes.body: Two hours opposite a man who has kept a wyrm's accounts for nineteen years. He is courteous, exhausted and entirely lucid. He has been waiting nine years for a Warden company to sit down and ask him something, and when it happens he answers every question in order and asks for nothing in return.

choices.label: Go on to the signet.

nodes.body: A charter put on the crown clerk's desk, which he reads, initials and files in the correct box. Then he explains what it changes, which is nothing: the office is not a Warden appointment, has never been one, and the ring does not read charters. He says all of that without any satisfaction at all.

choices.label: Go on to the signet.

nodes.body: A knife is put down in front of the crown clerk of Kar Ashen; he looks at it. Then he goes on writing, because the one thing nineteen years in that chair has taught him is exactly how little a knife matters in this chamber, and he explains that too, while he writes, without looking up.

The keeper's signet lies on the desk beside the ledger: nine-sided, warm, sized for whoever picks it up; the initials of the last four holders have worn off the shank. There is a hollow in the desk's wood where it has sat, and the hollow is deeper than nineteen years of one man's work.

choices.label: Take the signet off the desk.
Read the shank's worn initials.
Leave it; you have seen this twice.
Put it on to see whether it fits.

nodes.body: The signet taken off a working desk and put in a pocket rather than on a hand, which the crown clerk permits without comment. He enters it in his ledger as a transfer pending appointment, dates it, and then asks the captain to confirm the spelling of the company's name for the entry.

choices.label: Go on to the book.

nodes.body: Four sets of initials read off a worn shank by lamplight. Three are meaningless. The fourth belongs to a Reckoning legate who came up to Sarnhold with a coach and a writ, and who is at this moment somewhere in this chamber, and who has therefore held this office before and put it down again.

choices.label: Go on to the book.

nodes.body: A nine-sided signet is put on a finger to see whether it fits, and it fits exactly, as it has for nineteen holders. There is no ceremony. There has never been a ceremony. Putting it on is the appointment procedure in its entirety, which is written on the plate above the rack in the founders' hand.

The crown ledger lies open on the desk: eleven hundred pages in nine hands, the current hand nineteen years old. There are four blank pages at the back. After them there is a ruled column with a heading, and the heading is for a tenth hand, and the ruling was done in the founders' century.

choices.label: Read the last nine pages.
Read the four blank pages' headings.
Take the ledger off the desk and carry it.

nodes.body: Nine pages read over a clerk's shoulder: this month's deliveries, next month's notices. A standing entry for the crown door's own maintenance signed by the same hand every ninth day. The maintenance entry has been signed nine hundred years without a gap, in nine hands, and every hand signed it personally.

choices.label: Go and see the office rota.

nodes.body: The crown ledger is taken off the desk of a working clerk. He allows it, and notes it, and hands over the pen with it. The company is now carrying the only document that can appoint or discharge a ninth hand, which means the appointment is now in the company's baggage rather than in the chamber.

The office, explained by the man holding it: nine years' term, nine duties, a house in the counted city, a stipend paid quarterly, and a clause about what happens to the holder's household if the count is not kept. He explains the first four in a minute and takes eleven on the fifth.

choices.label: Ask what the household clause actually means.
Ask him why he took it in the first place.
Ask him whether he wants to be relieved.

nodes.body: The household clause, explained without evasion: the holder's family stands as surety and is entered in the ninth column on appointment. It is removed from the column only when the successor's family is entered. His own family has been in it for nineteen years, which is why the term has not ended.

choices.label: Go on to the decision.

nodes.body: The answer to why he took it: he was twenty-six, and the alternative was his sister taking it, and she had a child; the appointment plate had been on the rack for a month with the family's name already on it. He says all of that in about nine words and then goes back to the ledger.

choices.label: Go on to the decision.

nodes.body: The crown clerk is asked whether he wants to be relieved of the office. He answers yes, without hesitation, for the first time in nineteen years. Procedurally, that answer is the beginning of the appointment of whoever asked the question, and the plate above the rack sets out the rest of the procedure.

The door's own voice is not sound. It arrives in the chamber as arithmetic laid directly into five heads at once, and it opens by naming the company's dead: accurately, in order, with dates, including two that only one person in the company knows about. Then it waits, politely, for the company to catch up.

choices.label: Hear it out to the end of the offer.
Refuse to be addressed and turn your back.
Answer it in kind, with the account you carry.

nodes.body: An offer heard out to its end, complete with term, rate, security and a clause about the frontier's peace. It is delivered with the patience of something that has made this offer to nine hands before and has all the time there is. It takes eleven minutes and it is entirely coherent.

choices.label: Go on to the terms.

nodes.body: A back turned on Ashendrel in its own socket chamber, which it accepts without any evident feeling. It stops addressing the captain. It does not stop, and the arithmetic continues to arrive, and it is now being addressed to whoever else in the company is still listening, and two of them are.

choices.label: Go on to the terms.

nodes.body: The account carried up from Gallowmere is read aloud in the socket chamber to the thing the account is about. Clause nine of the founders' plate describes that form of address specifically. It calls it an acknowledgement of the debt by a party competent to acknowledge it, and it explains what follows.

The terms, set out plainly enough that a clerk could minute them: the count ends today, the ring opens, the arrears of nine hundred years are paid in one payment out of what is nearest, and the frontier is free of the Compact forever afterwards. There is no trick in the wording. Everybody looks for one.

choices.label: Write them down and say nothing else.
Ask what nearest means in the terms.
Agree to them, here, on the record.

nodes.body: The terms written down word for word by a hedge-thaumaturge whose hand shakes for the first time in three books, witnessed by a Reckoning sister and sealed with a Warden charter's own seal. Whatever else happens now, the offer exists on paper, in the founders' form, in a court's language.

choices.label: Go on to the price.

nodes.body: The question about nearest is asked and answered precisely, in figures: a counted city of eleven thousand, a fortress of four hundred. A company of five, in that order of proximity and in no other. The figures are given without emphasis, the way a clerk reads out a schedule of assets.

choices.label: Go on to the price.

nodes.body: Terms are agreed on the record in a socket chamber, in front of the crown clerk. There is a Warden seal on the agreement and a Reckoning sister as witness. The payment schedule begins with the word immediately, which was in the terms, and which everybody heard, and which nobody thought to negotiate.

The price is where the offer stops being abstract: one payment, taken at once, from the nearest principal. The door's own estimate of what that comes to has been written out in the crown ledger's tenth column in advance, in a clerk's hand, and the column has been ruled and waiting since the founding.

choices.label: Read the tenth column's figure.
Refuse to look at it and go to the ring.
Ask whether a smaller principal would serve.

nodes.body: A figure read in the tenth column of the crown ledger: a number of people and a date. It is written in the same neat hand as every other entry in the book, with the same abbreviations, in the same ink. It is the plainest sentence anybody has read in three books and it is four characters long.

choices.label: Go on to the oath.

nodes.body: The question is asked about whether a smaller principal would serve, and it is answered in the affirmative, with a figure. The figure is five. It is given in the same tone as everything else, and the crown clerk writes it in the margin without being asked, because that is what he does with figures.

choices.label: Go on to the oath.

nodes.body: The figure is refused, unread, which is the only genuinely cowardly decision available in this chamber. The company walks into the ring not knowing what it has been offered. It is therefore unable to refuse it properly, and unable to argue afterwards that it did not accept.

The last conversation before the ring is about the founders' oath, which Ashendrel offers in the founders' own form. That form is binding on it in a way nothing else in this mountain is, which is the whole reason the founders wrote it down. It requires a hand to swear on the other side.

choices.label: Take the oath in the founders' form.
Refuse the oath and hold to the charter.
Have Nyre take it as a sister of the Reckoning.

nodes.body: An oath taken in the founders' own form, which the collar plate sets out and the crown ledger records, and it binds both parties to terms neither can afterwards revise. It takes about a minute to say. Nobody in the chamber, including the crown clerk, has ever heard it said out loud before.

choices.label: Go on to the decision.

nodes.body: The oath refused and a Warden charter held up instead: a legal instrument of a state four hundred years old, addressed to an arrangement nine hundred years old, in a chamber that predates both. It is not a stupid decision. It is simply an instrument of the wrong jurisdiction, and everybody present knows it.

choices.label: Go on to the decision.

nodes.body: The founders' oath is taken by a sister of the Reckoning rather than by the captain, which is procedurally sound and which Nyre volunteers for before anybody can stop her. It makes her the party bound and not the company. She reads the form off the plate and gets every word of it right.

The ring's working stewards are nine of the crown clerk's household on the ninth-hour rota, and they have kept the sockets, trimmed the lamps and packed the collars here for their whole working lives. They are unarmed. They are also the only people in the mountain who know which collar is due today.

choices.label: Put the charter to them and stand them down.
Work the rota alongside them for one hour.
Ask which of them knows the collar work.
Clear the chamber by force; they are the count.

nodes.body: A charter put to nine stewards, who stand down formally, in writing, with the time entered. Then they stand in the gallery and watch, because they have nowhere else to be and the rota is at the ninth hour regardless of who is holding it, and somebody will have to do the collar work.

choices.label: Go on to the legate.
Send them out of the chamber entirely.

nodes.body: One hour worked on the rota alongside nine stewards, trimming lamps and reading collars and passing lead. It teaches the company more about this door than the whole city archive did, and by the end of it the senior steward is explaining the eighth collar's crack without being asked anything at all.

choices.label: Go on to the legate.

nodes.body: The question is asked and the collar man identified: a mason of sixty who has packed these collars for forty years. He knows what clause nine means in practice rather than in bronze, and he has never once been asked, and it takes him a moment to understand that the question is serious.

choices.label: Go on to the legate.

nodes.body: A socket chamber is cleared by force of nine unarmed household stewards at the ninth hour. That leaves the ring unattended for the first time in nine hundred years, for eleven minutes. The rota's own margin, cut into the wall in the founders' hand, is nine, and the excess is where everything after this comes from.

Nine stood-down stewards are sent out of the chamber entirely, which is correct procedure with civilians. It also removes from the room the only nine people who know which collar is due, on the day the eighth collar is due, in front of a company that has not read the rota's second page.

Prior Absolon Rell is here, in the socket chamber, having come up the wyrm-road ahead of the company with his coach left at Sarnhold. He has an appointment plate in his baggage. He greets the company by name and asks after their journey, and he is not surprised to see them and does not pretend to be.

choices.label: Arrest him on the charter, in front of witnesses.
Hear what he came up here to do.
Let him proceed and watch what he does.

nodes.body: A mother-house legate arrested in a socket chamber by a chartered company, in front of nine stewards, a crown clerk and a mason. All of them are willing to witness it. One of them writes it down, with the time, and asks the captain to sign the entry, which the captain does.

choices.label: Go on to the Guild.

nodes.body: Rell's own account of his purpose, given without embarrassment: the office falls vacant in nine days, the mother house has resolved to fill it from within the order, and he is here to be appointed. He considers that a service. He explains, at some length, why he considers it a service.

choices.label: Go on to the Guild.

nodes.body: A legate is allowed to proceed, and watched, which is the coldest decision available in this book. The appointment is properly made and correctly witnessed. The Reckoning holds the ninth hand of the crown door by nightfall, with a nine-year term and a household clause, and the company has minuted the whole thing.

Bruk Sunder is also here, with four delvers and a survey kit, entirely legally, on a Guild charter that predates the Warden charter by two hundred years. He has a copy of it with him. He offers it for inspection before anybody asks, which is the behaviour of a man who has read all of it.

choices.label: Read his Guild charter properly.
Order him out of the chamber.
Ask what the Guild intends to do with a wyrm.

nodes.body: A Guild charter read in full by two people who understand documents. It is genuine, older than the Wardens, and it grants mineral and salvage rights over precisely this chamber, in language that predates the Compact's own paperwork. There is no clause that excludes a living thing from the definition of a mineral deposit.

choices.label: Go on to the Rooks.

nodes.body: An order to leave is given to a Guild factor holding an older charter than yours, and he declines it courteously and has his delvers minute the exchange for the Guild's record. Then he goes back to his survey, and his survey is of the socket ring, and he is measuring the collars.

choices.label: Go on to the Rooks.

nodes.body: The question is asked of what the Guild intends, and answered fully, with figures, and the Guild intends to work the arrangement as a going concern. It has costed it. It has a nine-year plan with the counted city as the labour supply, and Sunder produces the plan, and it is a good plan.

Corrow's Rooks are in the gallery above the ring: eleven of them, chartered, armed, and working under a Warden commission that Thane did not mention because Thane did not issue it. They are not at the rail with the watchers. They are behind the watchers, spread out, covering the chamber's two doors.

choices.label: Fight them for the chamber now.
Get above them by the masons' scaffold.
Ask to see the commission they are working under.
Hold the ring and let them come down to you.

nodes.body: A fight in a socket chamber against eleven chartered mercenaries, in a room with nine warm sockets and a cracked collar in it. It is the worst possible place any of the twenty-two people present could have chosen. Every one of them knows it, and it happens anyway in the fourth minute.

choices.label: Go on to the last works.
Push them back up the gallery stair.

nodes.body: The masons' scaffold used to get above the gallery, which puts the company on the door frame looking down at eleven Rooks who have not thought about the roof. It takes four minutes. Corrow's lieutenant works it out on the third and cannot get his people turned round before the fourth.

choices.label: Go on to the last works.

nodes.body: A commission produced and read: signed, sealed, and issued by the Reckoning's mother house under a Warden counter-seal that Rell carries in his own baggage. It makes the Rooks lawful. It also makes the company's charter contested, which is a thing that can be argued in a court and not in this chamber.

choices.label: Go on to the last works.

nodes.body: A ring is held against eleven mercenaries coming down a gallery stair, which is good ground and the correct tactical choice. The eighth socket's cracked collar is nine feet behind the line. In the fourth minute somebody's whole weight goes into it, and the collar does what a cracked collar does.

Eleven Rooks are pushed back up a gallery stair by a company that is winning, which is the point at which winning stops being useful. The stair leads to the tithe hall. The tithe hall is where the ninth-hour delivery is waiting to be called, and the calling has already started.

The last works stand in the chamber's corner: the crown die on a portable anvil, brought down from the mint for the appointment, with a striker's hammer beside it and a blank already in the vice; the vice is a mason's vice. The blank has been filed and is ready for the tally to be cut.

choices.label: Take the die and break it here.
Read the blank in the vice.
Leave the works alone and go to the ring.
Cut the blank yourself, now, and see.

nodes.body: The crown die off its anvil and broken with a striker's hammer in four blows, in front of the crown clerk, the legate and the Guild, and it ends the cutting of irons in this mountain permanently; Sunder objects on the record. The crown clerk does not object at all, and writes down the time.

choices.label: Go on to the forge.

nodes.body: The blank in the vice, read with a lamp: founding gauge, crown tally, and a name already cut into the flank. It is the name Rell has been carrying an appointment plate for, cut in advance, in the mint's own hand, eleven days ago, which is the day the mint stopped cutting anything else.

choices.label: Go on to the forge.

nodes.body: A blank is cut on the crown die by the captain's own hand, to see what happens, which is what the die is for; it produces a finished ninth iron with a name on its flank. The name is not one the cutter chose, and the die does not have a mechanism for choosing names.

ending.title: A Name You Did Not Choose

nodes.body: The chamber's own small forge is kept for collar lead and iron work: hot, with a lead pot on it, a mason's tools laid out in order beside it, and a bench with nine years of chalk notes on the wall above it. Everything about it is the workshop of somebody who takes maintenance seriously.

choices.label: Melt lead and pack the eighth collar properly.
Use the forge to spoil the blank in the vice.
Put the crown iron in the fire and see if it goes.

nodes.body: An hour with a lead pot and a mason's tools, packing a cracked collar the way the rota specifies. It is not heroic in any way at all. It is also the thing most likely to keep this door shut for another century, and the mason works alongside the company and does not once take over.

choices.label: Go on to the wedge.

nodes.body: The blank in the vice spoiled with a hot iron, deliberately and thoroughly, which cannot be undone. No appointment can be made in this chamber until the mint cuts another one, and the mint takes nine days to cut and the die is standing on an anvil four feet from the vice.

choices.label: Go on to the wedge.

nodes.body: A founding-gauge crown iron is put into a working forge to see whether it will burn. It does not burn. It takes considerable exception to the attempt, in a chamber with eight of its fellows seated in the walls, and all eight of them take exception at the same moment and on the same count.

The wedge has been Vurma's idea since Hollowmarch: an iron driven crosswise through the ring's collars rather than into a socket, locking all nine into one piece that no hand can draw and no keeper can count. She has drawn it three times on three different walls. She has the placement worked out.

choices.label: Have Vurma set the wedge properly.
Have the mason check the wedge's bearing first.
Set it yourself, fast, before anybody stops you.
Wedge it with the founding iron from the chapel.

nodes.body: Vurma sets a wedge in the crown ring with forty years of Guild pathfinding behind the placement, which takes eleven minutes and two adjustments. It is the best piece of work anybody does in this book, and she does it in silence, and afterwards she puts her hand flat on it and leaves it there.

choices.label: Go on to the vigil.
Have her set a second wedge on the far side.

nodes.body: A mason of forty years' collar experience checks the wedge's bearing before it is driven, which finds two problems and fixes both, and moves the wedge four inches to the left. He explains the reasoning while he works. Vurma listens to all of it and then thanks him, which she does not often do.

choices.label: Go on to the vigil.

nodes.body: A wedge set fast by the captain's own hands before the legate can object. It holds. Nobody in the chamber will certify it as sound, because nobody was allowed to look at it before it went in, and Vurma says exactly that, out loud, twice, and then does not mention it again.

choices.label: Go on to the vigil.

nodes.body: A chapel founding iron is used as the wedge, which is a different alloy cut in a different century for a different door. It shears under the ring's nine-count load in the fourth minute, with the whole company standing inside the ring. The shearing takes the load with it into the collars.

A second wedge is set on the far side of the ring for redundancy, which is sound engineering in every context except this one. It puts two hard points into a collar system designed to distribute its load across nine. The ring's own count arrives at the pair of them from opposite directions.

A dwarf watch-alcove opens off the socket chamber, where the stewards rest between rota hours: a bench, a lamp, a water jug and a clear view of the whole ring. Somebody has cut a tally into the bench's edge over the years, in nines, and stopped counting it about four hundred marks in.

choices.label: Take three hours before you do anything.
Do not sit down. Finish this now.

nodes.body: Three hours on a steward's bench with the ring in front of you and the company asleep in shifts around you, and it is the last quiet anybody in this story gets, and everybody knows it at the time, and nobody wastes it talking. Kettle sleeps. Nyre does not, and nobody comments on either fact.

choices.label: Go to the decision.

nodes.body: The masons on the scaffold at the door frame are a master of sixty, two journeymen and an apprentice, working on the frame's upper collar as they have every ninth day for forty years. They work steadily. They do not stop when the company comes in, and the master nods without taking his hand off the stone.

choices.label: Ask the master what the frame is doing.
Order them off the scaffold on the charter.
Ask him what clause nine means in stone.

nodes.body: The master's answer about the frame, given in trade terms with his palm flat on the stone: the frame is spreading, has been spreading since autumn, and will need more than lead within the year; he has reported it four times. He has the copies of all four reports in his tool bag.

choices.label: Go up the scaffold.

nodes.body: A mason of forty years asked what clause nine means in stone, and he answers: the founders cut this frame so that it fails inward rather than outward. He has spent his whole working life maintaining that failure. He explains what maintaining a failure means, and it takes him four sentences.

choices.label: Go up the scaffold.

nodes.body: Four masons are ordered off a scaffold on a Warden charter in the middle of collar work, and they comply, because a charter is a charter. It leaves a partly-packed upper collar open on the day the eighth socket was already due, and the lead in the pot goes hard within the hour.

The masons' scaffold on the door frame is dwarf poles and planks, four levels of it, giving a hand's reach to the frame's upper collar and a clear view down into the socket ring. It has been up for forty years. Its lashings are renewed on a rota, and the rota is chalked on the bottom pole.

choices.label: Climb it and look at the upper collar.
Use it to get above the gallery and the Rooks.
Take it down; it is a way in for other people.
