nodes.body: The upper collar seen at a hand's reach: dwarf stone, spread a finger's width, packed and repacked with lead in nine hundred years of visible layers like the rings of a tree. The newest layer is eleven days old, and the layer under it is nineteen years old, and the gap between them is the whole story.

choices.label: Go on to the crane.

nodes.body: The scaffold used as a route above the gallery, which nobody in the chamber expects because scaffolds are furniture. It gives the company the only high ground in the room. This room has been fought over exactly once before, in the founders' century, according to a note cut into the frame at scaffold height.

choices.label: Go on to the crane.

nodes.body: A masons' scaffold is taken down to deny it to other people, which takes forty minutes of honest work. It also removes the only access to an upper collar that is spreading a finger's width and is due for packing today. The lead pot is on the forge, and the mason is standing beside it.

A dwarf crane stands over the ring, used for setting collar stone: a hook, a wire fall, a counterweight, and a bearing that is still greased and still turning after nine hundred years; it swings across the whole ring. There is a chalk mark on the floor showing where the counterweight sits when it is stowed.

choices.label: Rig the crane to draw a collar stone.
Rig it over the ninth socket for the seating.
Leave the crane; it is not your equipment.
Cut the counterweight and drop the fall.

nodes.body: The crane rigged to draw a collar stone under the mason's direction, which is exactly what it is for. It gives the company the ability to open or close the ring's stonework rather than only its irons. That is a different order of possibility, and it takes Ilsabet about four seconds to appreciate.

choices.label: Go on to the seal.

nodes.body: The crane rigged over the ninth socket, which is how the founders seated the first nine irons and how the ninth will be seated today by somebody. Rigging it puts that somebody's timing under the company's hand, and the legate watches the rigging from the desk without saying anything at all.

choices.label: Go on to the seal.

nodes.body: A nine-hundred-year-old counterweight is cut in a chamber with eight warm sockets and a scaffold in it. Eleven hundred pounds of dwarf stone arrives on the ring floor at the ninth minute, which is the minute the ring's own movement comes round. The two of those things together are what the founders' rota exists to prevent.

The founders' seal is cut into the chamber floor in front of the ring: nine hands in a circle around a door, and around them an inscription in the founders' own hand. The counted city has never translated it. It has been walked over by every keeper, steward and mason for nine hundred years.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet translate the floor inscription.
Stand on the seal and read the ring from it.
Cut the seal out of the floor and carry it.

nodes.body: A founders' inscription translated on a chamber floor after nine hundred years, by a hedge-thaumaturge kneeling on it with a lamp. It is not a dedication and not a warning. It is an apology, addressed to whoever is standing on it, from the people who built the arrangement, and it names what they did.

choices.label: Go to the decision.

nodes.body: A founders' seal is cut out of the chamber floor and carried, because it is the only apology anybody ever wrote for any of this. It is nine hundred pounds of dwarf flagstone. The company cannot get it up the wyrm-road, and the attempt takes four hours, and the four hours were the margin.

In the gallery above the ring, nine of the counted stand at the rail in shifts and watch the door, and they have watched it in shifts, without instruction from anybody living, for nine hundred years, and they are not guards; they have no weapons. They are simply always there, nine of them, and the shift changes on the hour.

choices.label: Ask them what they are watching for.
Get them out of the gallery before the hour.
Stand with them at the rail for one shift.
Clear them out; the gallery is a firing position.

nodes.body: The answer given by nine people at a rail: they are watching for the day the count stops, and the founders told the first nine to watch; each nine has told the next nine since. Nobody has ever stood them down, and no keeper has ever tried, and they are not entirely sure the keeper could.

choices.label: Go on to the hollow.
Ask them what they were told to do if it stops.

nodes.body: Nine watchers got out of the gallery before the ninth hour, with some difficulty and a good deal of patient argument. It is a kindness. It also means that for the first time in nine hundred years nobody is at the rail when the hour comes, and the rail is what the watching was from.

choices.label: Go on to the hollow.

nodes.body: One full shift stood at the rail with nine of the counted, in silence, watching a door breathe on a nine-count. It is the single most useful hour of preparation available in this chamber, and at the end of it the eldest watcher tells the company what changes in the rhythm before the hour turns.

choices.label: Go on to the hollow.

nodes.body: A gallery is cleared by force because it is a firing position, and nine watchers are put out of a place they have held in shifts for nine hundred years. On the way out the ninth of them explains, without rancour, what they were watching for and what they were told to do when they saw it.

The watchers are asked what they were told to do if the count stopped, and all nine of them answer at once, in the founders' own words, which they have had by heart since childhood, and the words are an instruction. The company is standing inside the instruction while they say it.

Vurma's hammer finds a hollow behind the ring wall: a void the founders left between the door frame and the rock, with a dwarf ladder in it and nine hundred years of undisturbed dust on the ladder's rungs. The access plate comes away in her hands, and it was made to come away in somebody's hands.

choices.label: Go down the founders' ladder.
Sound the void and map it from outside.
Wall the hollow up before anybody else finds it.
Send Kettle down alone to see.

nodes.body: The founders' ladder descended into a void nobody has entered since the founding. At the bottom there is a bench, a tool rack with its tools still in it, and a set of written instructions on the wall in nine bronze plates. The instructions are for dismantling the door, and they are complete.

choices.label: Go on to the bellows.
Take the dismantling instructions off the wall.

nodes.body: The void sounded and mapped from outside with a hammer and a wire, which tells Vurma its size and shape and one further fact: the door's frame is not attached to the rock in the way the entire counted city believes it is. She says that twice, and the second time she says what it means.

choices.label: Go on to the bellows.

nodes.body: Kettle down the founders' ladder alone with a lamp, and back in eleven minutes, white, and she describes a bench, a tool rack and a set of instructions in dwarf that she cannot read; Ilsabet can. Kettle also says that the dust down there has one set of footprints in it, and they are not hers.

choices.label: Go on to the bellows.

nodes.body: A founders' hollow is walled up to keep it from other people, with the company on the outside of it. That seals the only route by which the door could ever be dismantled, and the only apparatus for doing it, and the instructions for how. It takes two hours and it is entirely irreversible.

A set of nine-hundred-year-old dismantling instructions is taken off a founders' wall and carried up a ladder: nine bronze plates, forty pounds. The plates are the wall's own bracing. The founders fixed the instructions to the thing they were instructions for, which is either a joke or a precaution.

A dwarf bellows apparatus stands in the hollow, connected through the rock to the door's own frame, built by the founders for a purpose the crown clerk has never known about. The masons know. It is on their rota, once every ninth decade, and the rota's page for it has been blank for ninety years.

choices.label: Have the mason explain the bellows.
Work the bellows and see what it does.
Leave it; the founders left it for a reason.

nodes.body: The mason's explanation, given with real pleasure at being asked a professional question: the bellows cools the frame's upper collar. It has not been worked in ninety years, because the rota went out of use when the last master died. Working it now would buy this frame a decade, possibly more.

choices.label: Go on to the tithe box.

nodes.body: The bellows worked by two people for an hour, in a stone void, by lamplight, in silence. It drops the upper collar's temperature by a measurable amount and tightens the frame's spread by a hair. It is the most boring act of heroism in three books and it is unambiguously the most useful.

choices.label: Go on to the tithe box.

nodes.body: A founders' bellows is left alone on the principle that the founders left it there for a reason, which is true. The reason is that it must be worked every ninth decade. This is the ninetieth year, which is written on the plate above it, in the founders' hand, in figures.

The tithe box beside the ring is a dwarf strongbox where the counted city's tokens are collected after each delivery. It is full: nine hundred years of tokens, each one a household's name on a disc of fired clay. There is a tally slate on the lid, and the slate is written up to today.

choices.label: Read the tally slate on the lid.
Take the box; it is nine hundred years of evidence.
Leave it and go to the ring.
Empty it into the hollow and lose the tokens.

nodes.body: The tally slate read off the strongbox lid: this month's tokens, next month's requirement, and a note in the crown clerk's hand recording that the requirement has doubled since Kar Duhn shut. Under that, in the same hand, a second note recording that it doubled again after Hollowmarch.

choices.label: Go to the decision.

nodes.body: A dwarf strongbox of nine hundred years of household tokens taken and lashed to the barrow: ninety pounds of fired clay and the counted city's entire record of who paid what and when. Each token has a name on it. Nyre insists on carrying it herself for the first mile and then admits she cannot.

choices.label: Go to the decision.

nodes.body: Nine hundred years of household tokens are emptied into a founders' hollow to destroy the record. The record was the only proof that any of the eleven thousand ever paid anything. The city's arithmetic simply starts again from one the following morning, and everybody's arrears are recalculated from a clean sheet.

The ring at the ninth hour, with everything now known, and eight irons warm and one socket bright and empty. A crown iron somewhere in the room. A legate with an appointment plate, a Guild with an older charter, eleven Rooks on the stair, nine watchers at a rail, and a door breathing on a nine-count in front of five people.

choices.label: Go to the door and settle it.

nodes.body: The crown door of Kar Ashen stands at the end of the wyrm-road in a frame of stone older than dwarves: nine sockets in a ring, eight filled and warm, the ninth worn bright and empty. Behind it is Ashendrel, awake enough to be listening and far too large for the word awake to be of any use. The chamber is full of people with rotas and paperwork, and every one of them is waiting to see what five strangers do next.

choices.label: Set the crown iron in its socket and lock the door.
Draw the eight irons and unmake the Compact here.
Take the crown iron out of the mountain entirely.
Open the door a hand's width and look.
Hold to the terms Ashendrel named.
Withdraw. Three doors is a Warden war, not a commission.
Knock, as you knocked at the first two.

nodes.body: The crown iron goes into the ninth socket and the socket takes it the way a lock takes its own key, and all nine are warm now. The frame takes up the load with a sound like a building settling, and the count in the whole mountain stops in the middle of a number for the first time since the road was cut. Nobody in the chamber says anything for about nine seconds.

choices.label: Break the crown die so no tenth iron can be cut.
Take the keeper's ring; a count still needs a hand.
Get everyone out while the mountain is quiet.
Drive it in crooked and jam the socket forever.

nodes.body: The crown die is carried to the portable anvil and broken across it in four strokes, and dwarf steel comes apart in a way that dwarf steel is not supposed to come apart. Vurma goes over the floor on her knees afterwards twice, collecting fragments into a sack. She does not accept help, and she counts the pieces, and the number she reaches is the number she expected.

choices.label: Go up and out.

nodes.body: The ninth hand's ring lies on the keeper's desk, warm and sized for whoever lifts it. The arithmetic beside it is not complicated and the crown clerk sets it out in three sentences: nine irons hold a door without a keeper right up until something decides to test the arrangement. This door has Ashendrel behind it. A count kept honestly by somebody who hates the work is the difference between the two situations.

choices.label: Put it on. Somebody has to keep this one.
Leave it. Nobody in this company signs that twice.

nodes.body: The ring goes on, and the count arrives at the back of the skull like a schedule of payments read out by a patient clerk. It is not a voice and it is not a compulsion. It is an obligation with dates in it, larger than the two before it by an order nobody in the company can express, and the crown clerk stands up out of his chair for the first time in nineteen years.

choices.label: Take the company out.

nodes.body: This is the decision to unmake the Compact at its own crown, and it deserves being said out loud before anybody touches anything. Eight irons in eight warm sockets. Nine hundred years of instalments paid by people who were never consulted about any of it. And five people standing in front of the only arrangement that has ever kept a wyrm asleep, with two irons in a pack and a charter in a pocket.

choices.label: Draw one iron and watch what the door does.
Draw all eight at once and run for the stair.
Draw them, then wedge the ring with the crown iron.
Change your mind and seat the crown iron instead.

nodes.body: One iron out, and the door leans a quarter of an inch outward against its frame. Two, and the stone around the sockets begins visibly to sweat. Three, and something on the far side says the captain's name in the voice of the paymaster of Kar Duhn, who has been dead since the first book, and then asks a question about the account in the same voice.

choices.label: Re-seat all three and step back.
Keep drawing. Finish it.
Ask it what the whole account comes to.

nodes.body: Three irons go back into three sockets, put there by hands that are not remotely steady, and the door settles with the sound of a held breath let out slowly. The voice thanks the company by name, all five names, correctly. Then it adds the names of the two hands that held the office before this one, and the crown clerk sits down on the floor beside his own desk.

choices.label: Get out of the mountain.

nodes.body: The crown iron is driven crosswise through the socket ring instead of into it, dwarf iron biting dwarf iron until the whole ring is locked into a single piece that no hand can draw and no keeper can count. It is crude and permanent. It is also, Vurma says while she is still holding the hammer, the only thing anybody has done in three books that cannot be undone by somebody else's paperwork.

choices.label: Leave it wedged and go.
Test it. Put your weight on the door.

nodes.body: The arithmetic the company has been carrying since Gallowmere, taken to its end: the ninth iron is the count. A count that cannot be kept is a debt that cannot be collected. Three of the nine irons in one pack makes the Compact's arithmetic something that does not close, anywhere, ever again, and it makes the people carrying that pack the only thing standing between a frontier and a demand for payment.

choices.label: Wrap it with the other two and carry it out.
Seat it after all; a shut door beats leverage.
Carry it out in the open and let them come for it.
Sink it in the aqueduct on the way up.

nodes.body: Salt-cloth, oilcloth, and the middle of the pack, with the three irons laid so that none of them touches another, which Ilsabet arranges twice before she is satisfied. The mountain's whole attention arrives and settles on five people who are about to walk uphill with it. The watchers at the rail turn to follow the pack rather than the company, and they keep following it for as long as it is in sight.

choices.label: Up the wyrm-road, and quickly.

nodes.body: Ashendrel's terms, named on a ledge four miles up the road and repeated here by a voice that arrives as arithmetic rather than sound: the count ends, the doors open, and the arrears of nine hundred years are paid once, in one payment, out of what is nearest. The frontier is free of the whole arrangement afterwards. The crown clerk has heard the offer before. He is the only person in the chamber who has.

choices.label: Hold to the terms and open the ring as agreed.
Refuse the terms to its face and seat the iron.
Refuse the terms and withdraw entirely.
Ask what one payment means in numbers.

nodes.body: The terms are held to and the ring is opened in the order the wyrm gives, socket by socket, with the whole chamber watching and nobody interfering. The mountain goes quiet in a way that is not silence but attention. The road's entire arithmetic waits on one company's word, and for about eleven seconds the only sound in the socket ring is a mason's lead pot ticking as it cools.

choices.label: Stand where you are and let it pay itself.
Break faith at the last moment and run.

nodes.body: The terms are refused out loud, to something the size of the hall, in plain words. The crown iron goes into its socket while the refusal is still being spoken. The count resumes underneath it like a clerk continuing to write through an argument, and the voice does not answer the refusal at all, which is not the same as not having heard it.

choices.label: Go, before it finishes considering the refusal.

nodes.body: A hand's width of the crown door, held open on a pick haft with Dellach's boot braced against the frame. Warm air comes out of the gap in a rhythm that is not wind and never has been. There is light on the other side, and it is not lamplight, and it has been burning without fuel since before the legion cut the first station on this road.

choices.label: Look through it.
Put a lamp through first.
Shut it again without looking.
Speak through the gap.

nodes.body: What is behind the crown door: the hall is the inside of the mountain, and Ashendrel fills it the way water fills a cup, and standing in rows in front of it, counting, are the counted of nine hundred years. There is a gap in the ninth row. It is exactly five people wide, and it has been left open, and nothing else in the hall is untidy in any way.

choices.label: Shut it and seat the crown iron.
Shut it and get out of the mountain.
Walk into the gap. Somebody has to.

nodes.body: A lamp lowered through the gap on a rope burns steadily for four seconds, then goes out from the wick downward, which is not a thing lamps do. It comes back up the rope relit by nobody, with the flame a better colour than it was before. Ossa, who has trimmed wicks on this road since she was twelve, looks at that flame for a long moment and then puts her own lamp out.

choices.label: Look through, now that you have to know.
Reach through and take the lamp back.

nodes.body: The door is eased shut on nothing seen, the haft withdrawn, and the count resumes precisely where it left off without any comment. Five people stand in front of it having decided together not to know something. Each of them will privately want to know it for the rest of their lives, and two of them will eventually come back and ask, and one of those two will be told.

choices.label: Go up and out.
Make it a Warden matter and withdraw properly.

nodes.body: The honest option is said out loud in front of the crown door by Nyre, who has been assembling it since Hollowmarch and delivers it in four sentences, and this arrangement is nine hundred years old. Three doors is a Warden war and a war is Warden business. Five people with a charter and a barrow do not get to be the hinge of it twice, and they have already been the hinge of it twice.

choices.label: Out the way you came, and no souvenirs.
Out, but take the crown ledger from the mint.
Out, and burn the nine lamps of the ring behind you.
Out, and sell the road to the Guild on the way down.

nodes.body: Back to the mint for the crown ledger: eleven hundred pages of instalments in nine hands, with four blank pages at the end and a ruled column headed for a tenth. The blank pages are the interesting part. Somebody ruled them in the founders' century and nobody has needed them since, which means the arrangement was designed with a great deal more room in it than nine doors.

choices.label: Take it and go.
Take it and cut the tenth column out of it first.

nodes.body: Four hundred steps up, and Kar Ashen has changed its mind about the company, and the tally-yards are lit. The counted are standing in the streets facing the gate, not moving, in nines. The crown gate itself has closed to a thumb's width, and the wheelhouse's ratchet is turning under its own weight in a room with nobody in it.

choices.label: Force the crown gate with everything you have.
Go out by the foundry chimney.
Go out by the mason's postern under the wall.
Walk out in the ninth-hour file, counting.
Sit down on the wyrm-road. You are finished.

nodes.body: Five people, a pick haft, a Warden shield as a fulcrum, and a gate that is not being held shut by weight. Eleven minutes of the worst work anybody has done in three books, with the counted standing in the street behind and not one of them intervening. The gate gives an inch at a time. Nobody in the company is able to say afterwards what was actually resisting the lever.

choices.label: Get everybody through the moment it is wide enough.
Hold it and count them through by name.

nodes.body: The drowned foundry's chimney is ninety feet of soot-glazed dwarf brick with staples at the bends, breathing warm air that smells of a forge Kar Ashen has not lit since the founding. The staples are half missing at the top. From inside it, the ward's lamps are visible below as nine points of light in a pattern nobody wants to look at twice.

choices.label: Climb it in pairs and take the skin off your hands.
Send the strongest up first to haul the rest.

nodes.body: Out by the mason's postern under the outer wall, with the lead seal broken behind you and the corridor beyond lighting itself politely, one niche at a time, all the way back to the ring. It has the manner of a house seeing a guest off the property and then standing in the doorway to make quite sure they have gone.

choices.label: Get onto the road.

nodes.body: The ninth hour kept in the slag yard, and then the file forms in the street below: nine lamps lifted, the count started, everything on schedule, and the Ninth Sword walks out of Kar Ashen inside it with the rhythm right, three irons in one pack, and every hand out of sight. Nobody in the file turns round. The counted in the street stand aside for the file and not for the company.

choices.label: Break off at the gate and get clear.
Stay in the file to the end of the count. It is only nine.

nodes.body: The Ninefold Road goes down off the spine in a thaw with meltwater running the whole width of the paving. Sarnhold is two days below. The company carries whatever it decided to carry, and Nyre asks the question that has to be settled before anybody speaks to a Warden, which is not what happened but what the five of you are going to say happened, and in what order.

choices.label: Straight down to Sarnhold and the Commandant.
Two days at the ice gallery first; they are spent.
Put it to the company as a company. All five voices.
Send Kettle ahead to see who is waiting at the fortress.
Off the road and west, with what you carry.

nodes.body: Two days in the ice gallery with a brazier and no watch to keep, behind nine inches of clear ice with nine niches burning on the far side of it; Kettle sleeps eleven hours. Dellach's hands come back. Ilsabet writes the whole account out twice in case one copy burns, and then writes a third copy and gives it to Ossa without telling anybody.

choices.label: Walk into Sarnhold on the third morning.

nodes.body: The company council convenes on a switchback bench above a two-thousand-foot drop and runs for an hour; Dellach argues for the record. Nyre argues for her order's hearing. Kettle argues for the west road and no names at all, and argues well. Ilsabet argues for whichever choice puts the fewest copies of the truth into the fewest hands, and will not say which choice that is.

choices.label: Take it to the Commandant, all five names on it.
Write the report the Wardens will read in fifty years.
Let them argue it out and then decide alone.

nodes.body: Kettle back from the last switchback with a list, delivered flat: a Reckoning coach in the fortress yard with its horses still harnessed, a Guild train loading at the sally port, and eleven Warden cloaks on the gate that do not fit the men wearing them. She has counted all of it twice. She adds that the fortress chapel's bell is not ringing the hour and should be.

choices.label: Walk in anyway; there is nowhere else to walk.
Wait for dark and go in over the curtain wall.

nodes.body: Sarnhold in the thaw, with the whole frontier waiting on the yard cobbles. Commandant Iver Thane at the tower door. Prior Absolon Rell beside a coach with the Reckoning's seal on it, back down the road ahead of the company somehow. Bruk Sunder with a contract already drawn. And three of the Compact's nine irons in a pack on the captain's shoulder, which everybody in the yard is looking at and nobody mentions.

choices.label: Report to Thane, on the record, in full.
Go to the Reckoning hearing and name Rell.
Write the report the Wardens will read in fifty years.
Hear what the Guild is offering for the road.
Say the minimum, take the fee, and be gone by dark.
Hand the irons to the legate and be done with it.

nodes.body: Iver Thane reads it twice without a question, sets it down, squares the pages, and asks the three things a Commandant of the spine has to ask: what is shut, what is loose, and what is in the pack. He asks them in that order. Then he asks a fourth, which is not in any Warden manual: whether the company would say the same thing under oath in front of the mother house.

choices.label: Ask for the standing charter and a spine writ.
Hand over all three irons with the report.
Keep the three, and have him raise the frontier.
Put the crown ledger on the table and let him decide.
Tell him the door is shut and leave the rest out.
Tell him what Ashendrel offered, word for word.

nodes.body: The written report will outlive everybody in the room: dated, signed by five hands, sealed to the spine archive. It requires the captain of the Ninth Sword to set down in plain words what was done to the crown door and by whom, with the hours attached to each entry. The clerk who takes it down asks twice for clarification and both times the clarification makes it worse.

choices.label: Write that the company now keeps the count.
Write that the door is open, and how far.
Write that three irons were drawn and reseated.
Write that the ring is wedged and ask for masons.
Write that the crown iron left the mountain.
Write that the company did not go through the door.

nodes.body: The Reckoning hearing convenes in Sarnhold's chapel with four priors down from the mother house, and Absolon Rell takes his own minutes at the end of the table. Nyre stands up as a sister of the Reckoning with two dead brothers' worth of requisitions in her hand and a certified archive folder beside them. She has been drafting the first sentence of this since Rell's Gate.

choices.label: Testify in full, everything, on the record.
Testify, and hand the order one iron as surety.
Withdraw the accusation for what Rell is offering.

nodes.body: Bruk Sunder's contract is drawn and witnessed before the company reaches the yard, and the Guild wants the charts, the hours and the crown road, and it will pay in coin, in shares, and in a delving company's worth of silence. He has costed all three. He also has the older charter in his coat, and he does not need to produce it, and everybody in the room knows he has it.

choices.label: Refuse, and take the report to Thane instead.
Sell the road and take the shares.
Sell the charts but keep the hours.

nodes.body: Three of the nine irons kept, wrapped, and entered on the spine record as company property held in trust, which takes Thane's clerk three attempts to phrase in a way the archive will accept. Couriers go out the same night to every Warden post from Sarnhold to the Ledger cities. The Compact's arithmetic is broken at three doors at once, and it cannot be repaired by any hand that has not got an iron in it. A frontier that has been paying for nine hundred years now knows, in writing, what it has been paying for. And on the last page of the crown ledger, in the ruled column headed for a tenth hand, somebody has written the six remaining doors in order, with dates against each, and the nearest of them is Sarnhold's own chapel.

The charter is made standing and the writ is made spine-wide, and the Ninth Sword is entered in the Warden roll as a company of record with a seal of its own. Thane's first order under it reads, in his hand: hold the crown road, and report the hour of every lamp on it. It is signed, sealed, dated, and it is the first written acknowledgement in four hundred years that the hours matter.

Three irons handed across a Commandant's table and locked into a fortress strongbox with two Wardens on it day and night, on a rota Thane writes himself. The fee is paid in full with the hazard added and no argument about either. A crown door under the spine is shut tonight and will be shut in the morning, and the counted city's mint has nothing left to cut with.

Eleven hundred pages of instalments in nine hands laid on a Commandant's table, which makes them his problem, his career, and no longer the company's business at all. Thane reads the last twenty pages twice without speaking. He has the slow attention of a man who is finding his own fortress in a delivery schedule, and then finding his own predecessor's signature against one of the deliveries.

Absolon Rell named to his face in front of four priors of the mother house, with his own requisitions matched to the crown ledger by a sister of his own order and an archivist's certified copies beside them. He does not deny it. An order discovers that its frontier chapters have been paying a wyrm in people since before the Reckoning had a written rule, and that the paying was minuted.

Ashendrel's terms reported to a Warden Commandant word for word, written down, witnessed and sealed. It is the first time in nine hundred years that what the thing under the spine actually wants has been entered in a human record instead of paid quietly. Thane reads the terms four times. Then he asks whether they are still open, and nobody in the room can tell him.

A socket ring locked into one piece by an iron driven crosswise, reported in plain words and copied twice for the archive. A spine-wide request goes out the same week for masons, an engineer and a permanent watch. What the company did cannot be undone by any hand and cannot be trusted forever, and the report says both of those things in the same sentence, which is why the request is granted.

A short honest report that says the crown door is shut and stops there. The fee is paid, the company is thanked, and everybody is out of the yard by dark. Four people know that nine hundred years of arithmetic was left out of a Warden file on purpose, and none of the four ever raises it, and the fifth one stops sleeping properly some time in the following winter.

One iron handed to the Reckoning as surety and entered in its register under a number, which is the safest vault on the frontier and the one place the Compact has always been able to reach into. The company keeps a receipt with a seal on it. The receipt is worth exactly what the paper is worth, which Nyre says out loud in the chapel, on the record, for the minutes.

Written into the spine archive in the captain's own hand: the crown iron left the mountain in a company pack, which means the count cannot be kept and the door cannot be paid. Nobody in the room can say which of those two is worse. Thane files it, reads it twice, and then asks the clerk to leave, and asks the company one question that is not entered in the record.

Written into a Warden file by a captain who has now read three versions of the same clause: the crown door is shut, all nine irons are seated. The count is kept by the captain of the Ninth Sword. There will be a journey under the spine every ninth night for the rest of a life that now has a schedule attached to it, and the household clause is attached to the schedule.

The truth entered to the inch, as the oath requires. Sarnhold's evacuation order is posted before noon and the Ninefold Road is closed at both ends by the week's end. A company that did the honest thing sits on the yard cobbles watching a fortress load its carts, and Thane comes out at some point and stands with them, and does not say that they were wrong.

Three irons drawn and reseated, written down in exactly those words, with a Warden clerk copying it out twice. Then Thane asks the question nobody in three books has been able to answer, and everybody in this room has already considered: whether a socket that has been emptied once holds the same as a socket that has never been emptied at all. Nobody answers. He writes the question into the file.

A file recording that the company reached the crown door, described it accurately, touched nothing, and came back down. It is the most defensible sentence in the spine archive. It is also the one the Ninth Sword will be asked about in every station house, taproom and chapter house on this frontier for the rest of its working life, and the asking will never once be hostile, which is worse.

The fee taken for a report that says as little as a report can say, and the company out of the sally port before dark with the money split five ways on the road. The spine is somebody else's arithmetic now. Nobody says that out loud, and everybody has agreed to it, and by the second station down the road nobody is talking at all.

Three irons handed to Prior Absolon Rell in a fortress yard in front of witnesses, receipted properly, and loaded into a coach with the Reckoning's seal on the door. The coach turns south. It is not seen again by anybody who asks after it, and the receipt is produced at an inquiry two years later and is found to be entirely in order in every particular.

The accusation withdrawn for a chapter house, a pension, and nine years of the company's debts carried by the order. Nyre resigns her order in the corridor afterwards in one sentence. Rell writes it into his own minutes verbatim, and it is the only part of the whole proceeding that anybody who was there remembers a year later.

The crown road sold to the Sable Guild with shares and silence, signed in a fortress yard on a drum head. By midsummer a Guild train is working the tally-yards of Kar Ashen on a schedule the Guild does not understand and has not been told the price of. The company's shares pay out quarterly. They pay out for two quarters, and then the payments become irregular, and then they stop.

The charts sold and the hours kept back, which is exactly the half of the thing that gets people killed. A Guild train walks into Kar Ashen at the wrong hour of the ninth night with forty people and a clean bill of lading. The company is drinking in Sarnhold when it happens, and hears about it eleven days later, and knows immediately which half of the sale did it.

An argument above a two-thousand-foot drop allowed to run until it stops being an argument. Kettle goes west that afternoon. Nyre returns to her order with her own account, and Dellach walks into the tower alone with his. The Ninth Sword ends at the top of the road it survived, over a disagreement about paperwork, and every one of the five accounts filed afterwards is honest and none of them agree.

Off the Ninefold Road and west over the shoulder with three of the Compact's nine irons in the pack, no report, no fee and no charter. It is a defensible piece of arithmetic: the irons are safest where nobody knows they are. It also makes five people the only thing on the continent worth hunting, and the hunting starts before the thaw is over and does not stop.

Three knocks on the crown door, because it worked twice and neither time was an argument for a third. The door answers them: three knocks returned from the other side in the same rhythm, at a scale that takes the gallery's dust off the ceiling and the opinions out of everybody present. The mason drops his ladle. It is the last sound anybody in the chamber hears clearly.

The crown iron hammered in at an angle to jam the socket forever, which works, and which cracks the collar, and a ring of nine that has held since the founding discovers, in front of witnesses, that it is now a ring of eight and a wound. The mason says one word. The crown clerk closes his ledger and puts the pen down beside it, squarely, which is the last thing he does.

Eight irons pulled in under a minute and five people running for a stair a mile long. It is a plan that requires the crown door to open slowly. The crown door has had nine hundred years to consider how it would like to do this, and it turns out to have made arrangements, and the arrangements are not slow and were never going to be.

The fourth iron drawn while the voice is still being courteous about the account, and then the fifth. After that no further decisions are required of anybody in the gallery. The arrangement has concluded, and the account is being settled in the order in which it was opened, which means the counted city first and the fortress second and the company somewhere in the middle of a very long list.

The whole account asked for through three empty sockets, and given in full: itemised, with dates, with interest, with a note on arrears and a schedule of instalments. The figure is one that the company is standing inside of and has been standing inside of since Gallowmere. It is read out to the end. It takes eleven minutes, and it is not cruel, and that is the unbearable part.

One payment explained in numbers by something that does not use sound to explain anything. The arrears of nine hundred years, taken at once, from the nearest available principal. The nearest available principal is a fortress two days down the road, a counted city eleven thousand strong. A company of five standing in a gallery, and the order of proximity is not the order anybody would have chosen.

The terms held to the end, and the wyrm paying itself out of the row it was owed, and it takes eleven minutes. It is not violent. Afterwards the crown door stands open on a hall with nobody counting in it, and the road above is quiet for the first time since the legion, and the Compact is over, and the price of that is written in the ninth column in a clerk's neat hand.

Five people walk into a gap in the ninth row exactly five people wide. It is the most defensible decision anybody makes in three books, and it is made without any discussion at all, which is how the company knows it has been coming since the Barrow Moor. It closes the gap. It adjusts the schedule by nothing whatsoever, and it changes nothing else at all.

One sentence spoken through a hand's width of crown door, politely, with the haft still braced. The reply does not arrive as sound. It arrives as arithmetic: the company counted, priced, scheduled, and entered against an instalment which the record shows as falling due immediately. There is no argument available, because there is nothing in the reply that is wrong.

An arm through the gap for a lamp relit by nobody, and the lamp handed over properly, into the hand that reached for it, by something that has waited nine hundred years for a transaction it did not have to begin. It is careful not to spill the oil. That care is the detail that the last person out of the chamber cannot afterwards stop describing.

A shoulder put against a wedged crown door to establish whether the work holds, which it does, entirely, and would have gone on doing indefinitely. In the same second the thing on the other side puts its own weight against the same door, out of what can only reasonably be described as professional curiosity. The wedge holds. The frame does not, and the frame was cut to fail inward.

Three irons carried openly down the wyrm-road as an invitation, on the theory that whatever wants them will have to come out into lamplight to ask. On the first night the company discovers that it does not have to come out at all and never has. That it does not consider a lit dwarf gallery to be outside anything, and that the road has been inside the whole time.

The crown iron sunk in the aqueduct on the way up, which solves the problem until the summer draw-down. Then a Guild water detail finds a strip of warm metal on the channel bottom and sells it in Sarnhold market for two coppers to a clerk with southern horses. The clerk pays without haggling, which is the only detail in the whole transaction that anybody afterwards finds strange.

The nine lamps of the socket ring smashed and left burning as a gesture on the way out, which feels justified for two days. The mountain's answer does not arrive that night. It arrives on the ninth night at Sarnhold, in a file that comes up the switchbacks with its own lamps and its own list, and the list is read out at the gate before anybody thinks to close it.

The crown road sold to the Guild on the way down for coin and no receipt, and the commission returned unfulfilled with an excuse Thane cannot disprove and does not believe. A Guild banner goes up the Ninefold Road at midsummer with forty people under it. The company is four hundred miles south by then, which is not far enough, and learns that in the autumn.

The tenth column cut out of the crown ledger with a knife, because a blank column ruled and waiting is an invitation. It takes eleven minutes of careful work with the pages flat. The mint's own standing order describes that particular alteration as the one act that transfers the office to whoever performs it, and the standing order is four hundred years older than the knife.

A captain sits down on the wyrm-road because the legs have finished arguing about it. The company will not leave without its captain, which is what a company is for and why the whole arrangement has worked for three books. The road has been getting longer all evening. It is in no hurry at all, and it has nine miles of itself to be patient in.

The crown gate held on a shield fulcrum while five names are called through it in order, which is precisely what a dead Warden scratched a warning about on the inside of a shield two books ago. The shield is the same shield. The fifth name is answered from the far side in the captain's own voice, with the correct inflection, about a second early.

The strongest sent up the chimney first to haul the others, which puts one set of hands ninety feet up and four sets of boots on soot-glazed brick. The third staple above the bend has been waiting since the founding for exactly this order of climbing. It is the staple the whole load hangs from, and it comes out of the brick without any warning at all.

The file stayed with to the end of the count, because it is only nine and the rhythm is easy and the gate is right there. The ninth number arrives in open road air with the switchbacks visible below and Sarnhold's smoke on the horizon. Then the count starts again from one, without any gap at all, and the file turns round on the paving and starts back down.

Kettle's report is accurate in every particular, and the company goes over Sarnhold's curtain wall after dark rather than through its gate. That is how a chartered company becomes a matter for the provost rather than for the Commandant. By morning the irons are in a fortress strongbox, the charter is impounded, and the Reckoning's coach has been given leave to depart with an escort.
